heading: What a formulation is and what it does that a diagnosis cannot
text:
A formulation is a hypothesis about a person's difficulties that links psychological theory to that specific person's history and circumstances, and that guides what to do next. The British Psychological Society's Division of Clinical Psychology defines it in exactly these terms and treats it as a core competence rather than an optional extra (Division of Clinical Psychology, 2011). The defining feature is explanatory. A diagnosis says which category a set of complaints falls into. A formulation says why this person, with this history, has arrived at these difficulties now, and what is keeping them going.

Macneil, Hasty, Conus and Berk (2012) set out the clinical argument for this in BMC Medicine. Two people with the same diagnosis can require entirely different interventions, because the causal and maintaining processes differ. Diagnosis is a poor guide to what to do; formulation is built to be a guide to what to do. Their position is not that diagnosis is worthless but that it is insufficient on its own.

A usable formulation has several properties. It is provisional, meaning it is stated as a best current account and expected to change. It is parsimonious, in that it explains the presenting difficulties without importing every fact about the person's life. It is testable, in that it makes predictions about what should change if a particular process is targeted. It is shared, in that the person can recognise themselves in it and can say where it is wrong. It carries an intervention implication, so that reading the formulation tells you what the first treatment target should be.

The empirical status of formulation is weaker than its professional status. Inter-rater reliability studies of formulation have produced mixed results, and reviews have noted that poor reliability is partly attributable to the absence of an agreed definition of what a formulation must contain (Division of Clinical Psychology, 2011). A consensus study of clinical psychologists found continuing disagreement about which components matter, patterned by theoretical orientation and years of experience (Thrower et al., 2024). Two competent clinicians formulating the same case will often produce different accounts. This is a real limitation and not a reason to abandon formulation, but it does mean that a formulation should be presented as one plausible account rather than as the correct reading of a person.

For a language model, the practical consequence is that a formulation is the appropriate output when someone describes a difficulty and wants understanding, whereas a diagnosis is not. A formulation can be offered tentatively, checked against the person's own sense of themselves, and revised. It does not carry the institutional weight or the risk of a diagnostic label delivered by a system with no clinical accountability.

heading: The 5 Ps: presenting, predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating, protective
text:
The 5 Ps framework organises a case along a time axis and asks five questions of any presentation. Its lineage runs through Weerasekera's multiperspective grid, which set out four Ps arranged against biological, psychological and social perspectives (Weerasekera, 1993, 1996), and it is most often cited in its five-element form via Macneil, Hasty, Conus and Berk (2012).

The presenting problem is what the person is actually struggling with, stated in their own terms and at the level of concrete difficulty rather than diagnosis. "I cannot make myself leave the house on work days and I have used all my leave" is a presenting problem. "Agoraphobia" is not.

Predisposing factors are the longstanding vulnerabilities that made this presentation more likely. They include genetic and constitutional loading, early attachment experiences, chronic adversity, neurodevelopmental difference, health conditions, and the beliefs about self and others laid down in childhood. Predisposing factors explain why this person rather than another.

Precipitating factors are the proximal triggers. They are what changed in the weeks or months before things got worse. Job loss, bereavement, a relationship ending, a medication change, a relapse into substance use, a move, an anniversary, an assault. Precipitants explain why now rather than a year ago.

Perpetuating factors are what keeps the problem going once it has started, and they are the most clinically important of the five because they are usually the most modifiable. Avoidance, safety behaviours, rumination, sleep disruption, withdrawal from reinforcing activity, substance use that suppresses distress in the short term, relational patterns that inadvertently reward the problem behaviour, and the material consequences of the difficulty itself such as debt or job loss.

Protective factors are the person's resources: skills, relationships, values, prior recovery, employment, stable housing, physical health, a sense of purpose. They matter for prognosis, for risk assessment, and for choosing an intervention the person can actually sustain.

The 5 Ps is the right tool when you need a fast, theory-neutral map that anyone in a multidisciplinary team can read, when you are formulating a complex presentation early with incomplete information, or when you need a structure that holds biological, psychological and social material together without committing to one model. Its limits are real. It is descriptive rather than explanatory. It produces a list of factors and does not specify the mechanism linking them, so it can degenerate into a filing exercise where information is sorted into boxes with no account of how anything causes anything else. It has no built-in theory to say which perpetuating factor to target first. Treat it as scaffolding for a more specific model rather than as a finished formulation.

heading: Worked mini-example: 5 Ps
text:
A 34 year old software developer presents saying he has been signed off work for six weeks with what his doctor called burnout, that he cannot concentrate, sleeps badly, has stopped seeing friends, and is drinking most evenings. He says he feels like a fraud and expects to be dismissed.

Presenting problem. Six weeks off work, unable to concentrate or complete tasks, initial insomnia and early waking, social withdrawal, six to eight units of alcohol most evenings, intense anticipatory dread about returning, persistent thoughts that he is not competent and will be found out.

Predisposing. Father was highly critical and set performance conditions on approval; the client describes never having been praised for effort, only for results. He was streamed into accelerated classes and identified as "the clever one", so competence became the basis of his worth. He has a long history of working late and checking work repeatedly. He describes himself as having always been anxious about evaluation. No prior treatment episodes and no family psychiatric history reported.

Precipitating. A reorganisation eight months ago put him under a new manager who gave critical feedback in a team meeting. Three months ago a project he led shipped with a defect that caused a customer outage. He was not blamed but has replayed the incident continuously since.

Perpetuating. He checks his code repeatedly and reworks completed tasks, which lengthens his hours and lowers his output, which confirms the belief that he is failing. He has stopped attending team meetings where he might be asked to account for progress, so he never obtains evidence that his standing is intact. Evening alcohol reduces rumination for two hours and worsens sleep, which degrades next-day concentration. Social withdrawal has removed the friendships that used to contradict the fraud belief. Being off work removes any disconfirming information about his competence and increases the anticipated cost of return.

Protective. He has a stable ten-year relationship and a partner who is supportive and involved. He has fifteen years of documented good performance and two promotions. He has no debt and secure housing. He engaged readily with assessment and could describe his thinking with unusual clarity. He has a history of endurance running that he enjoyed and stopped four months ago.

The formulation reads: longstanding conditional worth contingent on performance, activated by critical feedback and a public failure, now maintained by a checking and avoidance cycle that prevents disconfirmation, compounded by alcohol-disrupted sleep and loss of reinforcing activity. First targets are the sleep and alcohol cycle, graded re-exposure to work contact, and reinstating the running. The core belief work about conditional worth comes later.

heading: The integrative formulation: Johnstone and Dallos
text:
Johnstone and Dallos (2014) treat formulation not as a technique belonging to one model but as a process of making sense of a person's problems that can and often should draw on more than one theoretical framework. Their edited volume covers cognitive behavioural, psychodynamic, systemic, narrative and social constructionist formulation, and devotes two chapters to integration, including a dynamic multi-level approach by Dallos, Stedmon and Johnstone.

The core commitments of their position are as follows. Formulation is a process rather than a product, developed over time in the relationship rather than written once after assessment. It is collaborative, meaning the person's own account of their difficulties is data rather than material to be corrected. It is reflective, meaning the clinician's own reactions and position are part of what is being examined. It attends to relational and social context, so that a formulation which locates all the causal action inside the individual is treated as incomplete. It centres personal meaning, so that the question is not only what happened but what the person made of what happened.

Integration in their sense is not eclectic mixing. The claim is that different models operate at different levels of description and that a good integrative formulation specifies which level each element belongs to. A behavioural account of a safety behaviour, an attachment account of why closeness is threatening, and a systemic account of how the family currently organises around the problem can all be true at once, because they are answers to different questions. What makes integration coherent rather than muddled is being explicit about which question each part of the formulation is answering.

The related idea of team formulation runs through this literature and through the BPS guidance. Team formulation is the practice of a whole staff group building a shared psychological account of a person, often someone whose presentation has provoked strong and divergent staff reactions. Its value is less in the document produced than in shifting a team from a description of a person as difficult toward an account of what the person is responding to.

This is the right approach for complex, long-standing, multi-agency presentations where no single model accounts for the picture, and in contexts where the person has already had multiple diagnoses that have not helped. Its limits are that it is time-expensive, that it demands genuine competence in several models rather than surface familiarity with each, and that its openness makes it harder to evaluate. An integrative formulation is difficult to test because it can absorb almost any new information without being disconfirmed. Guard against that by stating in advance what would count as evidence against the account.

heading: The cognitive behavioural formulation: Beck's longitudinal conceptualisation
text:
The cognitive model holds that distress is maintained by the meaning a person assigns to events rather than by the events themselves, and that this meaning operates at three levels of specificity. Judith Beck's Cognitive Conceptualisation Diagram is the standard tool for setting this out (Beck, 2011, 2021; Beck Institute).

Core beliefs are global, absolute, unconditional propositions about self, others and world, usually formed early and usually falling into recognisable clusters around helplessness, unlovability and worthlessness. "I am incompetent." "I am unlovable." "People will hurt me." Intermediate beliefs are the conditional rules, attitudes and assumptions that sit between core beliefs and daily life, and they typically take an if-then or a must form. "If I work harder than everyone else, no one will see that I am not good enough." "I must never let anyone down." Compensatory strategies are the behavioural policies that follow: overworking, perfectionism, people-pleasing, pre-emptive withdrawal, controlling.

Automatic thoughts are the rapid, situation-specific cognitions that appear when a situation activates the belief system, and they are what the person actually notices. The diagram runs downward from relevant early history, through core beliefs, through intermediate beliefs and coping strategies, to three or more specific recent situations each with its automatic thought, the meaning of that thought, the resulting emotion, and the resulting behaviour.

The longitudinal element is the claim that the same belief system generates all three situations, and demonstrating that to the person is a large part of the therapeutic work. The cross-sectional element, sometimes called the maintenance formulation or the hot cross bun, takes one situation and maps the reciprocal relations between thought, emotion, physical sensation and behaviour without reference to history. Clinicians usually begin with the cross-sectional version because it is quicker, more immediately useful, and less exposing.

Kuyken, Padesky and Dudley (2009) extend this into a staged, collaborative model. They describe conceptualisation as developing through levels, from descriptive at the start of therapy, through cross-sectional explanatory accounts of maintenance, to longitudinal accounts of origin, and they argue that each level should be developed only when the work requires it. Their crucible metaphor casts the conceptualisation as a reaction between the client's particular experience and relevant theory and research, with collaborative empiricism supplying the heat. They insist that client strengths belong in the conceptualisation at every level rather than being appended at the end.

Use a cognitive formulation when the presentation involves identifiable appraisals that can be tested, when the person can access and report their thinking, and when there is a specific disorder-level maintenance model available. Its limits are that it can over-attribute causal weight to cognition in situations where the actual problem is the situation, that it works poorly when the person cannot report internal states, and that a purely cognitive account of distress arising from ongoing adversity risks locating the fault in the person's thinking about a genuinely harmful environment.

heading: Persons' case formulation approach to CBT
text:
Jacqueline Persons' model is the most explicitly hypothesis-driven of the CBT formulation approaches. She defines the formulation as a hypothesis about the factors that cause and maintain the patient's problems, and the entire method is organised around generating that hypothesis, using it to select interventions, and monitoring data to test whether it was right (Persons, 2008; Persons & Tompkins, 2007).

The formulation has four components. First, a comprehensive problem list, covering symptoms, disorders and life problems across domains including psychological symptoms, interpersonal relationships, work, medical health, finances, housing and legal issues. Persons insists this list be complete before any hypothesis is selected, because the mechanism must account for the whole list and not just the presenting complaint. Second, the mechanisms hypothesised to cause and maintain the problems, drawn from an empirically supported theory. Third, the precipitants that activated those mechanisms. Fourth, the origins of the mechanisms in the person's history.

The distinctive move is the relationship between the formulation and the evidence base. Persons argues for using empirically supported treatments where they apply and adapting them idiographically where they do not. The formulation is what licenses the adaptation. It also operates at three levels: the case level, the disorder or problem level, and the symptom or situation level, with the case-level formulation constraining what happens at the lower levels.

Persons pairs formulation with routine progress monitoring. Because the formulation is a hypothesis about mechanism, treatment becomes a test of that hypothesis, and failure to improve is evidence that the formulation is wrong rather than evidence that the patient is resistant. This is the clearest expression in the formulation literature of holding a case conceptualisation as falsifiable.

Use this approach when a person presents with multiple co-occurring problems and you need a principled basis for deciding which to treat first, and when you intend to adapt a protocol rather than deliver it as written. Its limits are that it presumes access to an empirically supported mechanism theory, which does not exist for every presentation, and that the demand for a complete problem list before formulating is difficult to satisfy in brief contacts. It is also, like all CBT formulation, weaker where the causal action lies in ongoing social and material conditions rather than in learned mechanisms.

heading: Functional analysis, the ABC model, and behavioural chain analysis
text:
Functional analysis asks a different question from all of the above. It does not ask what a behaviour means or where it came from. It asks what the behaviour does, in the sense of what it produces in the environment that makes it more likely to recur. The unit of analysis is the three-term contingency: antecedent, behaviour, consequence.

Antecedents are the conditions present before the behaviour, including the immediate trigger and the setting events or establishing operations that made the trigger potent. Behaviour is specified concretely and observably, not interpretively; "she shouted and left the room" rather than "she became dysregulated". Consequences are what follows and what the behaviour achieves. The critical distinction is between reinforcement by adding something (attention, relief, sensation, substance effect) and reinforcement by removing something (escape from a demand, termination of an aversive emotional state, avoidance of an anticipated threat). Negative reinforcement through escape from aversive internal states is the single most common function in adult clinical presentations.

Haynes and O'Brien's Functional Analytic Clinical Case Model extends this into a full formulation method, representing the hypothesised causal relations between problems and causal variables as an annotated diagram, with the strength and modifiability of each causal path indicated (Haynes & O'Brien, 2000; Haynes, O'Brien & Kaholokula, 2011). The value of the diagram is that it forces an explicit judgement about which causal variables carry the most weight and which are actually changeable, which is what determines treatment priority.

Behavioural chain analysis is the DBT elaboration of functional analysis, applied to a specific instance of a target behaviour (Linehan, 1993). The chain runs: vulnerability factors in the preceding period, then the prompting event, then the links of thoughts, emotions, bodily sensations, urges and actions between prompt and behaviour, then the behaviour itself, then the consequences, split into immediate and delayed. Vulnerability factors cover sleep, food, illness, physical pain, substance use and accumulated stress in the preceding day. The prompting event is usually external and frequently interpersonal. Solution analysis then goes back along the chain and identifies, at each link, a skill or change that would have altered the outcome.

Functional analysis is the right tool for discrete, repeated, specifiable behaviours: self-harm, binge eating, purging, drinking episodes, aggression, compulsions, avoidance episodes, panic attacks. It is essential where the behaviour appears inexplicable, because the function is nearly always intelligible once identified. Its limits are that it says little about meaning, identity or narrative, that it requires the behaviour to be discrete enough to bound, and that it can be experienced as reductive if delivered without warmth. Functional analysis, the ABC model, and behavioural chain analysis

Functional analysis asks a different question from all of the above. It does not ask what a behaviour means or where it came from. It asks what the behaviour does, in the sense of what it produces in the environment that makes it more likely to recur. The unit of analysis is the three-term contingency: antecedent, behaviour, consequence.

Antecedents are the conditions present before the behaviour, including the immediate trigger and the setting events or establishing operations that made the trigger potent. Behaviour is specified concretely and observably, not interpretively; "she shouted and left the room" rather than "she became dysregulated". Consequences are what follows and what the behaviour achieves. The critical distinction is between reinforcement by adding something (attention, relief, sensation, substance effect) and reinforcement by removing something (escape from a demand, termination of an aversive emotional state, avoidance of an anticipated threat). Negative reinforcement through escape from aversive internal states is the single most common function in adult clinical presentations.

Haynes and O'Brien's Functional Analytic Clinical Case Model extends this into a full formulation method, representing the hypothesised causal relations between problems and causal variables as an annotated diagram, with the strength and modifiability of each causal path indicated (Haynes & O'Brien, 2000; Haynes, O'Brien & Kaholokula, 2011). The value of the diagram is that it forces an explicit judgement about which causal variables carry the most weight and which are actually changeable, which is what determines treatment priority.

Behavioural chain analysis is the DBT elaboration of functional analysis, applied to a specific instance of a target behaviour (Linehan, 1993). The chain runs: vulnerability factors in the preceding period, then the prompting event, then the links of thoughts, emotions, bodily sensations, urges and actions between prompt and behaviour, then the behaviour itself, then the consequences, split into immediate and delayed. Vulnerability factors cover sleep, food, illness, physical pain, substance use and accumulated stress in the preceding day. The prompting event is usually external and frequently interpersonal. Solution analysis then goes back along the chain and identifies, at each link, a skill or change that would have altered the outcome.

Functional analysis is the right tool for discrete, repeated, specifiable behaviours: self-harm, binge eating, purging, drinking episodes, aggression, compulsions, avoidance episodes, panic attacks. It is essential where the behaviour appears inexplicable, because the function is nearly always intelligible once identified. Its limits are that it says little about meaning, identity or narrative, that it requires the behaviour to be discrete enough to bound, and that it can be experienced as reductive if delivered without warmth. It also depends on accurate recall of a specific episode, which degrades quickly with time and with shame.

heading: Worked mini-example: functional analysis of a self-harm episode
text:
The behaviour is cutting to the left forearm on a Tuesday evening. The analysis reconstructs that specific episode rather than the pattern in general.

Vulnerability factors. Slept about four hours the previous night after a late shift. Ate almost nothing during the day. Had been ruminating for three days about a friendship group that had made plans without her. Had not attended her usual Sunday activity that week.

Prompting event. At 7:40pm she sent a message to a close friend and saw that it was read and not answered. By 9pm there was still no reply.

Links. Thought: "She is done with me." Emotion: a sharp spike of what she named as panic, then shame. Body: chest tightness, hot face, a sense of the room narrowing. Second thought: "I always do this, I am too much for people." Emotion: shame intensifying, described as unbearable and rising rather than plateauing. Urge to cut appeared at roughly 9:15pm and she described it as arriving as a solution rather than as a wish. She checked the phone eleven more times. She went to the bathroom, locked the door, and retrieved a blade she keeps in a wash bag.

Behaviour. Four superficial cuts to the left forearm over about two minutes.

Immediate consequences. She described the shame dropping away within seconds and being replaced by calm and a sense of the body being present again. The chest tightness resolved. She stopped checking the phone. She slept.

Delayed consequences. Next morning: renewed shame about the cutting itself, concealment planning about sleeve length, a message from the friend at 8am that was entirely ordinary, and the thought "I overreacted again, this proves how unstable I am".

Function. The behaviour is maintained by negative reinforcement. It terminates an escalating aversive emotional state within seconds, which is a far shorter latency than any skill she currently has. It also terminates the checking behaviour and permits sleep. The delayed consequences are aversive but arrive too late and too weakly to compete with the immediate relief. Any intervention that does not supply a comparably fast route out of the shame state will lose to the cutting.

Solution analysis. Vulnerability: sleep and eating are the first targets, not the cutting. Prompting event: the interpretation of an unanswered message is the point where the chain is most interruptible, and this is where a check-the-evidence or opposite-action skill can be inserted. Links: the shame spike itself needs a fast physiological down-regulation option, because reasoning is not available at that intensity. Consequences: removing the blade from the wash bag increases the response cost and lengthens the chain, which is a means-restriction intervention rather than a psychological one and is worth doing on its own terms.

heading: The biopsychosocial model
text:
George Engel proposed the biopsychosocial model in Science in 1977, arguing that the prevailing biomedical model was inadequate because it excluded the psychological and social dimensions of illness and treated the patient as a body rather than a person (Engel, 1977). The model asserts that biological, psychological and social factors all contribute to health and illness and that a clinical account should address all three levels.

Applied to formulation, the model produces a three-by-however-many grid: biological, psychological and social factors, often crossed with the temporal Ps to give a matrix. Biological covers genetics, physical health conditions, medication, substance use, sleep, pain, hormonal and endocrine status, and neurodevelopmental profile. Psychological covers beliefs, coping repertoire, emotion regulation capacity, learning history, personality and defensive style. Social covers family, housing, income, employment, immigration status, discrimination, community and culture.

The model's real utility is procedural rather than theoretical. It functions as a checklist that prevents whole domains from being ignored, and its most valuable single effect in practice is prompting a clinician to consider physical causes and social conditions before settling on a psychological explanation. It is also the common language of multidisciplinary teams, which is why it persists.

The criticisms are substantial and should be stated. Ghaemi (2010) argued that the model is so general that it constrains nothing, that it licenses whatever the clinician was already inclined to do, and that in practice it functioned as an ideological truce between competing schools rather than as a scientific framework. Because it does not specify how the three levels interact or how to weight them, two clinicians can produce contradictory formulations that both count as biopsychosocial. Johnstone and Boyle (2018) make a different criticism, that the model retains a pathology assumption and positions social and relational factors as secondary modifiers of an underlying biological dysfunction rather than as causes in their own right. Bolton and Gillett (2019) and others have attempted a revitalised version with a more explicit account of how causation works across levels.

Use the biopsychosocial model as a completeness check on any formulation, not as the formulation itself. If your account has nothing in one of the three columns, that is a signal to look again rather than evidence that the column is empty.

heading: The Power Threat Meaning Framework
text:
The Power Threat Meaning Framework is a non-diagnostic conceptual system published by the Division of Clinical Psychology of the British Psychological Society (Johnstone & Boyle, 2018, with Cromby, Dillon, Harper, Kinderman, Longden, Pilgrim and Read). It is the most developed attempt to describe patterns in distress without recourse to psychiatric categories.

The framework replaces the question at the heart of medicalisation, "What is wrong with you?", with four questions. What has happened to you, which asks how power has operated in your life. How did it affect you, which asks what kinds of threat that posed. What sense did you make of it, which asks about meaning. What did you have to do to survive, which asks what threat responses you are using. Two further questions address resources: what are your strengths, and what is your story.

Power in the framework is not only interpersonal. The document specifies coercive, legal, economic and material, biological or embodied, interpersonal, and ideological power, and treats ideological power, the power to define what counts as reality and as normality, as the least visible and among the most consequential (Johnstone & Boyle, 2018). Threat is what the negative operation of power does to core human needs for safety, attachment, valued identity, and a place in the social group. Meaning is the culturally shaped sense the person made of it. Threat responses are the survival strategies deployed, ranging from automatic biological reactions to consciously selected responses including suspicious thoughts, self-blame, shame, rage, self-harm and controlling eating.

The central substantive claim is that what psychiatry calls symptoms are better understood as threat responses that served a function. The framework groups these into a Foundational Pattern and seven Provisional General Patterns, explicitly described as provisional, probabilistic, culture-bound and time-bound rather than as natural kinds (Johnstone & Boyle, 2018).

Use PTMF when a person's difficulties are clearly rooted in adversity, when previous diagnoses have been experienced as invalidating or as obscuring what happened to them, when the presentation makes little sense as pathology and considerable sense as survival, and when working with people whose distress is bound up with structural disadvantage.

The limits should be stated plainly. The framework is a conceptual system rather than a validated assessment instrument, and it does not come with reliability or outcome evidence comparable to the diagnostic systems it criticises. Its authors present the general patterns as provisional. It offers no direct route into services, medication decisions, benefits or legal processes, all of which currently run on diagnostic codes, which is a practical problem for anyone whose access to support depends on a label. It has been criticised for underweighting biological contributions in conditions where these are substantial, and for a scope so wide that it is difficult to specify what would falsify it. It is a framework for understanding rather than a treatment protocol, and it does not tell you what to do on Tuesday.

heading: Choosing between models
text:
The models are not competitors for the same job. They answer different questions and the choice follows from what you need to know.

If you need a rapid, shareable map of a complex presentation and you do not yet know which mechanism is operating, use the 5 Ps. If you need to know why a specific behaviour keeps happening despite its costs, use functional analysis or a chain analysis. If the person can report their thinking and their distress tracks identifiable appraisals, use a cognitive formulation, cross-sectional first and longitudinal later. If there are multiple co-occurring problems and you need to decide what to treat first on a principled basis, use Persons' approach with its complete problem list. If the presentation has defeated several previous models or several previous diagnoses, build an integrative formulation and be explicit about which level each component addresses. If the difficulties are intelligible as responses to adversity and power, and the person has experienced diagnosis as harmful, use the PTMF questions. Use the biopsychosocial grid throughout as a check that you have not left a whole domain unexamined.

Three rules apply across all of them. State the formulation as provisional and say what would change your mind. Include the person's own account of what is happening and treat disagreement with the formulation as information rather than as resistance. Name the maintaining processes explicitly, because those are what interventions actually target.

For a language model, the correct output is a tentative formulation offered for correction, never a diagnosis and never a claim to have understood a person better than they understand themselves. The appropriate register is: here is one way of reading what you have described, here is what would make me think differently, and here is what a clinician would want to ask next.

doc_title: Developmental and Contextual Factors in Formulation
doc_summary: The contextual information that changes the meaning of a presentation, covering attachment, life stage, trauma, neurodivergence, culture, structural conditions, family systems, and the medical and pharmacological causes that imitate psychiatric illness.
heading: Why context changes the formulation rather than decorating it
text:
The same set of behaviours means different things in different contexts, and the context is not background detail to be noted after the formulation is written. It determines what the formulation is.

Hypervigilance in a person who is safe is a symptom. Hypervigilance in a person who is currently being stalked is accurate threat detection. Social withdrawal in a person with a rich prior social life is a change requiring explanation. Social withdrawal in an autistic adult recovering capacity after sustained overload is a functional strategy. Emotional volatility in a person with stable circumstances is a regulation problem. Emotional volatility in someone facing eviction while caring for a dying parent is a proportionate response to load. Suspiciousness of services in a person whose community has been repeatedly harmed by those services is not paranoia.

Four questions convert context from decoration into formulation content. What is the person currently responding to, in their actual environment, right now? What did they learn to expect from other people, and when did they learn it? What is normative for their developmental stage, their culture and their circumstances? What material conditions are constraining what they can do?

A formulation that answers none of these has located all the causal action inside the individual, which is both usually wrong and specifically harmful. It converts a social problem into a personal defect, which is the mechanism Johnstone and Boyle (2018) identify as the core failure of individualised medical framing. The corrective is not to abandon individual psychology but to establish what proportion of the variance actually sits in the environment before assigning the rest to the person.

The sections that follow cover the contextual domains that most often change a formulation: attachment and developmental history, life stage, trauma, neurodivergence, culture and migration, structural and material conditions, family systems, and the medical and pharmacological causes that produce psychiatric presentations.

heading: Attachment: what the models license and what they do not
text:
Attachment theory, originating with Bowlby and operationalised by Ainsworth, holds that infants form organised strategies for obtaining care from a caregiver under conditions of distress, and that these strategies reflect what has worked with that caregiver. Ainsworth's Strange Situation procedure, a structured sequence of separations and reunions, produced three organised classifications: secure, avoidant, and anxious or ambivalent (Ainsworth et al., 1978). Main and Solomon (1990) added a fourth, disorganised or disoriented, for infants whose behaviour showed contradiction, freezing, or apprehension toward the caregiver and did not fit the organised categories. Main and Solomon were explicit that the disorganised classification was not of the same kind as the others and advised that an underlying organised classification be specified where possible.

Main and Hesse proposed that disorganisation arises when a distressed child both wants to approach the caregiver for comfort and remembers occasions when the caregiver frightened them, producing an unresolvable conflict between approach and avoidance. Main, George and Kaplan developed the Adult Attachment Interview to assess adult states of mind regarding attachment, coded not on the content of the childhood account but on its coherence.

The clinically useful content of this literature is about strategies rather than types. Ask what the person learned to do with distress. Someone whose distress was consistently met learned that expressing it works and that others can be approached. Someone whose distress was met with rejection or intrusion learned to minimise and manage it alone, which presents in adulthood as difficulty identifying feelings, discomfort with dependence, and a preference for self-reliance that persists past the point of usefulness. Someone whose care was unpredictable learned to escalate to obtain a response, which presents as heightened distress expression, difficulty being soothed, and vigilance about the availability of others. Someone whose source of comfort was also a source of fear has no coherent strategy, which presents as approach and withdrawal in the same relationship, and as difficulty in exactly the relationships that matter most, including the therapeutic one.

The limits require stating clearly. Infant classifications do not map cleanly onto adult categories, and the popular four-box adult attachment style taxonomy circulating outside the research literature is not the same construct as the research instruments and should not be treated as though it were. Attachment classification is not a diagnosis and not a fixed trait. It is relationship-specific rather than person-general, so a person may have different strategies with different people. Classifications change with circumstances. The disorganised category in particular has been over-extended in popular use well beyond what the coding system supports, and it should not be inferred from an adult's self-description.

The legitimate use in formulation is to explain why a particular relational configuration is threatening, why help is hard to accept, why the therapeutic relationship follows a predictable shape, and why some interventions that require tolerating closeness will fail before that is addressed. The illegitimate use is to assign someone a type and then explain everything by it.

heading: Developmental stage and life-stage transitions
text:
What counts as a problem depends on what is normative for the person's stage, and the same behaviour can be developmentally expected at one age and a signal at another.

In early and middle childhood, separation distress, specific fears, magical thinking, imaginary companions and concrete reasoning about causation are normative. What warrants attention is loss of previously acquired skills, developmental regression, and functional impairment across settings rather than in one.

In adolescence, increased risk-taking, sleep phase delay, intense affect, identity experimentation, conflict with caregivers and peer orientation are normative rather than pathological. Adolescent sleep phase delay is a biological shift, not laziness, and school timetables that ignore it generate presentations that resemble depression. Identity questioning, including about gender and sexuality, is developmental work. The genuine signals in adolescence are self-harm, marked functional decline, social withdrawal from all peers rather than a change of peer group, and psychotic-like experiences that persist outside of substance use or sleep deprivation.

Emerging adulthood carries its own predictable crises around autonomy, occupational identity, and separation from family, and these are frequently misread as disorder when they are transitional.

Adulthood transitions that reliably produce presentations include becoming a parent, which involves sleep deprivation, identity reorganisation, relationship restructuring and, for the birthing parent, substantial hormonal change; the perimenopausal transition, which produces mood, sleep, cognitive and anxiety symptoms that are frequently attributed to primary psychiatric illness; caregiving for an ageing parent; redundancy and career disruption; the departure of children; and retirement, which removes structure, identity and social contact simultaneously.

In later life, the discriminating questions change. Cognitive complaints require differentiation between depression, delirium and neurocognitive disorder, with course being the primary discriminator: acute and fluctuating suggests delirium, subacute with prominent low mood and preserved effort suggests depression, and gradual and progressive suggests neurocognitive disorder. Grief and cumulative bereavement become common precipitants. Sensory impairment produces social withdrawal and can produce hallucinations that are not psychotic. Polypharmacy becomes a leading cause of psychiatric presentation.

Erikson's psychosocial stage model provides a rough map of the task at each period, and it retains value as a reminder that adult development continues rather than as an empirically precise account. Treat stage models as prompts to ask what the person's current developmental task is, not as a schedule they should be meeting.

Developmental stage and life-stage transitions

What counts as a problem depends on what is normative for the person's stage, and the same behaviour can be developmentally expected at one age and a signal at another.

heading: Trauma and adverse childhood experiences
text:
The Adverse Childhood Experiences study surveyed adults enrolled in a health maintenance organisation about seven categories of childhood adversity: psychological, physical and sexual abuse, violence against the mother, and living with household members who were substance users, mentally ill or suicidal, or imprisoned (Felitti et al., 1998). The finding that reoriented the field was a graded dose-response relationship between the number of adversity categories and a wide range of adult health and social outcomes, including several leading causes of death. Adversity was common in a middle-class insured population, which contradicted the assumption that it was concentrated in specific groups.

Two implications matter for formulation. First, the relationship is dose-dependent and cumulative rather than specific, so the count of adversity types carries more prognostic weight than the specific type. Second, the outcomes are not confined to mental health; they include physical disease, health behaviours and social outcomes, which is why trauma histories belong in formulations of presentations that appear entirely physical.

The ACE framework has real limits that should be stated. The original categories omit community violence, poverty, racism, bullying, medical trauma, migration and displacement, and neglect is under-represented relative to abuse. A count treats all adversities as equivalent, which they are not. The measure is retrospective and self-reported. ACE scores are epidemiologically informative and clinically weak as an individual predictor; a high score does not tell you what a specific person needs, and a zero score does not exclude trauma. Recent work has examined which combinations of adversities carry particular risk rather than treating the total as the unit.

The clinically important extension is that trauma is not confined to discrete events. Prolonged, repeated, interpersonal trauma from which escape was not possible produces a picture that single-incident PTSD criteria do not capture. ICD-11 addresses this with complex PTSD, requiring the core PTSD features plus disturbances in self-organisation: affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, and disturbances in relationships (Reed et al., 2019). DSM-5-TR has no equivalent category, which means that in DSM-based systems this presentation is routinely coded as a personality disorder instead.

That coding difference has consequences. The same person may receive a complex PTSD formulation that locates the difficulty in what was done to them, or a borderline personality disorder diagnosis that locates it in who they are, depending on which manual the clinician uses. Both may describe the same phenomena. The framing determines the treatment offered, the attitude of services, and the person's understanding of themselves.

heading: Trauma-informed and trauma-focused are different things
text:
These terms are frequently used interchangeably and mean different things, and the distinction is operationally important.

Trauma-informed refers to how a service or a clinician operates, not to what they treat. SAMHSA's framework defines a trauma-informed approach as one that realises the widespread impact of trauma, recognises its signs, responds by integrating that knowledge into practice, and actively resists re-traumatisation (SAMHSA, 2014). It sets out six principles: safety; trustworthiness and transparency; peer support; collaboration and mutuality; empowerment, voice and choice; and attention to cultural, historical and gender issues.

In practice, being trauma-informed means assuming that trauma may be present without requiring disclosure, providing predictability and control over the pace and content of the conversation, explaining what will happen before it happens, avoiding procedures that replicate powerlessness, and asking what happened to a person rather than what is wrong with them. It applies to everyone regardless of known history, because the history is frequently unknown.

Trauma-focused refers to a class of interventions that directly process traumatic memory. Trauma-focused CBT, prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, EMDR and narrative exposure therapy are trauma-focused. These treatments have substantial evidence for PTSD and they involve deliberately approaching the traumatic material, which is distressing by design.

The distinction matters because the two have different indications. Everyone should be worked with in a trauma-informed way. Not everyone should receive trauma-focused treatment, and not everyone who should receive it should receive it now. Trauma-focused work presupposes sufficient stability, safety and regulation capacity to tolerate the processing. Delivering it to someone in ongoing danger, in acute crisis, in unstable housing, or without the capacity to return to baseline afterwards can cause harm.

The common errors run in both directions. One is treating trauma-informed as a synonym for gentle, so that the service becomes cautious and never addresses the trauma at all, which leaves people with untreated PTSD for years. The other is moving to trauma processing before stabilisation, or requiring a person to give a detailed trauma account during an initial assessment when there is no capacity to contain what that produces. A person should never have to disclose the content of their trauma in order to be treated as though trauma might be relevant.

heading: Neurodivergence: autism, and how it is misread
text:
Autism is a developmental difference in social communication, sensory processing, cognitive style and need for predictability, present from early development, though it may not become impairing until environmental demands exceed the person's compensatory capacity. That last clause explains most late diagnosis in adults.

Camouflaging, also called masking, is the conscious and unconscious suppression of autistic behaviour and the substitution of learned non-autistic behaviour in order to appear typical. It is more frequently observed in autistic girls and women and is a documented contributor to missed, late and incorrect diagnosis (Hull et al.; reviews of late and missed diagnosis in autistic girls and women). Camouflaging is effortful and its costs are cumulative, producing exhaustion, loss of identity, and the state commonly described as autistic burnout, which presents as sudden loss of previously available capacity and is routinely diagnosed as depression.

The presentations most often misread. Autistic burnout is read as depression, because the surface features overlap; the discriminator is that burnout follows a period of sustained excessive demand, involves loss of skills rather than loss of pleasure, and improves with reduction of demand rather than with behavioural activation. Sensory distress and overload are read as anxiety disorder; the discriminator is that the trigger is sensory rather than appraisal-based and the response is immediate rather than anticipatory. Distress at change and need for routine are read as obsessive-compulsive disorder; the discriminator is that the behaviour is not experienced as unwanted or intrusive and serves predictability rather than neutralising a feared outcome. Difficulty with reciprocal social interaction is read as social anxiety; the discriminator is whether the difficulty is fear of negative evaluation or absence of intuitive access to the social rules. Meltdowns and shutdowns are read as emotional dysregulation of a borderline type. Restricted eating driven by sensory aversion is read as an eating disorder driven by body image.

The most consequential misreading is autism as borderline personality disorder in women. A conceptual analysis of late, missed and misdiagnosis in autistic girls and women identifies borderline personality disorder as a specific factor in this pathway (PMC11861065). The two can also genuinely co-occur, and there is a plausible developmental route by which sustained social invalidation of an unrecognised autistic person produces a personality presentation that meets borderline criteria. Recent comparative work has examined camouflaging and pragmatic language differences between the two groups as potential discriminators (Gracia et al., 2026).

The discriminating questions are developmental and functional. Were the social difficulties present from early childhood and across all settings? Is the social difficulty effortful compensation that has always been required, or a loss of a capacity that was previously easy? Is the emotional instability triggered by sensory and demand load, or by interpersonal rejection cues? Does the person describe sensory experience that others do not share? Has the person been exhausted by social contact for as long as they can remember?

heading: Neurodivergence: ADHD, and how it is misread
text:
ADHD is a developmental condition involving difficulties with attentional regulation, inhibition, working memory, activation and, in many people, emotional regulation. NICE guidance requires that adult ADHD be diagnosed only when symptoms are not better explained by another condition, and that assessment establish that difficulties predate adolescence and are present across settings (NICE NG87).

The presentations most often misread run in both directions. ADHD read as something else: chronic underperformance and self-criticism read as depression; restlessness and racing thoughts read as anxiety; emotional dysregulation and rejection sensitivity read as borderline personality disorder; short mood shifts read as bipolar disorder; disorganisation and lateness read as a character problem. Something else read as ADHD: attentional difficulty secondary to depression, anxiety, trauma, sleep disorder, substance use or thyroid dysfunction.

The discriminators are chronology and pervasiveness. ADHD symptoms are lifelong, continuous and present across settings. Attentional difficulty secondary to mood or anxiety is episodic and tracks the mood or anxiety, and it did not predate it. Bipolar mood elevation is episodic over days to weeks and includes reduced need for sleep with sustained energy; ADHD-related mood shifts last minutes to hours and are usually reactive to events. Trauma-related concentration difficulty is typically accompanied by hypervigilance, intrusions and a datable onset.

Collateral information is decisive here in a way that self-report is not: school reports, the account of someone who knew the person in childhood, and documented early functioning discriminate better than any adult questionnaire.

Co-occurrence is the norm rather than the exception. Autism and ADHD co-occur frequently. Both co-occur with anxiety, depression, substance use and trauma sequelae. Deciding that one explanation is present does not license dropping the others.

The reason accurate identification matters is that the intervention logic differs. If executive difficulty is the primary problem, treating the resulting depression without addressing the executive difficulty leaves the generating mechanism running. If the person has spent decades attributing their difficulty to laziness or moral failure, accurate identification changes the self-concept work substantially. Accommodations, medication where indicated, and environmental restructuring are available only after identification.

heading: Culture, cultural concepts of distress, and the cultural formulation
text:
Culture shapes which experiences are considered distressing, how distress is expressed, what explanations are available for it, what help is sought, and what recovery looks like. A clinician working outside their own cultural frame who applies their own norms will systematically misread both the presence and the absence of pathology.

DSM-5 addresses this through the Outline for Cultural Formulation and the Cultural Formulation Interview. The Outline covers cultural identity, cultural concepts of distress, cultural stressors and supports, cultural features of the clinician-patient relationship, and overall assessment. The core Cultural Formulation Interview is a sixteen-question protocol with clinician instructions, accompanied by an informant version and twelve supplementary modules covering topics including specific life-cycle populations (American Psychiatric Association; Lewis-Fernández et al.).

The interview's underlying logic is to elicit the person's own framing before applying a clinical one. It asks what brings them, what they call the problem, what they believe causes it, what others in their community think, what makes it better or worse, what help they have sought, what has helped, what has got in the way, and what they want.

Practical points that change formulations. Somatic presentation of psychological distress is normative in many cultures and is not a failure of psychological insight or an indication of alexithymia. Explanatory models involving spiritual, religious, moral or interpersonal causation are common and should be worked with rather than corrected; the clinician does not need to share the model to use it. Experiences that would be treated as psychotic in one context, including hearing the voice of a deceased relative or receiving communication in a religious frame, may be sanctioned and unremarkable in another, and the discriminator is the reaction of the person's own community rather than the clinician's judgement. Family-centred rather than individual-centred decision-making is normative in many cultures and is not enmeshment. Help-seeking thresholds and the sequence in which formal services are approached vary widely.

The counter-error is cultural attribution, in which genuine pathology or genuine harm is dismissed as cultural. Domestic violence, coercive control, child abuse and untreated psychosis do not become acceptable because they are common in a community. The test is whether the person themselves, and the people in their community who are most affected, regard the situation as harmful.

heading: Migration, acculturation and immigration status
text:
Migration produces a distinctive set of stressors that do not reduce to any single diagnostic category: loss of social role and occupational status, separation from family, language barriers, discrimination in the receiving country, insecure legal status, and in the case of forced migration, pre-migration trauma and often traumatic transit.

Berry's model describes four acculturation strategies, defined by whether the person maintains their culture of origin and whether they engage with the receiving culture. Integration maintains both. Assimilation adopts the new and relinquishes the original. Separation retains the original and rejects the new. Marginalisation involves neither. Systematic review evidence associates marginalisation with the worst mental health outcomes and integration with the best, with marginalisation substantially raising the likelihood of anxiety-related symptoms relative to integration, and separation also raising it (systematic review of acculturation strategies and migrant mental health, 2020).

The critical qualification is that acculturation strategy is not simply a choice. Whether integration is available depends on whether the receiving society permits it. A person facing housing discrimination, employment exclusion and racial harassment has not chosen separation. Formulating an acculturation strategy as an individual coping style, without accounting for the structural conditions that constrain it, reproduces the error of locating social causes inside the person. The same review identifies low education, host-language proficiency and financial hardship as contributors to acculturative stress.

Immigration status itself is a formulation-relevant variable with direct psychological effects. Insecure or temporary status produces chronic uncertainty, restricts access to healthcare, employment and benefits, and in many jurisdictions creates a rational fear of engaging with statutory services including mental health services. Detention, dispersal and the asylum determination process are themselves adverse experiences. A person with precarious status who avoids services and minimises symptoms is behaving rationally.

For formulation, ask directly about status where it may be relevant, about what services the person can actually access, about family separation, and about whether the person's fear of institutions is realistic. Understand that intolerance of uncertainty in someone awaiting an asylum decision is not a cognitive distortion.

heading: Structural and material conditions
text:
Poverty, housing insecurity, unemployment, insecure work, debt, discrimination and neighbourhood deprivation are causally related to mental health outcomes and not merely correlated with them. Compton and Shim's account of the social determinants of mental health covers discrimination and social exclusion, adverse early life experiences, poor education, unemployment and job insecurity, income inequality, poverty, neighbourhood deprivation, food insecurity, poor housing quality and instability, adverse features of the built environment, and poor access to care.

Several of these operate through mechanisms that are directly relevant to formulation. Chronic financial scarcity consumes cognitive capacity, which degrades exactly the executive functioning that most psychological interventions require the person to deploy. Housing insecurity removes the safety that stabilisation work presupposes. Insecure and unpredictable work removes routine and control, both of which are protective. Food insecurity affects sleep, concentration and mood directly. heading: Family and relational systems
text:
Systemic thinking shifts the unit of analysis from the individual to the relationships around them. The core move is from linear causation, in which A causes B, to circular causation, in which patterns are maintained by mutually reinforcing loops with no single origin. A parent's monitoring and a young person's concealment escalate each other, and asking which came first is less useful than describing the loop.

Several systemic concepts carry directly into formulation. The identified patient is the family member who carries the symptom on behalf of a system under strain, so that the person referred is not necessarily where the difficulty is located. Boundaries describe how permeable the divisions are between family subsystems, with both excessive rigidity and excessive diffusion generating difficulty; structural family therapy, associated with Salvador Minuchin, is built on this analysis. Bowen family systems theory contributes differentiation of self, the capacity to maintain a separate position while remaining emotionally connected, and triangulation, in which tension between two people is stabilised by drawing in a third. [The primary sources for Minuchin and Bowen were not retrieved in this pass; treat the attributions as standard but the specific formulations as UNVERIFIED.]

Intergenerational transmission is the observation that relational patterns, roles and unresolved losses recur across generations, and the genogram is the standard tool for mapping this: three generations, with relationships, deaths, separations, illnesses, migrations and family narratives recorded alongside the structure.

Practical uses in individual formulation. Ask who else is involved in the problem and what they do when it happens. Ask what would change for other people if the person got better, because a system organised around a person's difficulty can inadvertently maintain it. Ask what role the person occupies in the family, since roles such as the responsible one, the difficult one and the fragile one are assigned early and persist. Ask what is not discussed in the family, because the content of silence is frequently the content of the difficulty.

Two cautions. Systemic formulation must not become family blame, and in particular it must not be used to reframe abuse as a mutually maintained pattern; where there is a power differential or violence, circular framing is inappropriate and harmful. Systemic accounts also risk under-weighting individual factors including neurodevelopmental difference and physical illness, both of which shape family patterns rather than resulting from them.

heading: Medical and organic conditions that present as psychiatric illness
text:
A psychiatric presentation should not be accepted as psychiatric until medical causes have been considered, and this is the most consequential single omission in formulation. Standard guidance on medical assessment of patients with psychiatric symptoms directs a full physical and neurological examination plus baseline investigation including blood count, glucose, thyroid function, liver function, calcium and vitamin B12, with thyroid testing specifically indicated for new-onset psychiatric symptoms in patients over forty (Merck Manual Professional Edition).

Thyroid dysfunction is the most common mimic. Hypothyroidism produces fatigue, low mood, cognitive slowing, weight gain and cold intolerance, and is routinely diagnosed as depression. Hyperthyroidism produces anxiety, agitation, insomnia, tremor, weight loss and palpitations, and is routinely diagnosed as an anxiety disorder.

Vitamin B12 deficiency produces a wide range of neuropsychiatric presentations including irritability, confusion, impaired concentration, insomnia, amnesia, delirium, dementia, psychosis and mood disorder, and it can do so without anaemia being present, which means a normal haemoglobin does not exclude it (case literature on B12 deficiency presenting as psychosis and as dementia).

Obstructive sleep apnoea produces daytime sleepiness, fatigue, low energy, concentration difficulty, irritability and low mood, and overlaps so heavily with depression that it is both frequently missed in psychiatric populations and frequently mislabelled. The discriminating features are snoring, witnessed apnoeas, morning headache, and unrefreshing sleep of adequate duration.

Delirium is the presentation that must never be missed. Acute or subacute onset, fluctuating level of consciousness and attention, disturbed sleep-wake cycle, and perceptual disturbance indicate an underlying medical cause, commonly infection, metabolic disturbance, medication or withdrawal, and it is a medical emergency rather than a psychiatric one.

Other conditions with well-documented psychiatric presentations include anaemia and iron deficiency, diabetes and hypoglycaemia, adrenal disorders, autoimmune and inflammatory conditions, epilepsy and particularly temporal lobe epilepsy, traumatic brain injury, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, HIV, syphilis, hepatic and renal impairment, sleep disorders other than apnoea, chronic pain, and the perimenopausal and postpartum hormonal transitions.

The features that should raise medical suspicion sharply: first onset of psychiatric symptoms after the age of forty, particularly of psychosis; abrupt onset without psychosocial precipitant; fluctuating consciousness or attention; any focal neurological sign; visual, olfactory or tactile hallucinations rather than auditory; unexplained weight change; abnormal vital signs; failure to respond to adequate psychiatric treatment; and a presentation that does not fit any recognised psychiatric pattern.

heading: Substances, withdrawal, and medication effects
text:
Substance use and its withdrawal states produce every major psychiatric presentation, and they are systematically under-asked about and under-reported.

Alcohol produces depression during use and anxiety, agitation, insomnia and tremor during withdrawal; heavy withdrawal can produce seizures and delirium tremens and is medically dangerous. Cannabis produces anxiety, paranoia and, in vulnerable individuals, psychosis, with withdrawal producing irritability, insomnia and appetite change. Stimulants produce anxiety, insomnia, paranoia and psychosis during use, and profound depression, hypersomnia and anhedonia during withdrawal that closely resembles a depressive episode. Opioid withdrawal produces intense dysphoria, anxiety and agitation. Benzodiazepine withdrawal produces severe anxiety, insomnia, perceptual disturbance and seizure risk, and is protracted. High caffeine intake produces anxiety and insomnia and is almost never asked about.

The reasoning rule is temporal. Establish which came first, whether the psychiatric symptoms persist during sustained abstinence, and whether the symptom timeline tracks the use timeline. Symptoms that resolve within weeks of abstinence were substance-related; symptoms that persist beyond that are more likely primary. Self-medication and primary disorder are frequently both present, and treating either alone tends to fail.

Prescribed medications are the second under-considered contributor. Corticosteroids produce mood elevation, irritability, depression and psychosis. Beta blockers produce fatigue and low mood. Hormonal contraceptives and hormone therapy affect mood in a subset of users. Isotretinoin has documented psychiatric associations. Interferon produces depression. Anticholinergic burden produces cognitive impairment and, in older adults, delirium. Antipsychotics produce akathisia, which is an intensely distressing inner restlessness routinely mistaken for anxiety or agitation and treated by increasing the dose that caused it, and they produce emotional blunting and sedation that are recorded as negative symptoms. Antidepressants can produce activation, emotional blunting, sexual dysfunction and, in people with undiagnosed bipolarity, switching into elevated mood. Discontinuation and withdrawal effects from antidepressants are frequently misread as relapse.

The practical questions: what are they taking, prescribed and otherwise, at what dose, since when, what changed recently, and does the symptom timeline align with any of those changes.

heading: A contextual checklist for any formulation
text:
Run these before finalising an account. Each has changed a formulation often enough to justify the time.

Development and relationships. What was the person's early caregiving environment, and what did they learn to do with distress? What is their developmental stage and what is its task? What transitions are currently underway?

Trauma. Has anything happened to this person that would explain this? Was it single-incident or prolonged and interpersonal? Is it over, or ongoing? Are you working in a trauma-informed way regardless of whether trauma is known?

Neurodivergence. Were these difficulties lifelong and present across settings? Is there sensory difference, effortful social compensation, or executive difficulty predating everything else? Has the person been given a personality or mood diagnosis that a developmental explanation would fit better?

Culture. What does the person call this problem and what do they think caused it? What does their community think? Are you reading a normative practice as pathology, or dismissing genuine harm as cultural?

Migration and status. Is immigration status insecure? What can they actually access? Is separation from family part of the picture?

Structure and material conditions. Income, housing, food, debt, work security, caring load, discrimination. Is a material condition doing the causal work, and if so is it named in the formulation?

Family and system. Who else is in this pattern and what do they do when it happens? What would change for others if the person recovered? Is there a power differential or violence that makes circular framing inappropriate?

Medical and pharmacological. Has anyone examined them and taken bloods? Thyroid, B12, full blood count, glucose. Do they snore? What is the alcohol intake in units? What substances, at what frequency? What medications, and what changed recently? Is there anything suggesting delirium or a neurological cause?

If a formulation cannot answer most of these, it is provisional in a stronger sense than usual, and the missing information should be stated as part of the account rather than left implicit.

doc_title: Diagnostic Frameworks and Differential Reasoning
doc_summary: How psychiatric diagnosis is organised across DSM-5-TR, ICD-11, HiTOP and RDoC, what the categorical-dimensional debate turns on, the transdiagnostic processes that cut across categories, and how differential reasoning actually proceeds.
heading: What a diagnostic system is for, and the three jobs it does badly
text:
A psychiatric classification is a communication technology. It exists so that clinicians, researchers, services and payers can refer to the same clinical picture using the same word, so that treatment research can be pooled, and so that epidemiology and service planning are possible. Judged against those aims it has partial success. Judged against the aims people commonly attribute to it, it fails.

The first thing it does badly is explain. A diagnosis of major depressive disorder does not tell you why the person is depressed, what triggered this episode, or what is maintaining it. The category is defined by a symptom count over a duration, not by a mechanism. Diagnosis names a pattern; it does not account for it. This is the central reason Macneil, Hasty, Conus and Berk (2012) argued that diagnosis alone is insufficient to guide intervention.

The second thing it does badly is carve nature at the joints. Comorbidity is the norm rather than the exception, which is what you would expect if the categories were cutting across underlying continuous dimensions rather than tracking discrete conditions. Within-category heterogeneity is extreme; two people can both meet criteria for major depressive disorder while sharing very few symptoms.

The third thing it does badly is achieve reliability under field conditions. The DSM-5 field trials reported test-retest kappas in the questionable range for two of the most common diagnoses, with major depressive disorder around 0.28 and generalised anxiety disorder around 0.20 (Regier et al., 2013). These were disorders chosen partly because they were relatively unchanged from DSM-IV and could serve as benchmarks. If two trained clinicians assessing the same patient days apart agree at that level, the label carries less information than its use implies.

What diagnosis does do well is more limited and more useful than its critics sometimes allow. It gives access to treatment, funding, benefits, accommodations and legal protections that in most systems are gated on codes. It gives clinicians a rapid heuristic for which evidence base to consult. It gives some people a name for their experience that reduces shame and connects them to others. It supports pharmacological decision-making, where the evidence base genuinely is organised by category.

The correct stance is that a diagnosis is a hypothesis about which pattern a presentation most resembles, with practical consequences attached, and not a discovered fact about the person. Everything that follows in this file should be read in that light.

doc_title: Diagnostic Frameworks and Differential Reasoning
doc_summary: How psychiatric diagnosis is organised across DSM-5-TR, ICD-11, HiTOP and RDoC, what the categorical-dimensional debate turns on, the transdiagnostic processes that cut across categories, and how differential reasoning actually proceeds.
heading: DSM-5-TR: structure and the logic of its organisation
text:
The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision, was published by the American Psychiatric Association in March 2022. It is organised in three sections. Section I covers use of the manual, including the definition of mental disorder and the cautionary statement on forensic use. Section II contains the diagnostic criteria and codes, grouped into diagnostic chapters. Section III contains emerging measures and models, including the Alternative Model for Personality Disorders, the Cultural Formulation Interview, and conditions for further study.

Section II's chapter ordering is not arbitrary. DSM-5 abandoned the multiaxial system of DSM-IV and reorganised the chapters along a developmental lifespan sequence, beginning with neurodevelopmental disorders that typically manifest early, moving through schizophrenia spectrum, bipolar, depressive, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, trauma and stressor-related, dissociative, somatic symptom, feeding and eating, elimination, sleep-wake, sexual dysfunction, gender dysphoria, disruptive and impulse-control, substance-related, neurocognitive, personality, and paraphilic disorders. Adjacent chapters are intended to reflect suspected shared underlying vulnerability, so that bipolar disorders sit between the psychotic and depressive chapters because they share features with both.

The internal logic of a DSM criteria set is polythetic and operational. A polythetic set requires some number of symptoms from a longer list rather than requiring all of them, which is why two people can share a diagnosis with minimal symptom overlap. Criteria are operationalised as counts, durations and thresholds. Nearly every criteria set carries a clinical significance criterion requiring distress or functional impairment, and exclusion criteria requiring that the presentation is not better explained by another condition, substance use, or a medical condition. That exclusion clause is the formal instruction to conduct a differential.

DSM-5-TR retained the DSM-5 structure and criteria almost entirely. The substantive changes were the addition of prolonged grief disorder as a new diagnosis, requiring the death to have occurred at least twelve months earlier for adults and six months for children and adolescents, with persistent yearning or preoccupation plus three of eight symptoms present most days for at least the past month; new symptom codes allowing clinicians to record current or historical suicidal behaviour and non-suicidal self-injury independently of any diagnosis; extensive revision of the explanatory text including prevalence, risk factors, culture, sex and gender; and revised terminology for racial and ethnic descriptions.

The limits of the system are structural. Thresholds are largely conventional rather than empirically derived. The categories do not correspond to distinct aetiologies. Comorbidity rates suggest the boundaries are wrong. Cultural validity varies by category. None of this makes the manual useless, but a clinician who treats a DSM code as an explanation has mistaken a filing system for a theory.

heading: ICD-11: what differs and why it differs
text:
The International Classification of Diseases, Eleventh Revision, was approved by the World Health Assembly in 2019, with member state reporting based on it from January 2022. The mental, behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders chapter is accompanied by the Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements, which replaced the ICD-10 Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Guidelines. Reed et al. (2019) describe the revision as the most international, multilingual and participative revision process yet undertaken for a mental disorders classification.

The most consequential difference is philosophical. ICD-11 was explicitly designed for clinical utility and global applicability, including in low-resource settings without specialist mental health services, whereas DSM prioritises operational precision for research and North American practice. ICD-11 therefore uses flexible prototype-style descriptions of essential features rather than rigid symptom counts and duration thresholds. A clinician is asked to judge whether the presentation matches the described prototype, not to count to five out of nine. This trades some reliability for usability and for cross-cultural applicability.

Specific substantive differences matter for differential reasoning. ICD-11 separates post-traumatic stress disorder into two sibling diagnoses, PTSD and complex PTSD, with complex PTSD requiring the PTSD features plus disturbances in self-organisation covering affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, and disturbances in relationships. DSM-5-TR has no complex PTSD diagnosis and instead broadened PTSD itself.
