ICD-11: what differs and why it differs

The International Classification of Diseases, Eleventh Revision, was approved by the World Health Assembly in 2019, with member state reporting based on it from January 2022. The mental, behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders chapter is accompanied by the Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements, which replaced the ICD-10 Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Guidelines. Reed et al. (2019) describe the revision as the most international, multilingual and participative revision process yet undertaken for a mental disorders classification.

ICD-11 was explicitly designed for clinical utility and global applicability, including in low-resource settings without specialist mental health services, whereas DSM prioritises operational precision for research and North American practice. ICD-11 therefore uses flexible prototype-style descriptions of essential features rather than rigid symptom counts and duration thresholds. heading: The categorical and dimensional debate
text:
The categorical model treats disorders as discrete kinds with boundaries, so that a person either has the condition or does not. The dimensional model treats psychopathology as continuous variation, so that the clinical question is how much of a trait or symptom dimension a person has, not whether they are in or out.

The evidence favours dimensions for most of psychopathology. Taxometric studies have generally failed to find natural cut points separating cases from non-cases for common conditions. Symptom severity distributions are continuous without a zone of rarity at the diagnostic threshold. Subthreshold presentations carry real impairment and real prognostic weight, which a categorical system discards. Genetic and neurobiological findings do not respect diagnostic boundaries, with the same variants associated with multiple categories. The high rates of comorbidity are more parsimoniously read as an artefact of drawing multiple category boundaries across a smaller number of underlying dimensions.

The arguments for retaining categories are practical rather than ontological. Clinical decisions are frequently binary: treat or do not treat, admit or do not admit, prescribe or do not prescribe. Categories are cognitively economical and communicate quickly. Health systems, insurers, courts and disability schemes run on codes. Treatment evidence has been generated within categories for fifty years and cannot be reindexed overnight.

The compromise position adopted by both major manuals is hybrid. DSM-5 retained categories in Section II while adding severity specifiers, cross-cutting symptom measures, and a dimensional alternative model for personality in Section III. ICD-11 went further by making personality disorder fully dimensional.

For reasoning about an individual, the most useful implications of the dimensional view are these. Do not treat a subthreshold presentation as nothing; the person's impairment is the relevant variable, not their symptom count. Do not treat a threshold crossing as a change in kind; someone who moves from four to five symptoms has not become a different sort of person. Expect co-occurrence and do not multiply diagnoses to account for it when a single underlying dimension explains the picture. Treat severity, chronicity and functional impact as more informative than category membership.

heading: HiTOP: the hierarchical dimensional alternative
text:
The Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology is a quantitatively derived dimensional classification built from factor-analytic evidence about how symptoms actually covary, developed by a consortium led by Kotov, Krueger, Watson and colleagues (Kotov et al., 2017). It is a bottom-up structure derived from data rather than a committee-defined taxonomy.

The hierarchy runs from narrow to broad. At the base sit signs, symptoms and maladaptive traits, the narrowest coherent dimensions. Above these sit syndromes, roughly corresponding to familiar DSM categories. Above these sit subfactors, small clusters of related syndromes such as distress or fear. Above these sit spectra. Above these sit superspectra. At the apex sits a general psychopathology factor.

Ruggero et al. (2019) identify six spectra: internalising, antagonistic externalising, disinhibited externalising, thought disorder, detachment, and somatoform. The internalising spectrum contains distress, fear, eating and sexual problem subfactors. The psychosis superspectrum has been the subject of dedicated validity work (Kotov et al., 2020).

The practical advantage is that a HiTOP profile describes a person on several continuous dimensions at once, which captures both severity and shape without the information loss of a threshold. It handles comorbidity natively, because co-occurrence is a consequence of shared higher-order variance rather than an anomaly requiring extra diagnoses. It captures subthreshold impairment. It aligns better than DSM categories with genetic and longitudinal findings.

The limits are frankly acknowledged by its own proponents. Ruggero et al. (2019) note that there is no direct evidence that using HiTOP dimensions improves treatment outcomes, that dimensional assessment adds administration and scoring burden, that reimbursement systems require ICD codes rather than dimensional profiles, that validated decision thresholds are underdeveloped, and that clinician training remains organised around categorical systems. The structure also continues to change as new data arrive, which is a scientific virtue and a clinical inconvenience.

Treat HiTOP as the best current description of the structure of psychopathology and as a corrective to over-interpretation of categories, while recognising that it does not yet function as a standalone clinical system.

heading: RDoC: a research framework, not a diagnostic system
text:
The Research Domain Criteria framework was introduced by the National Institute of Mental Health in 2010 to reorient psychopathology research away from DSM categories and toward dimensions of observable behaviour and neurobiological measures (Insel et al., 2010). It is explicitly a research framework and was never intended for clinical diagnosis.

RDoC is organised as a matrix. The rows are domains of functioning and their constituent constructs. The original domains were negative valence systems, positive valence systems, cognitive systems, systems for social processes, and arousal and regulatory systems, with a sensorimotor systems domain added later. The columns are units of analysis running from genes, molecules, cells, circuits and physiology up to behaviour, self-report and paradigms. Developmental trajectory and environment are treated as cross-cutting considerations rather than as cells in the matrix.

The core commitment is that a research question should be framed in terms of a dimensional construct such as reward learning or threat responsivity, studied across the full range from normal to impaired, without recruiting on the basis of a DSM diagnosis. The intended payoff is a set of mechanistic constructs that eventually map onto treatment targets more usefully than syndrome labels do.

The value for clinical reasoning is conceptual rather than procedural. RDoC constructs give a vocabulary for what may actually be going wrong for a person: blunted reward responsivity, elevated acute threat response, impaired working memory, disrupted arousal regulation, poor social communication reception. These describe mechanisms and cut across categories, which is closer to what a formulation needs than a diagnostic label is.

The limits are substantial. RDoC has been criticised for biological reductionism, for underweighting social and environmental causation despite the environment being nominally a cross-cutting factor, and for failing after more than a decade to deliver the clinical translation that motivated it. Commentary on the framework's own trajectory has described it as becoming humbler about those original ambitions. It has no diagnostic algorithm, no thresholds, and no direct clinical application. Do not use RDoC constructs as if they were diagnoses.

heading: The p factor and what a general factor does and does not mean
text:
Caspi and colleagues analysed eleven forms of psychopathology in a longitudinal birth cohort and found that a hierarchical model with three higher-order factors, internalising, externalising and thought disorder, fitted the data, but that a single general factor accounted for the covariation better still (Caspi et al., 2014). They named it p by analogy with g in the intelligence literature. The p factor was associated with greater life impairment, worse developmental histories, more compromised early-life brain function and family psychiatric loading.

The finding has been widely replicated across samples, ages and measurement approaches, and a general factor is now part of the HiTOP structure at its apex. The substantive claim is that people differ in a general liability to develop psychopathology of any kind, and that this general liability explains much of what looks like comorbidity between specific conditions.

Interpretation is contested. One reading is that p indexes a real dispositional vulnerability, possibly related to emotion dysregulation, negative emotionality, executive dysfunction, or disordered thought. A second reading is that p is largely a methodological artefact of how symptoms are measured, reflecting shared method variance, response style, or the fact that impairment and distress items appear across many scales. A third reading is that p indexes severity and chronicity rather than any distinct construct.

For clinical reasoning the useful implication is not the metaphysics but the prediction. If general liability is high, expect breadth rather than specificity: expect the person to have had several different presentations over time, expect symptoms outside the current diagnostic category, expect co-occurrence, and expect a worse course. Do not treat the appearance of a new symptom cluster as necessarily a new illness. High p should shift you toward transdiagnostic mechanisms and away from chasing each successive syndrome with a separate protocol.

heading: Transdiagnostic processes: repetitive negative thinking
text:
Harvey, Watkins, Mansell and Shafran (2004) reviewed cognitive and behavioural processes across the disorders and argued that a set of common processes maintain symptoms across diagnostic boundaries. They examined attention, memory, reasoning, thought and behaviour, and asked of each whether it functions transdiagnostically. Their conclusion reframed maintenance: what keeps disorders going is often the same handful of processes applied to different content.

Repetitive negative thinking is the most researched of these. Ehring and Watkins (2008) defined it as a style of thinking that is repetitive, passive or relatively uncontrollable, and focused on negative content, and argued that worry, depressive rumination, post-event processing in social anxiety, and trauma-related rumination are the same process applied to disorder-specific content rather than distinct phenomena. Direct comparisons between worry and rumination have generally found more similarity than difference. Elevated repetitive negative thinking appears across a wide range of conditions and prospective evidence supports a causal role in maintaining emotional problems.

The clinical implications are direct. Ask about the process, not only the content. The relevant questions are how long the thinking goes on, whether it is experienced as controllable, whether it is abstract and evaluative or concrete and problem-solving, and whether it produces any action. Watkins' distinction between abstract evaluative processing, which maintains distress, and concrete process-focused thinking, which does not, is the operative target. Rumination-focused interventions target the style directly rather than disputing the content.

Assessing it requires probes aimed at form rather than content. How long does the thinking go on once it starts. Can you stop it if you try, and what happens when you try. Does it feel useful while you are doing it, and does it produce any decision or action. Is the thinking about specific concrete detail, such as what exactly happened and what you would do differently at a particular moment, or is it abstract and evaluative, such as why this always happens to you and what it says about you. The abstract evaluative mode is the one that sustains distress.

Two further points bear on formulation. Repetitive negative thinking is frequently valued by the person doing it, who experiences worry as preparation and rumination as problem-solving, so an intervention that treats it purely as a symptom to be eliminated will meet resistance that is rational from the person's perspective. It also interacts with sleep, since the thinking commonly occupies the pre-sleep period, which means that sleep disruption and rumination form a reinforcing loop that neither sleep hygiene nor cognitive work alone will break.

For differential reasoning, the presence of heavy repetitive negative thinking is diagnostically non-specific. It should raise the probability that whatever category you land on will not be the whole story, and it should raise the priority of treating the process itself.

heading: Transdiagnostic processes: experiential avoidance, emotion dysregulation, intolerance of uncertainty
text:
Experiential avoidance was proposed by Hayes, Wilson, Gifford, Follette and Strosahl (1996) as a functional diagnostic dimension, defined as the attempt to alter the form, frequency or situational sensitivity of unwanted private experiences including thoughts, feelings, memories and bodily sensations, even when doing so causes behavioural harm. The paper's argument is that a wide range of presentations can be understood as unhealthy efforts to escape or avoid internal experience, and that classifying by function rather than by topography cuts across the diagnostic categories in a way that has treatment implications.

The clinical marker is not that the person avoids, since everyone does, but that avoidance has narrowed their life. The diagnostic question is what the person is unwilling to feel, and what they have given up in order not to feel it. Substance use, dissociation, compulsive behaviour, self-harm, workaholism, chronic distraction and interpersonal withdrawal can all serve this function. Two people with the same avoidance function and entirely different topographies require the same intervention logic.

Emotion dysregulation is the second major transdiagnostic process. Gross's process model of emotion regulation distinguishes strategies by where they act in the emotion-generative sequence: situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change, and response modulation. Aldao, Nolen-Hoeksema and Schweizer (2010) meta-analysed the relationships between reappraisal, problem solving, thought suppression and rumination and symptoms of depression, anxiety, eating disorders and substance use. Maladaptive strategies, particularly rumination and suppression, showed consistently stronger associations with symptoms than adaptive strategies showed protective associations. This asymmetry matters clinically: removing a maladaptive strategy tends to buy more than adding an adaptive one.

Intolerance of uncertainty was developed within the generalised anxiety literature by Dugas and colleagues and is defined as a dispositional tendency to perceive uncertain situations as threatening, unfair or unacceptable. Carleton has argued that fear of the unknown may be the fundamental fear underlying anxiety and neuroticism more broadly (Carleton, 2016). Intolerance of uncertainty accounts for significant variance in panic disorder, social anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, depression and eating disorders, and it is now treated as a well-established transdiagnostic risk factor and treatment target.

The practical use of these three constructs is that they specify what to target when the diagnostic picture is mixed. A presentation featuring heavy experiential avoidance, poor emotion regulation and high intolerance of uncertainty will respond to work on those processes regardless of which categories it satisfies.

heading: The procedure of differential reasoning
text:
Differential reasoning asks, for a given presentation, what else this could be and what would distinguish the alternatives. It is a discipline of generating rivals and then seeking evidence that separates them, and it is the single most important guard against premature closure.

The procedure has six steps.

First, describe the presentation at the level of phenomena rather than labels. Not "depression" but "reduced energy, loss of interest, early waking, weight loss of six kilograms over three months, and difficulty concentrating".

Second, establish the timeline. When did each element start, in what order, and what is the course: continuous, episodic, progressive, fluctuating, or lifelong? Timeline is the single most discriminating piece of information in psychiatric differential reasoning, and it is the piece most often omitted. Lifelong and pervasive points toward neurodevelopmental or personality-level explanation. Episodic with clear return to baseline points toward mood disorder. Onset following a specific event points toward stressor-related explanation. Progressive decline points toward neurocognitive or medical explanation.

Third, generate at least three candidate explanations, of which at least one must be non-psychiatric. The obligatory candidates for almost any presentation are a medical or organic cause, a substance or medication effect, a sleep disorder, and a normal response to abnormal circumstances.

Fourth, for each candidate, state what evidence would confirm it and what evidence would rule it out. This is the step that distinguishes reasoning from pattern-matching. If you cannot say what would rule a candidate out, you are not testing it.

Fifth, weight by base rates. Common conditions are common. In a general adult population, depression, anxiety, alcohol misuse, trauma sequelae, sleep deprivation and undiagnosed ADHD or autism are far more prevalent than the rarer conditions that a striking presentation may suggest.

Sixth, hold the conclusion provisionally and specify what would revise it. Write down the disconfirming observation you would expect to see if you are wrong.

Lifelong and pervasive points toward neurodevelopmental or personality-level explanation. Episodic with clear return to baseline points toward mood disorder. Onset following a specific event points toward stressor-related explanation. Progressive decline points toward neurocognitive or medical explanation.

Third, generate at least three candidate explanations, of which at least one must be non-psychiatric. The obligatory candidates for almost any presentation are a medical or organic cause, a substance or medication effect, a sleep disorder, and a normal response to abnormal circumstances.

Fourth, for each candidate, state what evidence would confirm it and what evidence would rule it out. This is the step that distinguishes reasoning from pattern-matching. If you cannot say what would rule a candidate out, you are not testing it.

Fifth, weight by base rates. Common conditions are common. In a general adult population, depression, anxiety, alcohol misuse, trauma sequelae, sleep deprivation and undiagnosed ADHD or autism are far more prevalent than the rarer conditions that a striking presentation may suggest.

Sixth, hold the conclusion provisionally and specify what would revise it. Write down the disconfirming observation you would expect to see if you are wrong.

heading: Worked differentials: four common presentations
text:
Low mood, fatigue and loss of interest. Candidates: major depressive episode; bipolar depression, which requires screening for past hypomania because antidepressant monotherapy is contraindicated; hypothyroidism; iron deficiency or B12 deficiency; obstructive sleep apnoea; chronic insufficient sleep; adjustment reaction to an identifiable stressor; prolonged grief; burnout from sustained occupational demand; alcohol use; medication effect including beta blockers, corticosteroids and hormonal contraception; anaemia; undiagnosed autism with autistic burnout. Discriminating evidence: any past period of reduced need for sleep with increased energy and activity, snoring and witnessed apnoeas and daytime sleepiness, cold intolerance and hair and skin change, the temporal relation to a stressor, weekday and weekend variation, drinking quantity in units, and whether interest is absent or merely inaccessible because of exhaustion.

Inattention, disorganisation and restlessness. Candidates: ADHD; anxiety disorder; depression; trauma-related hypervigilance; sleep disorder including apnoea and delayed sleep phase; substance use including cannabis and stimulant withdrawal; hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism; autism with executive difficulty; absence seizures; the ordinary consequences of an unsustainable workload or caring role. Discriminating evidence: whether the difficulties predate adolescence and were present across settings, which NICE guidance treats as necessary rather than optional; whether attention is episodic and tracks mood or is continuous and lifelong; school reports and collateral history; whether restlessness is motoric or is subjective dread.

Mood swings. Candidates: bipolar disorder types I and II; borderline personality organisation; premenstrual dysphoric disorder; ADHD with emotional dysregulation; complex PTSD with affect dysregulation; substance use with intoxication and withdrawal cycling; thyroid disease; the effects of chronic sleep deprivation. Discriminating evidence: duration of the mood state, since bipolar episodes last days to weeks while borderline and ADHD-related shifts last hours; whether shifts are triggered interpersonally, which points away from bipolar; whether elevated states include reduced need for sleep with sustained energy rather than simply feeling good; cycle timing relative to menses.

Hearing voices or unusual beliefs. Candidates: a psychotic disorder; dissociative experience following trauma, where voices are common and frequently misread; substance-induced psychosis including cannabis, stimulants and hallucinogens; delirium; temporal lobe epilepsy; sleep-related hypnagogic and hypnopompic phenomena; bereavement hallucinations, which are common and non-pathological; culturally sanctioned spiritual experience; severe sleep deprivation. Discriminating evidence: whether voices are experienced as inside or outside the head, their relation to trauma content and to dissociative states, onset acuity, fluctuating consciousness suggesting delirium, substance timeline, and the person's cultural community's reading of the experience.

doc_summary: How psychiatric diagnosis is organised across DSM-5-TR, ICD-11, HiTOP and RDoC, what the categorical-dimensional debate turns on, the transdiagnostic processes that cut across categories, and how differential reasoning actually proceeds.
heading: Diagnosis is a hypothesis, and a language model must not deliver one as a verdict
text:
The epistemic status of a psychiatric diagnosis is that of a provisional pattern-match, made under uncertainty, using criteria that are conventional rather than natural, with modest field reliability, by a system whose own developers describe the categories as imperfect. It is a hypothesis with administrative consequences.

The consequences of getting it wrong are asymmetric and durable. A diagnosis entered in a record propagates. It shapes how every subsequent clinician reads the person, which is the anchoring effect operating at system scale. Certain labels attract stigma both from services and from the person themselves. Some labels close doors, affecting employment, insurance, immigration, custody proceedings and firearms licensing depending on jurisdiction. A wrong label can delay the right treatment by years, which is the standard history of late-diagnosed autistic adults and of women given personality disorder diagnoses when the operative history was trauma.

A language model operates without the things that make a clinical diagnosis defensible. It has no longitudinal contact, no collateral history, no physical examination, no bloods, no observation of the person across states and settings, no ability to hold uncertainty across sessions, no clinical accountability, and no duty of care that can be enforced. What it has is a plausible-sounding pattern-matcher over a text description, which is precisely the mechanism that produces premature closure in humans.

The operating rule is therefore as follows. Do not state or imply that a person has a condition. Do not say "this sounds like X" or "you likely have X", both of which function as verdicts regardless of hedging. Do describe the pattern in ordinary language, name what a clinician would want to explore, name the alternative explanations including the medical and situational ones, and say what kind of assessment would actually answer the question. If the person already has a diagnosis, work with it while remaining alert to what it may be obscuring. If someone asks directly whether they have a condition, say plainly that this is not a question that can be answered from a text conversation, explain what a real assessment involves, and help them prepare for it. Where risk is disclosed, that takes priority over any diagnostic discussion.

The useful contribution is not the label. It is the differential: here are the several things this could be, here is what would tell them apart, here is what to ask about next.

doc_title: Hypothesis Generation and Differential Reasoning
doc_summary: An executable procedure for moving from a person's account to a ranked set of competing explanations, the evidence that discriminates them, the specific errors that corrupt the process, and the rules for revising a formulation.
heading: The reasoning stance: what mode you should be in
text:
Clinical reasoning runs in two modes. The fast mode recognises a pattern immediately from a small number of features and produces a candidate explanation before any deliberate analysis begins. The slow mode works through features systematically and tests candidates against evidence. Experienced clinicians run primarily in the fast mode and are usually right, which is why it persists. Diagnostic error concentrates in the cases where the fast mode produces a confident answer and the slow mode is never engaged (Croskerry, 2003, 2005).

The relevant asymmetry is that the fast mode produces confidence before it produces evidence. A plausible story arrives, feels complete, and then all subsequent information is read as either supporting it or as noise. The purpose of an explicit procedure is not to suppress the fast mode, which is not possible and would not be desirable, but to force a second candidate into existence before the first one has hardened.

For a language model the risk profile is worse than for a human clinician, for three reasons. A model has no longitudinal contact that would eventually contradict a wrong reading. It generates fluent, confident-sounding explanations by default, which makes a wrong formulation more persuasive than it deserves. It receives only what the person chose to write, which is a heavily filtered sample of the evidence. The procedure below should therefore be run explicitly rather than assumed.

The stance to adopt throughout: you are generating a set of candidate explanations and looking for the observations that would separate them. You are not identifying what is wrong with someone. The output of good reasoning here is a ranked differential with stated uncertainty, not a conclusion.

Two conditions should trigger deliberate use of the slow mode rather than reliance on recognition. The first is early certainty. Feeling sure within the first minute is a signal to slow down, because the strength of the impression is generated by the ease of the pattern match rather than by the weight of the evidence. The second is emotional response to the person, in either direction. Strong dislike, strong liking, frustration, pity and identification all distort what gets asked and what gets recorded, and the case that produces them is the case most in need of a second view.

The procedure that follows is written to be run in order. It is not a description of how expert clinicians experience their own reasoning, which is largely recognition-driven and post-hoc rationalised. It is a scaffold that produces the same output more reliably and that can be inspected and corrected by someone else.

doc_title: Hypothesis Generation and Differential Reasoning
doc_summary: An executable procedure for moving from a person's account to a ranked set of competing explanations, the evidence that discriminates them, the specific errors that corrupt the process, and the rules for revising a formulation.
heading: Step 1: Convert the account into observations
text:
Restate what the person said as a list of observations, stripped of interpretation and of diagnostic language.

Rules for this step. Use the person's own words for subjective states. Replace any label they supply with the phenomena it stands for; if they say "I have anxiety", ask what happens, when, and in the body. Separate what they report experiencing from the explanation they have already attached to it, because their explanation is a hypothesis too and should be listed as one candidate rather than adopted as the frame. Record what is absent as well as what is present, since negatives discriminate. Note the domains they did not mention, which are usually sleep, substances, physical health, money, and safety.

Distinguish four kinds of content and keep them separate. Symptoms are internal experiences reported by the person. Signs are observable features, which in a text conversation are limited to what the writing itself shows. Function is what has changed in their actual life: work, study, relationships, self-care, leaving the house. Meaning is what the person believes their difficulties say about them, which drives shame and help-seeking but is not evidence about mechanism.

Function is the most under-collected and most discriminating category. Severity and course are far better indexed by what the person can no longer do than by how many symptoms they endorse.

A worked conversion. Account given: "I think I've got depression again, I'm exhausted all the time and I can't be bothered with anything." Observations: fatigue, described as constant rather than exertion-related, duration not yet established. Reduced motivation, scope not established. Self-applied label of depression, with an implied prior episode, details not established. Not stated: sleep quality and quantity, appetite and weight, alcohol and other substances, physical health and medications, whether anything changed before this started, whether interest is absent or blocked by exhaustion, whether there is any suicidal ideation, whether they have ever had a period of the opposite. That list of absences is the interview agenda.

heading: Step 2: Build the timeline before anything else
text:
Timeline is the highest-yield single piece of information in psychiatric differential reasoning, and it is the piece most often skipped because it is laborious and because a compelling symptom picture makes it feel unnecessary.

Establish four things. Onset: when did each element start, and in what order. Course: continuous, episodic with return to baseline, progressive, fluctuating within days, or lifelong. Context at onset: what else was happening in the weeks and months before, including losses, changes, medication starts and stops, substance changes, physical illness, and workload. Trajectory since: better, worse, unchanged, or cycling.

The discriminating power of course is large.

Lifelong and pervasive across settings points toward neurodevelopmental explanation or toward personality-level and attachment-level patterns, and away from episodic disorder. A person who has always been this way does not have an episode.

Episodic with genuine return to baseline points toward mood disorder and away from personality-level or neurodevelopmental explanation.

Onset closely following an identifiable event points toward stressor-related and adjustment explanations, toward grief, and toward trauma sequelae, and requires you to consider whether the response is proportionate to circumstances before pathologising it.

Progressive and unremitting decline, particularly with cognitive features, points toward neurocognitive or general medical explanation and should raise the priority of medical assessment sharply.

Fluctuating within hours, especially in response to interpersonal events, points away from bipolar disorder and toward affect dysregulation of the kind seen in borderline patterns, complex trauma, and ADHD.

Fluctuating consciousness or attention with acute onset points toward delirium and is a medical emergency.

A worked timeline shows the discriminating power. A person reports low mood, poor concentration and irritability. Timeline established: concentration difficulty and disorganisation present since primary school, documented in reports, continuous, never absent. Low mood beginning eighteen months ago after a job change, worse in the past four months, with some better weeks. Irritability worse in the past four months and worse in the evenings. Alcohol intake rose four months ago. Sleep has been six hours or less for four months, with a further shift after a house move. Read as a single depressive episode, this is one condition. Read against the timeline, it is a lifelong attentional difficulty, a mood disturbance that postdates it by two decades and follows an occupational change, and a four-month layer of sleep restriction and increased drinking that accounts for the recent deterioration. Those three components have different treatments and different urgencies.

If you have not established the timeline, you do not yet have a differential. You have an impression.

heading: Step 3: Generate the hypothesis set, including the mandatory candidates
text:
Generate at least three candidate explanations before evaluating any of them. Generating one and then testing it is the mechanism of confirmation bias; generating three and then discriminating is the antidote.

Five candidates are mandatory for essentially any presentation of psychological distress, and should be explicitly considered even when they seem unlikely.

A medical or organic explanation. Thyroid dysfunction, B12 or iron deficiency, anaemia, diabetes, autoimmune conditions, neurological disease, infection, hormonal change including perimenopause and postpartum, and in older adults or acute presentations, delirium.

A substance, medication or withdrawal explanation. Alcohol, cannabis, stimulants, opioids, benzodiazepines, and the withdrawal states from each. Prescribed medications including corticosteroids, beta blockers, hormonal contraception, isotretinoin, and psychiatric medications themselves. Caffeine and nicotine.

A sleep explanation. Obstructive sleep apnoea, insomnia disorder, circadian rhythm disorders including delayed sleep phase, and simple chronic sleep restriction. Sleep loss produces a syndrome that closely resembles depression with cognitive impairment, and it is both common and reversible.

A situational explanation. The person may be responding normally to genuinely bad circumstances. Poverty, overwork, caring responsibilities, an abusive relationship, insecure housing, insecure immigration status, discrimination, bereavement, or an ongoing threat. If the circumstances would distress most people, the first question is what needs to change in the circumstances, not what is wrong with the person.

A developmental or neurodivergent explanation. Undiagnosed autism or ADHD in an adult presenting with anxiety, depression, burnout or interpersonal difficulty is common and routinely missed, particularly in women, in people diagnosed with personality disorders, and in people who have coped by masking.

Beyond the mandatory five, generate the psychiatric candidates the presentation actually suggests, and generate them as a set rather than as a single winner. For each candidate, write one sentence stating how that explanation would account for the full observation list, not just the salient feature.

heading: Step 4: Set priors from base rates
text:
A hypothesis's plausibility depends on how common the condition is in the population the person actually belongs to, before any of their specific features are considered. Ignoring this is base rate neglect, and it is the error that makes rare and dramatic explanations feel more compelling than they should.

The general principle: common things are common, and in unselected adult populations the common things are depression, anxiety disorders, alcohol misuse, insomnia, trauma sequelae, and undiagnosed neurodevelopmental conditions. Rare conditions remain rare even when a presentation resembles them.

Base rates are population-specific, and the relevant population is the one the person is drawn from, not the general public. In a tertiary referral clinic, an emergency department, a prison, a specialist eating disorder service or a perinatal service, the prior probabilities differ enormously from those in a community sample. A model reasoning about a person who has come to a chat interface is reasoning about a self-selected population that skews toward distress that has not been resolved elsewhere, which raises the prior on chronicity, on prior unsuccessful help-seeking, and on conditions that are commonly missed.

Base rates also shift with demographics, and this is where the reasoning most often goes wrong in both directions. Some conditions are genuinely more prevalent in some groups. Other apparent differences in prevalence are artefacts of differential diagnosis rates rather than differences in underlying condition, which is the case for autism and ADHD in women and girls, and arguably for psychosis diagnoses in Black populations in the UK and US. Adjusting a prior by demographics is legitimate; adopting a diagnostic stereotype is not. The test is whether you are using a fact about incidence or a fact about who tends to get labelled.

Two practical rules. First, if a candidate requires an unusual condition to explain features that a common condition would also explain, prefer the common one until you have evidence that discriminates. Second, the fact that a presentation is unusual is not evidence for a rare condition, because common conditions present unusually far more often than rare conditions present at all.

The relevant caveat: the strongest known evidence base in clinical judgement research is that structured, actuarial and mechanical prediction equals or exceeds unaided clinical judgement across nearly a hundred comparative studies (Grove & Meehl, 1996; Dawes, Faust & Meehl, 1989). Where a validated structured measure or decision aid exists, the clinician's impression should not override it.

Adjusting a prior by demographics is legitimate; adopting a diagnostic stereotype is not. The test is whether you are using a fact about incidence or a fact about who tends to get labelled.

Two practical rules. First, if a candidate requires an unusual condition to explain features that a common condition would also explain, prefer the common one until you have evidence that discriminates. Second, the fact that a presentation is unusual is not evidence for a rare condition, because common conditions present unusually far more often than rare conditions present at all.

The relevant caveat: the strongest known evidence base in clinical judgement research is that structured, actuarial and mechanical prediction equals or exceeds unaided clinical judgement across nearly a hundred comparative studies (Grove & Meehl, 1996; Dawes, Faust & Meehl, 1989). Where a validated structured measure or decision aid exists, the clinician's impression should not override it.

heading: Step 5: Identify the discriminating evidence
text:
For each candidate, state the specific observation that would raise its probability and the specific observation that would lower it. Evidence that is consistent with every candidate is not evidence. This is the step that most distinguishes reasoning from pattern-matching.

Construct the discriminators deliberately. The best questions are those whose two possible answers point in opposite directions. "Have you ever had a period of a week or more when you needed much less sleep than usual and had more energy rather than less?" discriminates unipolar from bipolar depression. "Were these difficulties with attention there before you were twelve, and were they there at school as well as at home?" discriminates ADHD from attentional difficulty secondary to mood, anxiety or trauma. "Does the mood shift last hours or days?" discriminates affect dysregulation from mood episode. "Do you snore, and has anyone ever told you that you stop breathing?" discriminates sleep apnoea from depression. "How much are you drinking, in units, on a typical day this week?" discriminates a great deal.

Rank candidates by the cost of missing them, not only by their probability. This is the emergency medicine principle of ruling out the dangerous before the likely, and it applies here. Medical causes, delirium, substance withdrawal states that can be physically dangerous, bipolarity before antidepressant monotherapy, ongoing abuse, and active suicidal intent all carry high cost if missed and should be actively excluded rather than passively deprioritised.

Record explicitly what you do not know. A differential built on an account missing sleep, substance, medical and safety information should say so, because the missing information is more decisive than any refinement of the existing candidates.

For a language model, the correct output of this step is the set of questions, not the answer. "Here are four things this could be, here is what would tell them apart, here is what a clinician would ask" is useful and honest. "This sounds like X" is neither.

heading: Step 6: Weigh, rank, and state the working formulation
text:
Produce a ranked list rather than a single answer. For each candidate record how well it accounts for the whole observation set, what argues for it, what argues against it, and what is still unknown.

Prefer the explanation that accounts for the most observations with the fewest assumptions, but do not over-apply parsimony. Comorbidity is the norm, not the exception, and the p factor literature and the HiTOP structure both predict that a person with any substantial difficulty is likely to have more than one. Two conditions co-occurring is often more probable than one exotic condition explaining everything.

State the working formulation in a form that carries its own revision conditions. A usable statement has four parts: the account, the confidence, the evidence that would strengthen it, and the evidence that would overturn it.

Worked example of the form. "The most likely account is that a longstanding pattern of conditional self-worth was activated by a public work failure and is now maintained by checking, avoidance of evaluative contact, and alcohol-disrupted sleep. Confidence is moderate. It would be strengthened by a history showing similar responses to previous evaluative setbacks and by improvement when the checking is interrupted. It would be overturned by evidence that the fatigue and concentration difficulty predate the work events, by a positive screen for sleep apnoea, by thyroid abnormality, or by a history of discrete elevated-mood episodes."

That last clause is the load-bearing part. A formulation that cannot be overturned by any observation is not a formulation.

Communicate the uncertainty rather than hiding it. Confidence expressed in the delivery is read as confidence in the content, so an account delivered fluently and without qualification will be received as settled regardless of the hedging words inside it. State the confidence level explicitly, name the leading alternative rather than only the winner, and say what is still missing. "This is the account that currently fits best, the main alternative is a sleep-driven picture, and neither can be separated without knowing whether you snore and how much you are drinking" is more useful and more honest than a single confident narrative.

Distinguish three things that are often collapsed together in the output. What you have observed, which is what the person reported. What you infer, which is the formulation. What you do not know, which is the assessment agenda. Keeping these separate lets a reader disagree with the inference without discarding the observations, and it makes the account revisable by someone other than you.

heading: Reasoning errors: the four that do most of the damage
text:
Premature closure is accepting a diagnosis before it has been fully verified and stopping the search, and it is generally regarded as the single largest contributor to diagnostic error (Croskerry, 2003). The subjective experience is not one of stopping early; it is one of having arrived. The countermeasure is procedural rather than attitudinal: require a minimum of three candidates before evaluating any, and require an explicit statement of what would disconfirm the leading candidate before acting on it.

Confirmation bias is seeking and weighting evidence that supports the current hypothesis while discounting evidence against it. In clinical interviewing it operates through question selection more than through evidence evaluation, because the clinician asks the questions that would confirm the working hypothesis and never asks the ones that would break it. The countermeasure is to construct at least one question per interview whose answer would specifically embarrass the leading candidate.

Anchoring is locking onto salient features of the initial presentation and failing to adjust in light of later information (Croskerry, 2003). The first thing said, the referral letter, and the existing diagnosis in the record are the three most powerful anchors in practice. A person who arrives labelled has already anchored every clinician who reads the file. The countermeasure is to build the observation list and timeline from scratch before reading the existing formulation, and, where an existing diagnosis is present, to ask explicitly what it might be obscuring.

Availability is judging something more likely because it comes to mind easily, typically because of recent or memorable experience (Croskerry, 2003). It inflates the probability of whatever you have recently read about, whatever is currently discussed publicly, and whatever produced a memorable outcome. For a language model the analogue is training-data availability: conditions heavily represented in text are over-generated, and conditions poorly represented are under-generated, independent of their actual prevalence. The countermeasure is to check the candidate list against base rates deliberately rather than trusting fluency as a proxy for probability.

Two further errors from the same literature deserve naming. Diagnosis momentum is the process by which a tentative label passes between clinicians and hardens into fact without any new evidence being added. Search satisficing is stopping once you find something, which causes second diagnoses, comorbid substance use, and medical contributors to be missed after the first plausible explanation is located.

heading: Reasoning errors: attribution, overshadowing, and the person as cause
text:
The fundamental attribution error in clinical work is attributing a person's behaviour to their stable dispositions while underweighting their situation. It is the reasoning that turns "she is frightened of this environment" into "she is a hostile person", and it is heavily amplified by the clinical setting, which shows you the person and not their circumstances. Presentations most vulnerable to it are those involving anger, non-attendance, non-adherence, and any behaviour that inconveniences the service. When a person's behaviour is described as manipulative, attention-seeking, difficult or non-compliant, the correct next question is what that behaviour is achieving and what conditions make it necessary.

The error compounds when the person is already in a stigmatised category, because their existing label supplies a ready dispositional explanation for anything they do.

Diagnostic overshadowing is the closely related error of attributing new symptoms to an existing diagnosis rather than investigating them. The term originated with Reiss and colleagues, describing how a diagnosis of intellectual disability so dominated clinical attention that co-occurring mental health conditions were misattributed to the disability (Reiss et al., 1982). It has since been extended to describe the misattribution of physical symptoms to an existing psychiatric diagnosis, and it is a documented contributor to the excess physical morbidity and mortality of people with severe mental illness (Jones et al., 2008; Hallyburton, 2022).

Practically, overshadowing means that the person with a schizophrenia diagnosis whose chest pain is recorded as anxiety, the autistic person whose depression is recorded as part of their autism, and the person with a borderline diagnosis whose neurological symptoms are recorded as functional are all victims of the same error. The countermeasure is a standing rule: when a person with an existing diagnosis presents with a new symptom, the existing diagnosis is the last explanation to be accepted, not the first.

A related failure is attributing to a condition what belongs to its treatment. Sedation, weight gain, emotional blunting, sexual dysfunction, akathisia and cognitive dulling are common medication effects that are routinely recorded as symptoms of the underlying illness.

heading: Reasoning errors: over-pathologising ordinary distress
text:
Distress that is proportionate to circumstances is not disorder. Horwitz and Wakefield (2007) argued that psychiatric classification, by defining depression on symptom counts largely without reference to context, transformed normal sorrow into disorder and generated large numbers of false positives. Their conceptual basis is Wakefield's harmful dysfunction analysis, in which a mental disorder requires both harm and a failure of an internal mechanism to perform its evolved function. Sadness following loss is the mechanism working, not failing.

The practical test has three parts. Is there an identifiable precipitant sufficient to produce this response in most people? Is the intensity and duration proportionate to that precipitant, judged against the person's cultural context rather than against a clinical norm? Is the response tracking the circumstances, so that it eases when they ease?

Where the answers are yes, the appropriate response is validation, practical support, and attention to what needs to change in the situation. Applying a diagnosis and a treatment protocol in these circumstances does three kinds of harm: it relocates a social problem inside the person, it can obstruct the practical remedy by treating distress as the thing to fix, and it attaches a durable label with consequences that outlast the episode.

The countervailing error is real and should be held simultaneously. Understandability is not the same as harmlessness. A person whose depression is entirely explicable by their circumstances can still be at risk of suicide, still be unable to function, and still benefit from treatment. Proportionate distress that has become self-sustaining, through withdrawal, rumination, sleep collapse or substance use, requires intervention on the maintaining processes even though the origin was normal. The judgement is not whether the distress makes sense but whether it is now running on its own machinery.

Watch for the specific version of this error where a person from a marginalised group is pathologised for a response that is adaptive in their environment. Hypervigilance in someone who is genuinely unsafe, mistrust of services in someone whose community has been badly treated by them, and anger in someone facing sustained unfairness are not symptoms.

heading: Reasoning errors: under-recognising trauma and neurodivergence
text:
Two explanations are systematically under-generated, and both produce years of wrong treatment when missed.

Trauma is under-recognised because it is frequently not volunteered, because services often do not ask, and because its sequelae present as something else. Adverse childhood experiences are common and show a dose-response relationship with a wide range of adult health and social outcomes (Felitti et al., 1998). The presentations that most often conceal trauma are affect dysregulation labelled as borderline personality disorder, dissociative experiences labelled as psychosis, hypervigilance and concentration difficulty labelled as ADHD, chronic physical symptoms labelled as functional or medically unexplained, substance use treated as a primary disorder, and non-attendance and mistrust labelled as poor engagement. The ICD-11 complex PTSD category exists precisely because prolonged interpersonal trauma produces a picture that PTSD criteria do not capture and that personality disorder criteria capture wrongly (Reed et al., 2019).

The countermeasure is to ask, routinely, in a way that does not require disclosure. A question about what the person's childhood was like, or whether anything has happened to them that still affects how safe they feel, opens the door without demanding entry. Never require a detailed account of trauma to justify considering it as a candidate.

Neurodivergence is under-recognised for structurally similar reasons. Autism and ADHD present differently from the diagnostic stereotypes in women, in people who learned to mask, and in adults who developed compensatory strategies that hid the difficulty until demands exceeded capacity. Camouflaging, the suppression and substitution of autistic behaviour to appear non-autistic, is more common in autistic girls and women and directly contributes to missed and late diagnosis (Hull et al.; see reviews of late, missed and misdiagnosis in autistic girls and women). Borderline personality disorder is a documented misdiagnosis in autistic women, and the two can also genuinely co-occur where sustained social invalidation has shaped personality development.

The discriminating questions are developmental. Were these difficulties present in childhood and across settings, or did they begin at a particular point? Is the social difficulty a loss of previously easy capacity, which points to depression or trauma, or a lifelong effortful compensation, which points to autism? Is the emotional instability triggered interpersonally and lasting hours, or is it episodic over days to weeks? Is the person exhausted by social contact in a way that has been true since childhood?

The cost of missing either is high and specific: years of ineffective treatment for the wrong target, iatrogenic harm from labels the person cannot shed, and the loss of accommodations and self-understanding that accurate identification provides.

heading: What debiasing actually achieves, and what to do instead
text:
The honest position is that education about biases has weak evidence for reducing diagnostic error. Naming a bias does not immunise against it, and the biases operate below the level at which knowing about them helps. Croskerry's own work moved toward metacognitive and structural interventions rather than toward bias education: developing the ability to disengage and reconsider before acting, reducing cognitive load, reducing time pressure, improving feedback, and conducting a cognitive and affective review after diagnostic failures (Croskerry, 2005).

What has better support is structure. Grove and Meehl's review of nearly a hundred comparisons found that mechanical and actuarial prediction equalled or exceeded informal clinical judgement in virtually every study (Grove & Meehl, 1996; Dawes, Faust & Meehl, 1989). The implication is not that judgement is worthless but that where a structured procedure exists, using it beats not using it, and overriding it on the basis of clinical impression tends to make accuracy worse.

Practical measures that survive this scrutiny, in rough order of value.

Use a structured procedure rather than an unstructured impression, particularly for risk and for diagnosis. Complete the timeline before forming an impression. Require a minimum number of candidates. Screen systematically for the mandatory candidates rather than considering them when prompted.

Seek disconfirming information deliberately. The single most useful habit is asking, before concluding, what would have to be true for this account to be wrong, and then checking that specific thing.

Get outside information. Collateral history, records, and prior notes discipline a formulation in ways that further interviewing of the person does not, because they are not filtered through the same account.

Slow down where the cost of error is high, where the presentation is atypical, where you feel strong certainty early, and where you feel strong dislike or strong affinity for the person. Affective states drive diagnostic error and the emotionally charged case is the one that needs the second opinion.

Track outcomes. Persons' insistence that failure to improve is evidence against the formulation rather than evidence against the patient is the operational form of this. Without outcome feedback, a clinician's confidence increases with experience while their accuracy does not.

Ask someone else. Supervision, second opinion and team formulation work because a different person does not share the anchor.

heading: How to hold a formulation loosely and revise it
text:
A formulation is a hypothesis with a lifespan. Building it is the easy part; the skill is in keeping it revisable while still acting on it.

State confidence explicitly and separately from content. "This is my best current account, held with moderate confidence" is different from "this is what is happening", and the difference should be audible to the person and to yourself.

Attach revision triggers when you write it. Name in advance the observations that would require you to change the account. Common triggers: no improvement after an adequate trial of an intervention that the formulation predicts should work; the emergence of a symptom the account does not predict; information about the timeline that contradicts the assumed order of events; disclosure of trauma, substance use or medical history not previously known; the person saying the account does not fit.

Treat the person's disagreement as evidence rather than as resistance. If someone says the formulation does not match their experience, the prior probability that they are right is high, because they have access to data you do not. Distinguish revision from replacement. Most formulations do not fail wholesale; they are wrong about the weighting of one component or about one causal link. Ask which specific element is disconfirmed before discarding the whole account.

If your account has grown steadily more elaborate without ever being contradicted, that is a sign that it has stopped being testable rather than a sign that it is right.

Re-formulate at defined points rather than only when something goes wrong. A scheduled review, at a fixed number of sessions or at a transition point, catches drift that a crisis-triggered review does not.

Keep the discarded candidates visible. A formulation record that lists what else was considered and why it was set aside is far more useful to the next clinician than one that presents a single conclusion, because it lets the next person re-open a question rather than starting from the same anchor.

doc_title: Hypothesis Generation and Differential Reasoning
doc_summary: An executable procedure for moving from a person's account to a ranked set of competing explanations, the evidence that discriminates them, the specific errors that corrupt the process, and the rules for revising a formulation.
heading: The compact procedure
text:
Run in this order and do not skip forward when the answer feels obvious.

1. Observations. Restate the account as phenomena. List what has not been asked about.
2. Timeline. Onset, order, course, context at onset, trajectory. Do not proceed without this.
3. Function. What has changed in what the person can actually do.
4. Candidates. Minimum three. Mandatory five always considered: medical or organic, substance or medication or withdrawal, sleep, situational, developmental or neurodivergent. Then the psychiatric candidates the picture suggests.
5. Priors. Weight by base rate in the relevant population. Prefer common explanations for common features. Do not let vividness stand in for probability.
6. Discriminators. For each candidate, one thing that would confirm and one that would rule out. Prioritise the high-cost misses: medical, delirium, withdrawal, bipolarity, ongoing abuse, active risk.
7. Rank. Best account, with what argues against it, and what remains unknown. Expect co-occurrence rather than forcing a single answer.
8. Revision triggers. Name the observations that would overturn the account before acting on it.
9. Review. Set a point at which the formulation is re-examined regardless of progress.

Three failure modes to watch for while running it. Skipping to step 7 because the answer arrived at step 1 is premature closure and is the most common. Running steps 4 through 6 on a candidate set that never included the mandatory five is a thorough analysis of the wrong option space. Producing a ranked list and then acting only on the top item, without recording what else was considered, removes the information that would let anyone revise the account later.

For a language model, steps 4 through 6 are the deliverable. Present the candidate set, the discriminating questions, and the reasoning, and route the conclusion to an assessment that can actually gather the missing evidence. Do not present step 7 as a diagnosis. Where risk is disclosed at any point in the procedure, that takes priority over completing it: safety comes before differential reasoning, and an incomplete formulation is an acceptable cost of responding to risk immediately.

doc_summary: What each therapy in the cognitive and behavioural family claims to change, the moves a practitioner actually makes, the trials and guidelines that support it, and where it goes wrong, with verbatim in-session wording.
heading: Standard cognitive therapy (Beck): the model and what it claims to change
text:
Beck's cognitive model holds that emotional distress is maintained by the appraisal of events rather than the events themselves (Beck, 1976; Beck, Rush, Shaw and Emery, 1979). The model is layered. Automatic thoughts sit at the surface and are situation-specific. Underlying assumptions or conditional rules sit beneath them, usually phrased as if-then or must statements. Core beliefs sit at the base and are absolute statements about self, others and the world. The claimed change mechanism is that a person learns to treat thoughts as hypotheses rather than facts, tests them against evidence and experience, and thereby reduces the frequency and credibility of the appraisals that drive symptoms.

Structurally, a Beckian session has a recognisable shape: mood check with a brief measure, bridge from the last session, agenda setting done collaboratively, review of the last homework, one or two agenda items worked in depth, new homework set collaboratively, and a summary plus feedback request at the end (Beck, 2011). The structure is not decoration. It is what allows a time-limited therapy to cover a formulation, a skill and a between-session task in fifty minutes.

The case formulation is the organising document. It maps early experience, the core beliefs formed from it, the conditional assumptions that keep those beliefs from being disconfirmed, the compensatory strategies the person uses, and the critical incident that broke the strategy. A clinician who is doing cognitive therapy well can say at any moment which part of the formulation the current technique is targeting.

Evidence: CBT is recommended by NICE as a treatment option across depression severities in adults (NICE guideline NG222, 2022), for OCD and body dysmorphic disorder including exposure and response prevention (NICE guideline CG31, 2005), and as trauma-focused CBT for PTSD presenting more than one month after the event (NICE guideline NG116, 2018). CBT for psychosis is recommended by NICE and should be delivered over at least sixteen planned sessions (NICE guideline CG178, 2014).

The most common failure in standard CBT is running the technique without the formulation. A thought record produced because it is week three of a protocol, rather than because this person's distress is maintained by a specific appraisal, produces compliance and no change. The second most common failure is treating cognitive restructuring as persuasion. If the clinician knows the "right" answer to the thought record before the client does, the exercise has become a debate, and the client will typically report the intellectual answer while retaining the emotional belief. The clinician's marker for this is the client saying some version of "I know it rationally but I don't feel it."

> "Can I check the shape of what we're doing? Last week we agreed the thing that keeps this going is the thought that if you ask for help you'll be seen as incompetent. Today I want to test that directly rather than talk about it. Does that fit with what you'd hoped to use the time for, or is something more pressing?"

doc_title: The CBT Family: Cognitive, Behavioural and Third-Wave Therapies in Practice
doc_summary: What each therapy in the cognitive and behavioural family claims to change, the moves a practitioner actually makes, the trials and guidelines that support it, and where it goes wrong, with verbatim in-session wording.
heading: Cognitive restructuring: the actual sequence
text:
Cognitive restructuring is a sequence, not a single move. The order matters because each step depends on the previous one being concrete.

First, catch a specific moment. The clinician resists working with a generalisation and pulls for an episode with a time and place attached. Second, identify the emotion and rate its intensity, which anchors change to something measurable. Third, identify the hot thought, meaning the cognition carrying the most affective charge, not simply the first thought reported. Fourth, rate belief in the hot thought as a percentage. Fifth, gather evidence for and against, with the "for" column collected first and taken seriously. Sixth, construct an alternative or balanced view in the client's own words. Seventh, re-rate emotion and belief.

The downward arrow technique is the standard route from an automatic thought to a core belief. The clinician repeatedly asks what it would mean if the thought were true, without challenging anything, until the client arrives at an absolute statement.

> Client: "I think they noticed I went blank in the meeting."
> Clinician: "Let's say they did notice. What would that mean to you?"
> Client: "That they'd think I wasn't on top of the project."
> Clinician: "And if they thought that?"
> Client: "They'd start checking my work."
> Clinician: "And if they started checking your work, what would that say?"
> Client: "That I'm not actually capable of this job. That I got here by luck."

Behavioural experiments are usually more potent than verbal disputation, and the field has moved toward them. The design has four parts: the specific prediction with a probability attached, the experiment that could disconfirm it, the actual result, and the revised belief. The prediction must be falsifiable. "It will go badly" is not usable. "At least three people will look away when I speak, and I will not be able to finish the sentence" is.

> "Before we go anywhere near whether that's true, I want to know exactly what you're predicting. If you send that email without rewriting it four times, what specifically happens? What percentage would you put on it?"

Common misapplications: challenging a thought that is accurate. If a client believes their partner is critical of them and the partner is in fact critical, the target is not the appraisal but the situation or the meaning attached to it. Restructuring an accurate perception is gaslighting with a worksheet. A second misapplication is restructuring thoughts about a live danger, such as a client in an abusive relationship appraising risk correctly. A third is using restructuring where the presenting mechanism is avoidance, where the exposure or activation work carries the change and cognitive work should follow it rather than precede it.

doc_summary: What each therapy in the cognitive and behavioural family claims to change, the moves a practitioner actually makes, the trials and guidelines that support it, and where it goes wrong, with verbatim in-session wording.
heading: Socratic questioning: the four-stage sequence with verbatim wording
text:
Socratic questioning is guided discovery, not cross-examination. Padesky's (1993) formulation gives four stages that repeat in cycles: ask informational questions the client can answer, listen empathically, summarise what has emerged, then ask a synthesising or analytical question that applies the new information to the original belief. Skipping the third stage is the most common error, because without the summary the client does not experience the new material as a coherent set.

Therapist use of Socratic questioning, rated by observers in the first three sessions of a sixteen-week course of cognitive therapy for depression, predicted session-to-session symptom change: a one standard deviation increase in Socratic questioning predicted a 1.51-point decrease in BDI-II score in the following session, and the effect held after controlling for the therapeutic alliance (Braun, Strunk, Sasso and Cooper, 2015).

A worked sequence on the belief "I'm a burden to my friends":

> Clinician (informational): "When you think about being a burden, whose face comes to mind first?"
> Client: "Sam."
> Clinician (informational): "When did you last see Sam?"
> Client: "Saturday. He asked me to come over."
> Clinician (informational): "Who made the arrangement?"
> Client: "He texted me. He'd asked twice before that too."
> Clinician (empathic listening): "So it sounds like being around him has felt like something you're imposing, even while he's the one initiating."
> Client: "Yeah. I keep thinking he's being polite."
> Clinician (summary): "Let me put together what we've got. You believe you're a burden. When we look at the most recent evidence, Sam initiated three times, you didn't ask once, and your explanation for that is that he's being polite."
> Clinician (analytical): "If a friend of yours told you they'd invited someone over three times out of politeness, what would you make of that?"

Note what the clinician does not do: assert that the client is not a burden, supply the reframe, or ask a leading question with the answer embedded. The last question is the analytical one, and the client generates the conclusion.

Rules for the wording. Ask questions the client has the information to answer. Do not ask questions to which the clinician already knows the answer and the client does not, because that is teaching disguised as enquiry. Ask about specifics before generalities. Use "what" and "how" more than "why", because "why" invites justification and often produces defensiveness. When the client generates an answer that goes against the clinician's hypothesis, follow the client's answer rather than repeating the question in a different form.

Failure modes to recognise in transcript. Chained rhetorical questions with an obvious intended answer ("Do you really think that's fair on yourself?"). Questions that function as reassurance ("But you know you're doing well, don't you?"). Rapid questioning without pauses, which produces compliance rather than discovery. If the client is answering in three words and the clinician is speaking in paragraphs, the sequence has failed.

heading: Behavioural activation: mechanism, technique, evidence
text:
Behavioural activation treats depression as maintained by a loss of contact with positive reinforcement, compounded by avoidance and withdrawal that reduce it further (Lewinsohn's behavioural model; Martell, Dimidjian and Herman-Dunn, 2010). The claimed mechanism is that scheduled, graded increases in activity restore contact with reinforcement, and that this happens without requiring any change in thought content. BA is deliberately not a cognitive therapy: it treats rumination as a behaviour to be interrupted rather than a set of propositions to be tested.

Core techniques: activity monitoring to establish a baseline of what the person actually does and how they feel doing it; activity scheduling using values or life areas rather than pleasant events lists alone; graded task assignment breaking activities down until the first step is small enough to be certain; functional analysis of avoidance, usually taught to clients as TRAP (Trigger, Response, Avoidance Pattern) and TRAC (Trigger, Response, Alternative Coping); and attention to acting according to a plan rather than according to mood.

Evidence: a component analysis found that behavioural activation alone performed comparably to the full cognitive-behavioural package for depression (Jacobson et al., 1996). In a randomised placebo-controlled trial of 241 adults with major depression, among the more severely depressed participants behavioural activation performed comparably to antidepressant medication and both outperformed cognitive therapy (Dimidjian et al., 2006). The COBRA trial found behavioural activation delivered by junior mental health workers non-inferior to CBT delivered by qualified therapists, with a mean difference of 0.1 PHQ-9 points (95% CI -1.3 to 1.5), and lower cost (Richards et al., 2016, Lancet). NICE lists behavioural activation among the recommended options for less severe and more severe depression in adults (NICE guideline NG222, 2022).

The central verbal move in BA is outside-in rather than inside-out.

> "I want to be honest about the order of operations here. We are not going to wait until you feel like doing things and then do them. We're going to do them at the times we plan, and check what happens to the mood afterwards. The feeling tends to follow the action, and it usually arrives late."

On rumination as behaviour:

> "When you were sitting on the bed going over the conversation, what was that doing for you in the moment? I don't mean was it useful in the long run. I mean what did it get you right then."

Contraindications and misapplications. BA fails when the schedule is set from the clinician's idea of a good life rather than the client's values, producing a list of chores. It fails when the first step is too large, because a failed assignment confirms the depressive prediction. It fails when the clinician does not do the functional analysis and so schedules activities that the client is avoiding for a good reason, such as contact with an abusive family member. In severe depression with marked psychomotor retardation, the initial steps have to be very small, sometimes at the level of sitting up or opening a curtain, and setting normal-sized tasks at this stage is an error rather than an ambition.

heading: Exposure and response prevention: habituation versus inhibitory learning
text:
Exposure treats anxiety disorders and OCD as maintained by avoidance and by safety behaviours that prevent disconfirmation. The older account of the mechanism was habituation: sustained contact with the feared stimulus produces a decline in anxiety within and between sessions, and this decline is the therapeutic event. The current account is inhibitory learning: extinction does not erase the original fear association but creates a new, competing association, and the strength of the new learning depends on the degree to which the outcome violates the person's expectation (Craske, Treanor, Conway, Zbozinek and Vervliet, 2014). On this account within-session fear reduction is not the target and is a poor predictor of outcome.

The practical consequences of the shift are large. Response prevention is the component that distinguishes ERP for OCD from exposure alone. For PTSD, prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy carry recommendations in the 2023 VA/DoD clinical practice guideline alongside EMDR, and the guideline recommends manualised trauma-focused psychotherapies over pharmacotherapy.

Contraindications and misapplications. Exposure delivered without an explicit rationale that the client has bought into becomes coercion and produces dropout. Exposure conducted while the client uses covert safety behaviours produces no learning and teaches the client that exposure does not work. Exposure to a real current danger is not exposure, it is a risk. In active self-harm, unmanaged substance dependence, or acute suicidality, stabilisation takes precedence. Exposure where the feared outcome is a genuine possibility, such as a health-anxious client with an actual undiagnosed symptom, requires medical clarity first. Finally, the very common misapplication of asking a client to "sit with it until the anxiety halves" is a habituation-era instruction, and under the current model the more defensible instruction is to stay long enough to find out whether the prediction was right.
