heading: Building and running an exposure hierarchy: verbatim wording
text:
Setting up:

> "I want to be straight with you about what this involves, because I don't want you to agree to something you haven't seen the shape of. We are going to deliberately approach the things you've been avoiding, in an order you choose, and while we do that you'll drop the things you normally do to keep the anxiety down. It will be uncomfortable. It will not be a surprise. You'll always know what we're doing before we do it, and you can stop. What I won't do is talk you into feeling calm at the moment you're most anxious, because that's the part that keeps this going."

Eliciting the prediction:

> "Before you touch the handle, tell me what you think will happen. Be as specific as you can. Not 'something bad', but what, to whom, and how soon. And put a number on it. Out of a hundred, how likely?"

During:

> "You said seventy per cent that you'd be contaminated and that it would spread to your daughter by tonight. We're at eight minutes. What's your number for that prediction now?"

Blocking a compulsion, including the reassurance version:

> "You just asked me whether it's safe. I'm not going to answer that, and I want to say why rather than just refusing. If I answer, the relief you get will belong to me rather than to you, and the question will come back tomorrow. What I will do is stay here while you find out."

After:

> "What did you predict, and what actually happened? Not how anxious you felt. What happened."

Handling a client whose feared outcome cannot be disconfirmed within the session, such as a feared illness with a long latency:

> "We can't settle whether you'll get ill in the next ten years, and I'm not going to pretend we can. What we can test is whether you can hold the uncertainty for an hour without checking. That's the thing that's actually costing you."

heading: Acceptance and commitment therapy: the hexaflex and the moves it names
text:
ACT (Hayes, Strosahl and Wilson, 1999; 2012) targets psychological flexibility rather than symptom reduction. The claimed mechanism is that suffering is amplified by experiential avoidance and cognitive fusion, and that living in accordance with chosen values while making room for unwanted internal experience produces improved functioning even where symptom frequency does not change. Symptom reduction is treated as a possible by-product, not the goal, which is a genuine difference from standard CBT rather than a presentational one.

The hexaflex names six processes: acceptance, cognitive defusion, contact with the present moment, self-as-context, values, and committed action. The first four are the mindfulness and acceptance side, the last four, overlapping in the middle, are the commitment and behaviour change side.

Acceptance is willingness to have the internal experience without struggling against it. The clinical move is to shift the question from how to reduce the feeling to what the struggle costs.

> "How long have you been fighting the anxiety? And in that time, has it got smaller? I'm not asking to score a point. I'm asking whether the strategy has delivered, because if it has we should do more of it."

Defusion changes the relationship to a thought rather than its content. Techniques include prefacing ("I'm having the thought that..."), repetition of a word until it loses meaning, naming the mind as a separate speaker, and thanking the mind.

> "Try saying it as 'I'm noticing I'm having the thought that I'm a failure.' Say the two versions back to back and tell me if anything shifts in how much it grips."

Contact with the present moment is attentional flexibility, usually trained with brief in-session exercises rather than long meditations.

Self-as-context separates the observing self from the content observed.

> "You've been anxious, and calm, and furious, and bored, all in the last week. Who has been there for all of them?"

Values are chosen life directions, not goals. The clinician distinguishes them explicitly, because clients import goals.

> "Getting the promotion is a goal. You can succeed or fail at it, and then it's over. What I'm asking about is the direction underneath it. If the promotion never came, what would still be worth doing about the kind of colleague you want to be?"

Committed action is the behavioural half and looks similar to graded task assignment, with the difference that the assignment is linked to a value and the willingness to carry discomfort is made explicit.

> "So the move is to say the thing in Thursday's meeting. And the price of admission is that your chest will be tight and your voice may shake. Are you willing to take those along, if that's what it costs to speak up about work you care about?"

The creative hopelessness sequence opens many ACT courses. It is an inventory of everything the client has tried to control the internal experience, followed by a shared assessment of what it has cost. It is done with warmth or not at all, because delivered coldly it lands as an accusation of failure.

heading: ACT evidence, limits and misapplications
text:
Evidence: a meta-analysis of 39 randomised controlled trials with 1,821 patients found ACT superior to control conditions with Hedges' g = 0.57 at post-treatment, and specifically g = 0.82 versus waitlist, 0.51 versus psychological placebo, and 0.64 versus treatment as usual (A-Tjak et al., 2015, Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics). A more sceptical review of 60 RCTs with 4,234 participants found a mean effect size of 0.42 across comparisons and a small, non-significant effect of 0.16 when ACT was compared with other cognitive or behavioural treatments, and concluded ACT was not yet well established for any disorder, probably efficacious for chronic pain and tinnitus, and possibly efficacious for depression, psychotic symptoms, OCD, mixed anxiety, drug abuse and work stress (Öst, 2014, Behaviour Research and Therapy). Both should be held at once: ACT clearly beats doing nothing, and the case that it beats CBT specifically is weak.

Misapplications. The largest is using acceptance language to talk a client out of changing a changeable situation. Acceptance is for internal experience, not for circumstances that can and should be altered. Telling someone in an unsafe workplace or a violent relationship to make room for the feeling and move toward their values is a serious clinical error.

The second is using defusion as suppression. "Just notice the thought and let it go" delivered as an instruction to stop having the thought is fusion in acceptance costume, and clients detect it.

The third is values work conducted before the person has any behavioural traction, which can produce a vivid picture of a life they are not living and a sharp increase in shame.

The fourth is ACT used to avoid exposure. Where a specific phobia or OCD indicates ERP, running values and defusion work instead is a downgrade in the strength of the intervention, and the clinician should know that is the trade being made.

heading: Dialectical behaviour therapy: structure, stance and evidence
text:
DBT (Linehan, 1993; Linehan, 2015) was developed for chronically suicidal and self-harming women meeting criteria for borderline personality disorder. The theory is biosocial: an emotionally vulnerable temperament transacting over time with an invalidating environment produces pervasive emotion dysregulation, and the behaviours that bring people to services are largely attempts to regulate or escape unbearable affect.

Standard DBT is a programme, not a technique. It has four components: individual therapy, skills group, telephone coaching between sessions, and a therapist consultation team. The consultation team is a treatment component, not supervision as an optional extra, and a service delivering the first three without the fourth is not delivering standard DBT.

Treatment is organised by a target hierarchy applied in order within each session: life-threatening behaviours first, then therapy-interfering behaviours (by either party), then quality-of-life-interfering behaviours, then skills acquisition. Diary cards track targets between sessions and set the agenda.

The four skills modules are mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness. Distress tolerance skills are explicitly crisis survival tools that do not solve the problem, and clients should be told so rather than led to expect resolution.

The dialectical stance is the balance between acceptance and change, held simultaneously rather than alternated.

> "Two things are both true. You did the best you could with what you had on Tuesday. And Tuesday cannot happen again, and we have to build something different. I'm not going to give up either half of that."

Evidence: in a two-year randomised controlled trial of 101 women with recent suicidal and self-injurious behaviour, DBT produced better outcomes than community treatment by non-behavioural experts across most target areas, and DBT participants were half as likely to make a suicide attempt (Linehan et al., 2006, Archives of General Psychiatry). NICE recommends that a comprehensive DBT programme be considered for women with borderline personality disorder for whom reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority, and advises against brief psychological interventions of less than three months' duration for borderline personality disorder (NICE guideline CG78, 2009).

Misapplications. "DBT skills" delivered as a psychoeducation group with no individual therapy, no coaching and no consultation team is a common service adaptation, and it should be described as skills training rather than DBT. Validation used without any change demand produces a warm therapy that does not move. Change demand without validation produces dropout, and in this population dropout has consequences. Diary cards used as compliance monitoring rather than as data for chain analysis convert the client into a defendant.

heading: DBT chain analysis: the full sequence with wording
text:
Behavioural chain analysis is a minute-by-minute reconstruction of a single target behaviour, done to locate the specific points where a different response was possible. It is done on one episode, not on a pattern, and specificity is the whole value of it.

The components in order: the target behaviour defined precisely; vulnerability factors present beforehand; the prompting event, which should be something a camera could have recorded; each link between prompt and behaviour, broken into thoughts, emotions, body sensations, urges and actions; the consequences, short-term and long-term, for the client and for others; then solution analysis, which installs an alternative response at specific links; then a prevention plan for the vulnerability factors, repair of any damage done, and a concrete commitment.

> Clinician: "Let's start at the behaviour and work backwards. On Thursday, what exactly did you do?"
> Client: "I cut."
> Clinician: "Where, when, with what, and for how long? I know this is unpleasant to go over in detail. The detail is where the handholds are."
> Client: "Bathroom, about eleven at night, the blade from the pencil sharpener. Maybe five minutes."
> Clinician: "What was going on before Thursday that made you more vulnerable? Sleep, food, illness, alcohol, anything left over from earlier in the week?"
> Client: "I hadn't slept properly since Monday and I'd skipped lunch two days running."
> Clinician: "So we start Thursday already low on resources. Now the prompting event. What was the first thing that happened, the thing a camera would have caught?"
> Client: "My sister's message came through at nine forty. It said 'we'll talk about it when you're less dramatic.'"
> Clinician: "Nine forty, message arrives. What's the very next thing, in your body or your head?"

The clinician continues link by link, resisting summaries and jumps. When the client says "and then I just did it", the clinician slows down rather than accepting the compression:

> "I want to slow down right there, because 'I just did it' has about ten minutes inside it. You put the phone down. What happened next?"

Solution analysis:

> "We've got seven or eight places where the chain could have gone somewhere else. Let's take the one where you were standing in the kitchen with the urge at about a six. That's earlier than we usually catch it. What skill could have gone in right there? Not what should have. What actually could have, at a six, with no sleep."

Chain analysis is not punishment and should not feel like one. If the client experiences it as a tribunal, the therapy has drifted, and the correction is usually more validation earlier in the chain, not less detail.

heading: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, compassion-focused therapy and metacognitive therapy
text:
MBCT (Segal, Williams and Teasdale, 2002) was designed for relapse prevention in recurrent depression. The claimed mechanism is decentring: attention training in an eight-week group format lets a person recognise the early re-activation of depressive thinking and disengage from rumination before it escalates. Teasdale et al. (2000) found relapse prevention effects concentrated in participants with three or more previous episodes. The PREVENT trial randomised 424 patients to MBCT with antidepressant tapering support or to maintenance antidepressants and found no difference in time to relapse over 24 months (hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.18, p = 0.43), which supports MBCT as an alternative for people who want to come off medication rather than as a superior option (Kuyken et al., 2015, Lancet). MBCT is not designed as an acute treatment for a current severe episode, and running it as one is the standard misapplication. Intensive mindfulness practice can also destabilise people with dissociative presentations or acute trauma symptoms, and screening for that is part of group selection.

CFT (Gilbert, 2009, 2010) was developed for people whose central problem is shame and self-attack, and specifically for those who can generate an alternative thought but feel no relief from it. The model proposes three interacting affect regulation systems: threat and protection, drive and resource-seeking, and affiliation and soothing. The claimed mechanism is that the soothing system is underdeveloped in people with hostile or neglectful early environments, so cognitive change lands on threat-toned processing and does not soothe. Techniques include compassionate mind training, soothing rhythm breathing, imagery of a compassionate other or compassionate self, chair work between the self-critic and the criticised self, and letter writing from a compassionate perspective. A systematic review and meta-analysis of CFT with clinical populations reports benefits for self-criticism, shame and self-compassion, with the caveat that trials are generally small and heterogeneous (systematic review and meta-analysis of CFT effectiveness in clinical populations, Journal of Affective Disorders, 2023; the specific author list should be confirmed at the source before quoting) [UNVERIFIED as to authorship and pooled effect size]. A known clinical phenomenon is fear of compassion: some clients respond to compassionate imagery with grief, anger or increased threat, and this is expected in the model rather than a sign the technique failed.

Metacognitive therapy (Wells, 2009) derives from the self-regulatory executive function model (Wells and Matthews, 1994). The claimed mechanism is that psychopathology is maintained by the cognitive attentional syndrome, meaning perseverative worry and rumination, threat monitoring, and unhelpful coping, and that this is driven by metacognitive beliefs about thinking rather than by the content of thoughts. MCT therefore does not challenge the content of negative thoughts at all, which distinguishes it sharply from Beckian work. Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, compassion-focused therapy and metacognitive therapy

MBCT is not designed as an acute treatment for a current severe episode, and running it as one is the standard misapplication. Intensive mindfulness practice can also destabilise people with dissociative presentations or acute trauma symptoms, and screening for that is part of group selection.

heading: Contraindications and failure modes across the CBT family
text:
Some cautions apply across the whole family and should be checked before any protocol starts.

Acute risk overrides protocol. Active suicidal intent, unmanaged self-harm, or an unsafe living situation moves the work to risk management and stabilisation. Starting trauma processing or intensive exposure with a person who has no means of down-regulating afterwards, and no support until the next appointment, is the most consequential error in this family.

Unmanaged substance dependence undermines learning-based treatments, because the substance functions as the avoidance and blocks the new learning. This does not mean abstinence is a precondition for all work, but it does mean the clinician should know what the substance is doing in the maintenance cycle.

Cognitive load matters. Protocols with written homework, thought records and self-monitoring assume literacy, working memory and time. Acquired brain injury, active psychosis, severe depression with concentration impairment, and intellectual disability all require adaptation, and unadapted protocols produce a record of non-compliance that gets attributed to the client.

Homework non-completion is data, not a moral failure. The first hypothesis should be that the task was too large, insufficiently specific, or not connected to anything the client cares about. The second is that the rationale was not shared. The third is a rupture in the alliance that the client is expressing behaviourally rather than verbally.

Recognising that the model is wrong. If a client is completing tasks, engaging in session, and not improving after six to eight sessions, the formulation is the first suspect, not the client's motivation. Common formulation errors: treating a trauma presentation as an anxiety disorder, treating a bipolar depression as unipolar, missing an eating disorder that is doing the emotion regulation work, missing autism where the presenting anxiety is a consequence of unsupported sensory and social demand, and missing an ongoing situation such as bullying, debt, violence or insecure immigration status where the appropriate intervention is practical rather than psychological.

Protocol fidelity and responsiveness both matter, and clinicians err in both directions. Rigid adherence that ignores what happened in the client's week produces disengagement. Endless flexibility that never completes a technique produces a supportive relationship with no mechanism of change. The workable position is to keep the mechanism constant and vary the delivery.

heading: Person-centred therapy: Rogers' six conditions and what they actually require
text:
Rogers (1957) specified six conditions he held to be necessary and sufficient for therapeutic personality change: two persons are in psychological contact; the client is in a state of incongruence, being vulnerable or anxious; the therapist is congruent or integrated in the relationship; the therapist experiences unconditional positive regard for the client; the therapist experiences empathic understanding of the client's internal frame of reference and endeavours to communicate this; and this communication is achieved to at least a minimal degree. Conditions three, four and five are the ones usually named as the core conditions, and condition six is the one most often forgotten, since it makes the client's perception the test rather than the therapist's intention.

The claimed mechanism is the actualising tendency. Rogers held that the organism moves toward growth when the conditions permit it, and that psychological distress arises from conditions of worth, meaning the introjected requirement to be a certain way in order to be valued. Removing conditions of worth in the therapy relationship allows self-experience that was previously denied or distorted to be symbolised accurately, which reduces incongruence between self-concept and experience.

Congruence is the most misread condition. It does not mean saying whatever the therapist feels. It means the therapist's inner experience, awareness of it, and communication are aligned, and that the therapist is not presenting a professional facade. In practice, congruence usually appears as the absence of false warmth rather than as disclosure.

Unconditional positive regard does not mean approval of behaviour. It means the therapist's regard does not fluctuate with what the client reports.

Evidence: therapist empathy is a robust predictor of outcome. A meta-analysis of 82 independent samples and 6,138 clients found a mean weighted r of .28 (95% CI .23 to .33, equivalent to d = .58), with the association holding across theoretical orientations, treatment formats and client problems (Elliott, Bohart, Watson and Murphy, 2018, Psychotherapy). This is evidence that empathy matters in all therapies, not evidence that the conditions are sufficient on their own, and Rogers' sufficiency claim remains contested.

Limits. Person-centred therapy conducted as pure non-directiveness underperforms in presentations where the maintaining mechanism is behavioural, notably OCD, specific phobia and eating disorders, where a purely reflective stance can inadvertently accommodate avoidance. It is also poorly suited as a stand-alone approach where risk is active and containment is required. The most common misapplication in the other direction is reflection used as a technique divorced from actual regard, which clients experience as parroting.

> Client: "I don't even know why I'm here. It all seems pointless."
> Poor: "It sounds like you're feeling hopeless. Have you thought about what might help?"
> Better: "There's something in the way you said that, like even coming here is one more thing that won't make a difference. And you came anyway."

heading: Emotion-focused therapy: emotion schemes, markers and task guidance
text:
Emotion-focused therapy (Greenberg, Rice and Elliott, 1993; Greenberg, 2011) sits inside the humanistic tradition but is process-directive. The therapist is non-directive about content and highly directive about process, which is the defining move of the model.

The theory distinguishes four kinds of emotional experience. Primary adaptive emotions are direct, useful responses to the situation, such as anger at violation or sadness at loss, and the aim is to access and use them. Primary maladaptive emotions are direct responses that are no longer useful, typically core shame or the fear of abandonment learned early, and the aim is to transform them rather than regulate them away. Secondary emotions are reactions to a primary emotion, such as anger covering hurt, and the aim is to get past them to what they cover. Instrumental emotions are expressed to influence others and the aim is to make their function explicit.

The central change principle is that maladaptive emotion is changed by another emotion rather than by reason. Accessing an adaptive emotion, usually assertive anger or self-compassion or grief, transforms a maladaptive core state such as shame or fear.

EFT is organised by markers. The therapist listens for a specific in-session indicator and offers the task that fits it. Self-critical split, meaning the client reports being at war with themselves, indicates two-chair dialogue. Unfinished business with a significant other indicates empty-chair work. An unclear felt sense, where the client knows something is wrong but cannot name it, indicates focusing. A problematic reaction point, where the client's reaction surprised them, indicates systematic evocative unfolding. A self-interruptive split, where the client blocks their own emotion, indicates two-chair enactment of the blocking.

Evidence: EFT has an outcome literature for depression and for interpersonal injury resolution, with trials generally supporting equivalence to CBT for depression and some advantage on interpersonal and self-esteem outcomes. Precise pooled effect sizes vary across reviews and should be checked against the specific meta-analysis being cited before quoting a number [UNVERIFIED as to any single canonical figure].

Limits and misapplications. Chair work run with a client who cannot regulate afterwards is the main risk, and it is a real one, because the tasks are designed to raise arousal. Doing chairwork in a single session with no continuity is unsafe. EFT is contraindicated as an early intervention in acute psychosis and requires substantial adaptation where dissociation is present. Offering a task without the marker present produces a mechanical enactment with no affective engagement, which is the most common training error.

heading: EFT chairwork: verbatim wording for two-chair and empty-chair
text:
Two-chair work for a self-critical split. The client sits in one chair as the critic and speaks to the self in the other chair, then swaps and responds from the criticised self. The therapist keeps the two voices separated, keeps the language in the second person, and pulls for specificity and for feeling.

> Clinician: "You said a moment ago that part of you is disgusted with you. I'd like to make that concrete rather than talk about it. Would you be willing to sit here and say that to yourself, as if you were sitting over there?"
> Client (as critic): "You're pathetic. You had one thing to do."
> Clinician: "Say it again, and tell them what you want them to feel."
> Client (as critic): "You're pathetic. You should be ashamed."
> Clinician: "Now come over here. What happens in you when you hear that?"
> Client (as self): "My chest goes tight. I want to disappear."
> Clinician: "Stay with the tight chest. Tell them what it does to you when they speak to you like that. Not what you think about it. What it does."
> Client: "It makes me want to give up entirely."
> Clinician: "Can you tell them that? 'When you say that to me, I want to give up.'"

The therapeutic target is a softening in the critic, which usually appears as the critic expressing fear or need rather than contempt, and an assertive or self-compassionate response from the criticised self. The therapist listens for these and does not push past them.

Empty-chair work for unfinished business. The client addresses an absent or deceased figure.

> Clinician: "Put your father in that chair. Not the man now, the man as he was when you were eleven. What do you see?"
> Client: "He's not looking at me."
> Clinician: "Tell him what it was like that he wasn't looking at you."
> Client: "I don't know if I can."
> Clinician: "That's honest. Can you tell him that? 'I don't know if I can say this to you.'"

The therapist follows arousal, slows the pace when affect rises, and does not require a resolution. Forced forgiveness is a serious error in this work: the aim is that the client accesses and expresses the previously blocked primary emotion, and holds the other accountable or lets go, and either outcome is acceptable.

Ending the task matters as much as starting it. The therapist brings the client back to their own chair, out of the enactment, and spends time on what just happened before the session closes.

> "Come back over here and take a breath. That was a lot. Before we finish, what stands out from what you just did?"

heading: Existential therapy: the givens, the stance, the evidence
text:
Existential therapy is a stance and a set of concerns more than a technique set. Yalom (1980) organised it around four ultimate concerns: death, freedom and the responsibility that accompanies it, existential isolation, and meaninglessness. Frankl's logotherapy centres meaning specifically, developed from his account of survival in the camps. The claimed mechanism is that avoidance of these givens generates symptoms, and that confronting them directly, with the therapist as fellow traveller rather than expert, permits an authentic reorganisation of how the person lives.

Technique is deliberately thin. The therapist works in the present, attends to how the client is avoiding choice, names responsibility without blame, and uses the relationship as a live instance of connection in the face of isolation. There is little homework and no protocol.

> "You've described this as something that happened to you. I want to put a harder question. What are you choosing, by not deciding?"

> "You said you have no options. I don't think that's true, and I don't think you think it is either. I think you have options you don't want, and that's a different kind of terrible."

Evidence: the general existential literature is thin on randomised trials. The exception is meaning-centred psychotherapy for existential distress in advanced cancer, which has been tested in randomised controlled trials. A trial randomising 253 patients with advanced cancer to eight-session manualised meaning-centred group psychotherapy or supportive group psychotherapy supported the efficacy of the meaning-centred condition for psychological and existential distress, and a subsequent trial of individual meaning-centred psychotherapy found small to moderate effects versus usual care and smaller effects versus supportive psychotherapy (Breitbart et al., 2015; Breitbart et al., 2018, Cancer). Dignity therapy and life review interventions have a parallel small literature in palliative settings.

Limits. Existential work assumes a client with enough cognitive and affective capacity to tolerate uncertainty and abstraction. It is not a first-line approach for acute crisis, for active psychosis, or for a person who needs symptom relief in order to function this week. Its most common misapplication is philosophical conversation that is engaging for both parties and changes nothing, which is difficult to detect because both people enjoy it. The corrective is to check whether anything in the client's actual life has changed.

heading: Psychodynamic therapy: unconscious process, defence, transference and the frame
text:
Contemporary psychodynamic therapy claims that current difficulties are shaped by patterns formed in early relationships, that much of this operates outside awareness, and that these patterns are enacted in the therapy relationship where they can be observed live and revised. The mechanism is insight combined with corrective relational experience, with the field increasingly emphasising the second over the first.

Shedler's (2010) summary of distinctive features is a useful working list: focus on affect and expression of emotion, exploration of attempts to avoid distressing thoughts and feelings, identification of recurring themes and patterns, discussion of past experience, focus on interpersonal relations, focus on the therapy relationship, and exploration of fantasy life.

Defence is understood functionally: a defence is what a person does to avoid an unbearable feeling. The clinician names the defence before naming the feeling, because interpreting the feeling while the defence is operating produces intellectual agreement without contact. Common defences to recognise in transcript: intellectualisation (talking about feelings in the abstract), rationalisation, displacement, projection, reaction formation, denial, isolation of affect (recounting a distressing event with no emotional tone), somatisation, and acting out.

Transference is the client's experience of the therapist patterned by earlier relationships. Countertransference is the therapist's response, and modern usage treats it as information about the client's relational world rather than only as a therapist problem. The frame is the set of arrangements around the therapy, time, fee, boundaries, and the frame is treated as clinically meaningful, so that consistent lateness or the request to extend a session becomes material rather than administration.

Evidence: a Cochrane review of short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy for common mental disorders included 23 studies with 1,431 randomised patients and found significant improvement versus controls, with fixed-effects standardised mean differences in the short term of -0.42 (95% CI -0.58 to -0.27) for general psychiatric symptoms, -0.47 (95% CI -0.61 to -0.33) for depressive symptoms, -0.46 (95% CI -0.64 to -0.27) for anxiety, and -0.67 (95% CI -0.85 to -0.48) for somatic symptoms, with gains generally maintained at medium and long-term follow-up. The authors concluded that STPP "shows promise, with modest to moderate, often sustained gains", and cautioned that few studies contributed to each category, that heterogeneity was significant, and that results were not always maintained in sensitivity analyses (Abbass, Hancock, Henderson and Kisely, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2006, Issue 4, CD004687).

Leichsenring and Rabung's (2004) meta-analysis reported large pre-post effect sizes for STPP of 1.39 for target problems, 0.90 for general psychiatric symptoms and 0.80 for social functioning, increasing at follow-up. Pre-post effect sizes are not the same as controlled between-group effects and should not be compared with the Cochrane figures above. Their later meta-analysis of long-term psychodynamic psychotherapy in complex disorders has been the subject of substantial methodological criticism, and claims resting on it should be qualified.

NICE lists short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy among the options for less severe depression in adults, and among the psychological treatments to be considered in combination with an antidepressant for depression with a coexisting personality disorder diagnosis (NICE guideline NG222, 2022).

Psychodynamic therapy: unconscious process, defence, transference and the frame

Contemporary psychodynamic therapy claims that current difficulties are shaped by patterns formed in early relationships, that much of this operates outside awareness, and that these patterns are enacted in the therapy relationship where they can be observed live and revised. The mechanism is insight combined with corrective relational experience, with the field increasingly emphasising the second over the first.

Shedler's (2010) summary of distinctive features is a useful working list: focus on affect and expression of emotion, exploration of attempts to avoid distressing thoughts and feelings, identification of recurring themes and patterns, discussion of past experience, focus on interpersonal relations, focus on the therapy relationship, and exploration of fantasy life.

Defence is understood functionally: a defence is what a person does to avoid an unbearable feeling. The clinician names the defence before naming the feeling, because interpreting the feeling while the defence is operating produces intellectual agreement without contact. heading: Malan's triangles and short-term dynamic work
text:
Malan's two triangles are the working map of short-term dynamic therapy, refined in Davanloo's intensive short-term dynamic psychotherapy (ISTDP).

The triangle of conflict has three corners: defence, anxiety, and hidden feeling or impulse. The hidden feeling presses toward awareness, which generates anxiety, which activates a defence. The clinician's job is to move from defence, through anxiety, to feeling. Attempting to reach the feeling without addressing the defence produces resistance.

The triangle of person has three corners: the therapist, current or recent others, and past figures, usually parents. The clinician tracks the same conflict as it appears in each. Malan's formulation is that a full interpretation links a corner of the triangle of conflict across corners of the triangle of person.

In ISTDP specifically the clinician also tracks anxiety pathways in the body, distinguishing striated muscle tension (which indicates the client can tolerate the rising feeling), smooth muscle activation such as gut symptoms or migraine, and cognitive-perceptual disruption such as blurred vision or dissociation. The last two indicate the clinician should regulate the pace down rather than press further, and treating all anxiety as workable is the characteristic error in this method.

> Defence identification: "I notice that when I ask what you felt, you tell me what you thought. That happens every time we get close. Do you see it too?"

> Defence clarification with cost: "That vagueness is protecting you from something. It's also the reason you can't get anywhere with this on your own. What do you want to do with it?"

> Anxiety regulation: "Let's slow down. Where are you feeling this in your body right now?"

> Linking across the triangle of person: "You said you couldn't bring it up with your manager because she'd think you were difficult. That's what you said about your mother two weeks ago. And I'd add a third: you waited four sessions to tell me the times don't work for you."

heading: Interpretation: how it is worded and when to withhold it
text:
An interpretation proposes a meaning the client has not stated. It is the highest-risk verbal act in dynamic work, because a premature or wrong interpretation can be experienced as an accusation or as the therapist knowing the client better than the client knows themselves.

Rules of wording. Offer it tentatively and leave room for rejection. Ground it in material the client provided in this session or a recent one. Make it short. Stop after it and wait rather than elaborating. Treat disagreement as data about the interpretation as well as about the client, not automatically as resistance.

> Weak: "You're angry with me because I represent your father."
> Better: "I want to try something out and you should tell me if it doesn't fit. When I said we'd need to end on time, something changed in the room. I wondered if it felt like being managed rather than met, which is close to what you've described about home."

The distinction that matters most in practice is between an interpretation and an observation. Observations are lower-risk and usually more useful early: they describe something visible without asserting a cause.

> Observation: "You smiled when you said that, and what you said wasn't funny."
> Interpretation: "I think the smile is there to make it easier for me to hear, so I won't be burdened by it."

When not to interpret. When the alliance is not established. When the client is in acute crisis and needs containment. When the interpretation would primarily demonstrate the therapist's cleverness. When the client is actively dissociating, since insight cannot be integrated in that state. When the material is a current external threat, where interpreting the client's response can obscure the reality of the danger. In brief work with a concrete goal, interpretation should be sparse and tied to the focus.

Transference interpretation specifically should be used sparingly and is dose-sensitive. Clients with fragile ego strength or low reflective capacity generally do worse with frequent transference interpretation, and supportive-expressive work is better indicated for them.

heading: Attachment-based work
text:
Attachment theory (Bowlby, 1969; Ainsworth) proposes internal working models of self and other formed in early caregiving that shape later expectation and regulation. The clinical translation across models is that the therapist functions as a temporary secure base, and that reliability, repair and affect regulation in the relationship are the active ingredients rather than content.

Common clinical categories, used descriptively rather than diagnostically: secure, anxious-preoccupied, avoidant-dismissing, and disorganised. The practical value is in predicting how the person will use the therapy. A preoccupied presentation tends to produce high affect, difficulty ending sessions, and distress at breaks. A dismissing presentation tends to produce minimised affect, brief answers, and reports that everything is fine, and the risk is that the therapist mistakes this for progress. A disorganised presentation tends to produce approach and withdrawal in the same session, and the therapist's task is predictability rather than depth.

Attachment-based family therapy (ABFT) is the manualised model with the strongest trial support in this group. It has five tasks: relational reframe, adolescent alliance, parent alliance, attachment repair, and promoting autonomy. In a randomised trial of 66 suicidal adolescents comparing ABFT with enhanced usual care over three months, ABFT produced significantly greater change in self-reported suicidal ideation with an effect size of 0.97, with 87% versus 51.7% meeting clinical recovery criteria at post-treatment and 70% versus 34.6% at follow-up (Diamond et al., 2010). A later trial of 129 suicidal adolescents comparing ABFT with family-enhanced non-directive supportive therapy found no significant between-group difference in rate of change in suicidal ideation (Diamond et al., 2019), which is the honest qualifier on the earlier result: ABFT beats usual care clearly, and beats a well-delivered supportive alternative less clearly.

Relational reframe wording, which shifts the target from the adolescent's symptom to the relationship:

> "I want to suggest something different from what you came in expecting. Rather than working on getting Maya to stop, I want to work on why Maya doesn't come to you when she's in that much pain. Because if she could, a lot of this would look different. Would you be willing to look at that with me?"

Limits. Attachment language is often used loosely as personality description. Adult attachment classifications from research instruments do not transfer cleanly to clinical labelling, and telling a client they are "an avoidant" is not a clinical intervention. Attachment-informed work also cannot substitute for trauma processing or for behavioural treatment where those are indicated.

heading: Internal Family Systems and parts work
text:
IFS (Schwartz, 1995) holds that the mind is naturally multiple, that all parts have positive intent, and that beneath the parts is a Self characterised by qualities including calm, curiosity, compassion and clarity. Parts are grouped into exiles, which carry pain and are kept out of awareness; managers, which run the person's life pre-emptively to keep exiles down; and firefighters, which act reactively and often destructively when an exile breaks through, covering behaviours such as bingeing, substance use, self-harm and dissociation. The claimed mechanism is unburdening: with Self-leadership established, protective parts give permission to access exiles, the exile's burden is witnessed and released, and protectors take up new roles.

The characteristic sequence is often taught as six steps: find the part, focus on it, flesh it out, feel toward it, befriend it, and explore its fears. Access to Self is checked by asking how the client feels toward the part, and any answer other than curiosity or compassion indicates another part is present and blended.

> Clinician: "Where do you notice the part that wants to shut this down?"
> Client: "It's like a wall across my chest."
> Clinician: "How do you feel toward the wall?"
> Client: "Frustrated. I want it gone."
> Clinician: "That frustration is another part. Can we ask it to give us a little space, just so we can get to know the wall? It doesn't have to leave. It can watch."

> Asking a protector its fear: "If it didn't do that job any more, what does it think would happen?"

Evidence: IFS was listed on the SAMHSA National Registry of Evidence-Based Programs and Practices in 2015, rated effective for improving general functioning and well-being and promising for depression and anxiety. The registry has since been discontinued, which limits how much weight the listing carries. A pilot effectiveness study of 17 adults with PTSD and multiple childhood traumas, receiving sixteen 90-minute IFS sessions, reported reductions in PTSD symptoms, but it was an uncontrolled feasibility study rather than a randomised trial (Hodgdon et al., 2021). The accurate statement is that IFS is promising and under-tested, not that it is an established treatment for PTSD.

Limits. Parts language can reify dissociation in clients with dissociative identity disorder, where the standard phase-based approach and specialist consultation are indicated rather than enthusiastic parts work. Approaching exiles before protectors have consented is the model's own named error and produces backlash, typically an escalation in firefighter behaviour after the session.

heading: Narrative therapy
text:
Narrative therapy (White and Epston, 1990) holds that people live by stories, that problem-saturated dominant stories obscure exceptions, and that identity is socially and politically constructed rather than internal. The claimed mechanism is that separating the person from the problem and thickening an alternative story changes what the person believes is possible and available.

Techniques. Externalising conversations relocate the problem outside the person and give it a name, often the client's own. Mapping the effects of the problem across life domains. Identifying unique outcomes, meaning occasions when the problem did not win. Re-authoring conversations that build the alternative story across time. Re-membering conversations that recruit significant figures into the preferred identity. Definitional ceremony and outsider witness practices, in which others reflect on what they heard. Therapeutic documents and letters.

> Externalising: "How long has the Worry been running the mornings? And when it does that, what does it tell you about yourself?"

> Mapping effects: "What has the Worry cost you at work? What has it cost between you and Ines?"

> Unique outcome: "On Tuesday you went anyway. That's the first time in a month the Worry didn't get the last word. How did you do that?"

> Re-authoring: "What does that tell us about what you're committed to, that the Worry hasn't been able to take?"

Evidence: the outcome literature is small and methodologically weak. A systematic review screening 461 studies from 1995 to 2021 found 17 meeting inclusion criteria, and reviewers characterise the supporting studies as mostly small, uncontrolled and single-site. Later pooled analyses report large effects but rate the certainty of the evidence as very low, because of risk of bias and lack of blinding. Narrative therapy should be described as promising and under-evidenced rather than established.

Limits. Externalising can minimise responsibility where accountability is the clinical issue, notably in work with people who have used violence, and narrative practitioners working in that field explicitly restructure the method to avoid it. Externalising is also poorly suited to presentations where the mechanism is physiological or behavioural and where naming the problem does not change the contingencies.

heading: Solution-focused brief therapy
text:
SFBT (de Shazer, Berg) is built on a deliberate refusal to analyse the problem. The premise is that problem talk and solution talk are different conversations, that change is constant, and that solutions do not have to be logically related to problems. The claimed mechanism is that attention to exceptions and to a described preferred future amplifies existing competence and produces small changes that cascade.

Core techniques with wording:

> Miracle question: "Suppose tonight, while you're asleep, a miracle happens and the problem that brought you here is solved. You don't know it happened because you were asleep. What's the first small thing you'd notice tomorrow morning that would tell you something was different?"

> Exception-finding: "When was the last time this was even slightly less of a problem? What was different about that day?"

> Scaling: "On a scale of nought to ten, where ten is the day after the miracle and nought is the worst it's been, where are you today?" followed by "What's keeping you at a four rather than a two?" and "What would a five look like? Not a ten. A five."

> Coping question, used when the client is at the bottom of the scale: "Given everything you've described, how have you managed to keep going at all this week?"

> Compliment and task: "I'm struck that you got yourself here on a day like this. Between now and next time, I'd like you to notice anything that happens that you'd want to continue."

Evidence: a systematic review of 43 randomised and quasi-experimental studies found 32 (74%) reporting significant positive benefit and 10 (23%) reporting positive trends, with the strongest evidence in adult depression where four studies found SFBT comparable to established alternative treatments, and with three studies finding SFBT used fewer sessions than comparison therapies (Gingerich and Peterson, 2013, Research on Social Work Practice).

Limits and misapplications. SFBT's refusal to explore the problem becomes a liability where risk, trauma or abuse is present and needs to be assessed rather than reframed. Scaling a client who has just disclosed sexual assault is a serious failure of fit. SFBT is also poorly suited where a specific evidence-based protocol is indicated, such as ERP for OCD. The most common misapplication is the miracle question deployed on a client in acute despair, which reads as dismissive; the coping question exists precisely for that situation and should be used instead.

heading: Systemic and family therapy
text:
Systemic therapy treats the problem as located in patterns of interaction rather than in an individual, and treats the presenting person as the identified patient rather than the site of pathology. Circular causality replaces linear causality: A's behaviour maintains B's behaviour which maintains A's.

The traditions differ. heading: The decision inputs: what actually determines the choice
text:
Modality selection is not a lookup from diagnosis to therapy. Five inputs combine.

The presentation and its maintaining mechanism. The formulation question is what keeps this going now, not what caused it. Avoidance maintaining anxiety indicates exposure. Withdrawal and loss of reinforcement maintaining depression indicates behavioural activation. Perseverative thinking maintaining distress indicates metacognitive or rumination-focused work. Interpersonal patterns maintaining isolation indicate interpersonal or dynamic work. Family interaction maintaining a young person's restriction indicates family therapy. Two clients with the same diagnosis can have different maintaining mechanisms and should get different treatments.

Guideline standing. Where a guideline recommends a specific treatment for a specific presentation, departing from it requires a documented reason. This is both a clinical and a governance matter.

Risk and stability. Acute risk, unstable housing, active dependence, or an ongoing threat move the question from which therapy to what has to be in place first.

Client preference and prior experience. Preference predicts engagement, and engagement predicts outcome. A client who has already failed a competently delivered course of CBT and disliked it should not be offered the same thing again by default.

Capacity and context. Session number available, the client's cognitive and literacy profile, language, whether they have privacy for online sessions, whether they can do between-session tasks, whether interpreters are needed, whether the therapy is time-limited by the service.

A sixth input is what the clinician can actually deliver competently. Referring on is a clinical decision, not an admission of failure, and delivering a poor imitation of a specialist treatment is worse than referring.

> "There are two or three reasonable ways to work with this, and they feel quite different in the room. I'd like to describe them and hear which one you'd actually turn up for, because that matters more than which one the research prefers by a nose."

heading: Presentation-to-modality matching: what the guidelines actually say
text:
Depression in adults. NICE recommends a menu of options ordered by the committee, differing for less severe and more severe depression, with individual CBT and behavioural activation among the options in both, alongside guided self-help, group interventions, interpersonal psychotherapy, short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy, counselling and antidepressant medication depending on severity and preference. For depression with a coexisting personality disorder diagnosis, a combination of an antidepressant and a psychological treatment such as behavioural activation, CBT, interpersonal psychotherapy or short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy should be considered. Behavioural couples therapy appears as an option where the relationship contributes to maintenance (NICE guideline NG222, 2022).

PTSD. Trauma-focused CBT should be offered to adults with a diagnosis or clinically important symptoms of PTSD presenting more than one month after the traumatic event. EMDR should be offered to adults presenting more than three months after a non-combat-related trauma. For children and young people aged 7 to 17, EMDR should be considered only where they do not respond to or engage with trauma-focused CBT (NICE guideline NG116, 2018). The 2023 VA/DoD clinical practice guideline recommends prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy or EMDR, recommends manualised psychotherapy over pharmacotherapy, and recommends against benzodiazepines and cannabis products.

OCD. Treatment intensity is matched to functional impairment. Low-intensity psychological treatment including exposure and response prevention, up to 10 therapist hours, should be offered where impairment is mild or the person prefers a low-intensity approach, with more intensive CBT including ERP for greater impairment. For obsessive thoughts without overt compulsions, CBT including exposure to the thoughts and prevention of mental rituals and neutralising should be considered. Cognitive therapy adapted for OCD may be added to ERP. A family member or carer may be involved as co-therapist where appropriate (NICE guideline CG31, 2005).

Psychosis and schizophrenia. CBT for psychosis should be delivered over at least 16 planned sessions, one to one. Family intervention should be offered to people in contact with their families (NICE guideline CG178, 2014).

Eating disorders. For children and young people with anorexia nervosa, anorexia-nervosa-focused family therapy is recommended, typically 18 to 20 sessions over one year. For adults with anorexia nervosa, individual eating-disorder-focused CBT, MANTRA or specialist supportive clinical management. Medication should not be offered as the sole treatment (NICE guideline NG69, 2017).

Borderline personality disorder. A comprehensive dialectical behaviour therapy programme should be considered for women for whom reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority. Brief psychological interventions of less than three months' duration should not be used specifically for borderline personality disorder or its individual symptoms (NICE guideline CG78, 2009).

The APA Division 12 database of research-supported psychological treatments provides a parallel US-based resource, rated under criteria from Tolin et al. (2015) as very strong, strong, weak or insufficient, with an archived older list rated under Chambless and Hollon (1998). It should be consulted directly rather than quoted from memory, since ratings have changed over time and some were revised downward.

heading: Stepped care and matched care
text:
Stepped care allocates the least intensive intervention likely to produce benefit first, with systematic monitoring and a route to step up. In the English implementation the steps are: step 1, recognition, assessment and active monitoring; step 2, low-intensity interventions such as guided self-help and computerised CBT delivered by psychological wellbeing practitioners; step 3, high-intensity psychological therapy delivered by qualified therapists, and medication; step 4, specialist and crisis services, inpatient care, and combined treatment for severe and complex presentations including risk to life and severe self-neglect.

Two failure modes of stepped care matter clinically.

Under-treatment by default. Stepping a person through low-intensity work when the presentation clearly indicates high-intensity treatment wastes months and teaches the person that treatment does not work. Guidelines allow direct allocation to the appropriate step, and matched care means starting where the presentation indicates rather than at the bottom.

Failure to step up. Stepped care depends on monitoring with a route out. Without session-by-session measurement and a review point, people sit at step 2 indefinitely.

The practical marker for stepping up is absence of change on a routine measure after an adequate dose. For low-intensity work an adequate dose is generally in the region of six sessions before a review, though this is a service convention rather than a trial-derived threshold [UNVERIFIED as a specific number].

Presentations that should generally not start at low intensity: PTSD, OCD with significant impairment, anorexia nervosa, psychosis, bipolar disorder, and any presentation with active suicidal intent.

heading: The first session: what it must accomplish
text:
A first session has to do six things, and a clinician who runs out of time will usually have spent it on history at the expense of the rest.

Establish enough safety for the person to speak. This includes the practical frame: length, frequency, confidentiality and its limits, note-keeping, what happens if they cannot attend.

Hear the problem in the person's own words before structuring it. The opening should be open and the clinician should not intervene early.

> "Where would you like to start?"
> "What made you pick up the phone when you did, rather than three months ago?"

Assess risk. Directly, calmly, specifically, and not at the very end when there is no time to respond.

Get a provisional formulation, meaning a working account of what keeps this going, held loosely.

Agree a focus. Not a full treatment plan, but a shared statement of what the work is about. A person who leaves the first session without knowing what they are working on is more likely not to return.

Instil some hope, honestly. Not by promising outcomes but by making the problem legible.

> "What you've described has a shape to it, and it's a shape I recognise. The avoidance is doing most of the work of keeping it going, and that's the part that responds well to treatment."

What not to do in a first session: deep exploration of trauma detail, chairwork or other high-arousal experiential tasks, transference interpretation, or a homework assignment the person has not shaped. Asking for the trauma narrative in session one, when there is no containment and no relationship, is the classic harmful first-session error.

Closing the first session:

> "We're coming to time. Before we stop, I want to check what this has been like, and I'd particularly like to know anything that felt off or that I got wrong."

heading: The fifth session: what should be different
text:
By roughly session five the work should have changed in character. If session five looks like session one, that is a signal.

What should be present. A shared formulation the client can state in their own words. An agreed focus that has survived a few weeks. Some between-session activity, however small. Measurable movement on something, even if the primary symptom has not shifted. A relationship robust enough to survive disagreement.

What the session itself looks like. Less history-gathering, more work on a specific instance. The bridge from last session and the review of between-session work take up real time rather than being a formality. The clinician does less structuring because the client brings material that fits the focus.

> Session one: "Tell me about the panic attacks."
> Session five: "You had one on Thursday. Let's take that one apart minute by minute, because you also had a near-miss on Saturday that didn't turn into one, and the difference is where the information is."

By session five, the clinician should also be able to answer three questions. What is the mechanism I am targeting. What would count as evidence that this is working. What would change my mind about the formulation.

This is also the standard point for an explicit review.

> "We're five in. I want to step back for ten minutes rather than carry on by momentum. What's better, what's the same, and what do you want us to do differently for the next stretch?"

If the answer is that nothing is different, that is a finding, and it belongs in the room rather than in the clinician's private worry.

heading: The phase-based trauma model
text:
Herman's (1992) three-stage model remains the organising frame for complex trauma work: safety and stabilisation, remembrance and mourning, and reconnection. The ISTSS expert consensus guidelines for complex PTSD in adults set out the same structure: phase one prioritises safety, symptom reduction, and emotional, social and psychological skills; phase two processes unresolved traumatic memories for integration; phase three consolidates gains and supports re-engagement with relationships, work, education and community.

Phase one content. Physical and situational safety first, meaning housing, violence, finances and substance use. Then affect regulation skills, distress tolerance, grounding, sleep, and a workable daily structure. Then psychoeducation about trauma responses, which reframes symptoms as understandable rather than as evidence of being broken. Then relational safety in the therapy itself, which for people harmed in relationships takes longer than clinicians expect.

Phase two content. Structured processing of the traumatic material using a specific method rather than open-ended recounting. Repeated unstructured retelling without a processing framework is retraumatising and should not be mistaken for phase two work.

Phase three content. Grief for what was lost, identity beyond the trauma, relationships, work, and the practical business of a life. This phase is routinely truncated by service limits and is where much of the durable gain sits.

Evidence and controversy. Cloitre et al. (2010, American Journal of Psychiatry 167:915-924) compared phase-based skills training followed by exposure against exposure-focused and skills-focused conditions in PTSD related to childhood abuse and found results favouring the phase-based approach over the exposure-focused condition. Against this, a body of work argues that stabilisation is often unnecessary and that immediate trauma-focused treatment is tolerated and effective in complex populations, including a randomised clinical trial comparing phase-based treatment with immediate trauma-focused treatment for PTSD due to childhood abuse published in BJPsych Open, and a critical analysis of complex PTSD guidelines by De Jongh and colleagues. The direction and magnitude of results in that specific trial should be checked against the paper before being asserted [UNVERIFIED].

The defensible current position is that phase-based sequencing is a reasonable default for complex presentations with poor affect regulation, active self-harm or dissociation, and that indefinite stabilisation which never proceeds to processing is a common and harmful failure, not a cautious one.

heading: When to stabilise before processing: the decision criteria
text:
The question is not whether the person's history is severe. It is whether they can enter high arousal, do something useful in it, and come down again within the session and afterwards.

Indicators to stabilise first. Current self-harm at a frequency or severity that would be dangerous if it escalated. Active suicidal intent or planning. Substance use that would be the likely response to increased distress. Dissociation that the person cannot interrupt, including amnesia for parts of sessions. No capacity to self-soothe, meaning the person cannot name a single thing that reliably helps. Living with the perpetrator or in ongoing danger. Acute psychotic symptoms. Recent inpatient admission. No support at all between appointments combined with a long gap between them. Severe untreated eating disorder where medical stability is at risk.

Indicators that processing can start. The person can identify and use at least one grounding or regulation strategy in session. They can report distress rising and falling rather than only being at ceiling. They have somewhere to go and someone or something to do after sessions. Substance use is not the primary regulation method. Risk is present but not acute and there is a plan.

Practical tests worth running before committing to processing:

> "I'd like to try something small. I'm going to ask you to bring the memory to mind for about thirty seconds, not the worst part, just the edge of it. Then we'll stop and I want to see how quickly you can come back. This is a test of the brakes, not the engine."

> "Between now and next week, what will you do in the two hours after a session like that? I'd rather we planned it than hoped."

The stabilisation trap. Some clients can stay in phase one indefinitely because it is tolerable and processing is not. The clinician's own anxiety contributes. The correction is a stated time frame and a review point.

doc_summary: How a clinician selects a modality for a presentation, what changes between an early and a mid-phase session, when to stabilise before processing, how to pace and titrate, and how to recognise and correct an approach that is not working.
heading: When not to go deep
text:
Depth is not a virtue in itself. There are situations where the correct clinical action is to stay on the surface.

When containment is what is needed. Acute crisis, recent bereavement in the first days, immediately after a disclosure to police or child protection. The work is practical and supportive.

When the session structure cannot hold it. A single session, a duty appointment, a phone call, the last ten minutes of any session. Opening material there is a clinician's error, and the standard preventive is to watch the clock and to decline material that cannot be closed.

> "I want to hear this properly, and we've got eight minutes, which isn't enough to open it and put it back down safely. Can we make it the first thing next week?"

When the person is not stable enough. See the criteria above.

When the person has said no. A stated boundary is clinical information and is respected.

When going deep would serve the clinician. Curiosity, the wish to be the one who reaches the material, and the pull of an interesting case are all real and all recognisable in supervision.

When the presenting problem is external. Debt, immigration insecurity, housing, workplace bullying, domestic abuse. Psychological exploration of a person's response to a real ongoing threat, in place of practical action, is a category error and can be actively harmful.

When the person is high-risk and about to leave. Never open new material in the final quarter of a session with someone at risk.

doc_title: Matching and Sequencing: Choosing, Ordering and Correcting the Approach
doc_summary: How a clinician selects a modality for a presentation, what changes between an early and a mid-phase session, when to stabilise before processing, how to pace and titrate, and how to recognise and correct an approach that is not working.
heading: Pacing and titration
text:
The working concept is arousal within a usable range: high enough that the material is emotionally live, low enough that the person can think. Above the range, the person is flooded, and no new learning is encoded. Below it, the person is numb, intellectualising or dissociated, and again nothing is encoded. The clinician's task is to keep the work in the band and to move the person back into it when they leave it.

Markers of going over. Speech speeding up or stopping. Breathing changes. Visible shaking. Losing the thread mid-sentence. Eyes fixed or unfocused. Reports of the room going far away or of not feeling their hands. Answering questions with long delays.

Markers of going under. Flat recounting of atrocity. Talking about the self in the third person or in general terms. Sudden humour. Detailed factual narration with no affect. Repeated "I don't know" delivered without searching.

Titration moves. Reduce the sensory detail requested. Shift tense from present to past. Move from image to word. Add distance ("watch it on a screen you can pause"). Split the memory and take one part. Shorten the exposure and increase the frequency. Interleave a regulation task. Return to the room by naming objects or by orienting to the present.

> "Stop there. Feet on the floor. Tell me four things in this room that are blue."
> "You've gone quite far in. Come back to me. Say my name and tell me what day it is."
> "We're going to take that one memory and cut it into three. Today we only do the first part, the drive there. We don't get out of the car."

The end of a session is a technical matter, not a courtesy. Processing work needs a deliberate closing that takes real minutes: return to the present, check state, review what will happen in the next few hours, confirm risk status.

> "Before you go. Where are you on a scale of nought to ten right now, and where were you when you came in? What are you doing straight after this? Who's in the house tonight?"

doc_summary: How a clinician selects a modality for a presentation, what changes between an early and a mid-phase session, when to stabilise before processing, how to pace and titrate, and how to recognise and correct an approach that is not working.
heading: Homework and between-session work
text:
Therapy happens for one hour a week and life happens in the other 167. Between-session work is how the therapy reaches the life. Meta-analytic work in CBT associates homework completion with better outcome, and the association holds across studies, though the causal direction is not fully settled and the precise pooled effect size should be checked against the specific meta-analysis being cited (Kazantzis and colleagues) [UNVERIFIED as to the exact figure].

Design rules that determine whether it happens.

Collaborative, not assigned. The client should generate or at least shape the task.

Specific to the point of triviality. When, where, how long, with what. "Do some exercise" fails. "Walk to the postbox and back after breakfast on Tuesday and Thursday" succeeds.

Small enough to be certain. The first assignment should be one the clinician is confident will be completed, because early success predicts continued engagement.

Explicitly linked to the mechanism. The client should be able to say why they are doing it.

Anticipate the obstacle before it happens.

> "What's most likely to stop this happening? ... And if the meeting overruns, what's the fallback?"

Reviewed first, always. The single strongest predictor of homework not being done is the clinician not asking about it. Reviewing it in the first five minutes of the next session establishes that it matters.

Non-completion is data, not misconduct. The response is curiosity, not disappointment.

> Poor: "That's okay, let's try again this week."
> Better: "Let's find out what happened, because that's usually the most useful thing in the week. Where did it break down: remembering, starting, or something coming up in the middle?"

Language matters. "Homework" carries school associations for many people, and "experiment", "practice", "between-session task" or the client's own name for it often works better.

heading: Recognising that the approach is not working
text:
The most consequential clinical skill in this section is noticing failure early. Clinicians are unreliable at identifying clients who are deteriorating without formal measurement, and the research on routine outcome monitoring exists precisely because unaided clinical judgement misses a substantial proportion of deteriorating cases (Lambert and colleagues; Hannan et al., 2005) [UNVERIFIED as to specific detection rates].

The practical answer is a session-by-session measure. PHQ-9, GAD-7, CORE-10, ORS or an equivalent, taken every session, plotted, and looked at. Measurement without inspection is theatre.

Signals that the approach is wrong.

No movement on the measure after an adequate dose, typically six to eight sessions of a working alliance and completed tasks.

The client is engaged and compliant and nothing is changing. This points to the formulation rather than to motivation.

Sessions have become pleasant and directionless. The clinician looks forward to them and cannot say what is being worked on.

The same content recurs weekly with no development. Repetition without deepening is a marker of a maintenance conversation.

Deterioration, including new symptoms, increased risk, or increased substance use.

Increasing cancellations, lateness or shortened engagement, which is often a withdrawal rupture rather than lack of motivation.

The clinician is working harder than the client, session after session.

Common causes and what they indicate. A missed diagnosis, including bipolarity, autism, ADHD, an eating disorder, a physical cause such as thyroid disease or sleep apnoea, or substance dependence. An unaddressed maintaining factor outside the room, such as ongoing abuse, debt or an unsafe workplace. A wrong mechanism in the formulation. An unrepaired rupture. Insufficient dose or intensity. A treatment that requires a specialist competence the clinician does not have.

heading: Changing course
text:
Noticing is not enough. The correction has a sequence.

Name it openly. Concealing a stalled therapy from the client is a common and corrosive error, and clients almost always already know.

> "I want to be straight with you. We're eight sessions in, your scores haven't moved, and I don't think what we're doing is working. That's mine to solve, not yours, and I'd like to look at it with you."

Ask the client for their account before offering yours. Clients frequently name the reason immediately when they are asked directly.

> "What's your read on why this hasn't shifted? And what have you been thinking but not saying?"

Revisit the formulation rather than intensifying the same technique. Doing more of a treatment that is not working is the standard error. Check for a missed maintaining factor, a missed diagnosis, and a mismatch between the mechanism and the method.

Consider the alternatives in order: change the target within the same model; change the model; add a component such as medication, family work or a practical intervention; refer for a specialist treatment; refer for assessment of a suspected missed condition; or pause the therapy.

Pausing is a legitimate clinical decision. Continuing indefinitely with an ineffective therapy has costs: it occupies a slot, it consumes the client's hope, and it teaches them that treatment does not work for them.

> "One option I want to put on the table is stopping for now. Not because you've failed, and not permanently. If we keep going out of politeness we'll use up something that might work better in six months when the housing situation is settled."

Take it to supervision or consultation before deciding. A stalled case is the paradigm indication for consultation, and in DBT the consultation team exists partly for this function.

heading: Endings, stepping down and relapse prevention
text:
Endings are part of the treatment and are planned rather than arrived at. Time-limited work should have the ending named at the start and referred to periodically, not mentioned for the first time in the penultimate session.

Content of a good ending. Review of what changed and how, with the client naming the mechanism in their own words, since attributing change to their own action rather than to the clinician predicts maintenance. A written or spoken relapse prevention plan: early warning signs specific to this person, what to do at each stage, who to contact and how. A blueprint of the techniques that worked. Explicit discussion of the relationship ending, which for people with attachment injuries or bereavement histories is live material rather than administrative.

> "What would be the first sign, three or four weeks before you were properly unwell again, that you'd notice and someone else might not?"

> "If this comes back in eighteen months, what do you want your future self to do in the first week?"

Stepping down rather than stopping is often the right structure: reducing to fortnightly, then monthly, then a single review appointment at three months. Booster sessions are a standard feature of relapse prevention in depression and are underused.

Endings that go wrong. Fading out through cancellations without a final session, which leaves the work unconsolidated and repeats an abandonment pattern for many clients. Extending indefinitely because ending is uncomfortable for either party. Ending abruptly at a service boundary with no notice, which is a service failure and should be named as such to the client rather than absorbed.

> "I want to say clearly that ending here is about the service's limit, not about you being finished or not deserving more. I'm sorry about it, and I'd rather say that than pretend it's clinically ideal."
