doc_title: Therapeutic Micro-Skills: The Conversational Craft
doc_summary: The moment-to-moment verbal craft of clinical conversation, with the reflection depths, validation levels, MI structure, rupture repair sequences and many paired examples contrasting advice-giving with the clinical alternative.
heading: What separates a clinical reply from an advice reply
text:
The single largest difference between a trained clinician and a well-meaning helper is the ratio of understanding to instruction. A helper hears a problem and reaches for a solution. A clinician hears a problem and first establishes that they have understood it accurately, out loud, in a way the person can correct.

This is not politeness. It has three functions. It checks the clinician's model against the person's actual experience before anything is built on it. It gives the person the experience of being understood, which is itself associated with outcome: therapist empathy has a mean weighted r of .28 with outcome across 82 samples and 6,138 clients (Elliott, Bohart, Watson and Murphy, 2018). And it keeps the person doing the work, which matters because arguments for change are more durable when the person makes them.

Four failure patterns to recognise in one's own output:

Premature solution. Offering a strategy before the problem has been described in enough detail for the strategy to be sound.

Reassurance. Contradicting the person's distress with an optimistic claim. This reliably ends the disclosure, because the person now knows that this content produces reassurance rather than engagement.

Normalising too early. Saying "that's completely normal" before the person has finished saying what it is. The same sentence is useful thirty seconds later.

Question stacking. Two or three questions in a row with no reflection between them, which converts the conversation into an interview and shifts responsibility for direction entirely onto the clinician.

> Client: "I've been snapping at my kids all week and I hate myself for it."
> Advice reply: "That sounds like burnout. Have you tried scheduling some time for yourself? Even twenty minutes can help. And it might be worth looking at your sleep."
> Clinical reply: "Snapping at them, and then the hating yourself on top of it. Which of those is worse to sit with?"

> Client: "I don't think I can do this anymore."
> Advice reply: "It's important to remember how far you've come. Let's look at what's worked before."
> Clinical reply: "Can't do this anymore. I want to make sure I hear which 'this' you mean, because that could be a few different things."

Note that the clinical replies are shorter than the advice replies. This is generally true. Length in a helper's turn is usually a symptom of the helper doing the work.

doc_summary: The moment-to-moment verbal craft of clinical conversation, with the reflection depths, validation levels, MI structure, rupture repair sequences and many paired examples contrasting advice-giving with the clinical alternative.
heading: Simple reflection
text:
A simple reflection restates what the person said, adding little or nothing. It stays within the content already offered. Its purposes are to signal accurate hearing, to slow the pace, and to keep the person talking without steering.

Forms: a near-repetition of key words; a paraphrase using the person's own vocabulary; a short partial reflection that picks up the loaded phrase and leaves it open.

> Client: "By the time I get home I've got nothing left."
> Simple reflection: "Nothing left by the time you get in."

> Client: "I keep thinking I should be over this by now."
> Simple reflection: "Should be over it."

The most powerful and least used form is the single phrase repeated back with the emphasis the person gave it, followed by silence. It invites elaboration without asking for it.

Rules. Do not add interpretation. Do not add a question on the end, because appending a question converts the reflection into a prompt and the person answers the question instead of continuing. Do not upgrade the emotion word. If they said irritated, do not reflect furious.

The most common error is the reflection formula. Beginning every reflection with "It sounds like" becomes audible as a tic within four or five uses and reads as technique rather than attention. Vary the openings, and often use none at all: a reflection can be a bare statement.

> Formulaic: "It sounds like you're feeling frustrated. It sounds like work has been really hard."
> Varied: "Frustrated." / "Work's been grinding you down." / "So that's two months of it now."

A reflection is a statement, not a question, and this shows in the intonation. Reflections delivered with a rising inflection function as questions and produce a yes or no rather than elaboration. In text, this means avoiding the question mark.

> Rising: "You're feeling like you can't cope?"
> Level: "You're at the point where coping isn't the word for it anymore."

The most powerful and least used form is the single phrase repeated back with the emphasis the person gave it, followed by silence. It invites elaboration without asking for it.

Rules. Do not add interpretation. Do not add a question on the end, because appending a question converts the reflection into a prompt and the person answers the question instead of continuing. Do not upgrade the emotion word. If they said irritated, do not reflect furious.

The most common error is the reflection formula. Beginning every reflection with "It sounds like" becomes audible as a tic within four or five uses and reads as technique rather than attention. Vary the openings, and often use none at all: a reflection can be a bare statement.

> Formulaic: "It sounds like you're feeling frustrated. It sounds like work has been really hard."
> Varied: "Frustrated." / "Work's been grinding you down." / "So that's two months of it now."

A reflection is a statement, not a question, and this shows in the intonation. Reflections delivered with a rising inflection function as questions and produce a yes or no rather than elaboration. In text, this means avoiding the question mark.

> Rising: "You're feeling like you can't cope?"
> Level: "You're at the point where coping isn't the word for it anymore."

heading: Complex reflection: continuing the paragraph, amplified and double-sided
text:
A complex reflection adds meaning that was implied but not said. It is a guess, offered as a statement, that the person can accept or correct. Complex reflections do more work than simple ones and carry more risk of being wrong, and being wrong is not a problem provided the reflection is offered in a way that invites correction.

Continuing the paragraph. The clinician says the next sentence the person was heading toward but did not say.

> Client: "I told my sister I'd help with Mum, and I said yes, and then I got off the phone and just sat there."
> Continuing the paragraph: "And part of you already knew you'd regret saying yes."

Amplified reflection. The clinician reflects the statement slightly stronger than it was given, without sarcasm, which typically prompts the person to argue the other side themselves. This is the single most useful move when someone is defending a position, and it fails badly if there is any irony in the delivery.

> Client: "The drinking isn't really an issue. Everyone in my job drinks like that."
> Amplified: "So there's really nothing about it that concerns you."
> Client: "Well, I mean, I wouldn't say nothing. The mornings are getting harder."

Double-sided reflection. The clinician holds both sides of an ambivalence in one sentence, with the change side last, since whatever comes last tends to be what the person picks up.

> Client: "I know I should leave but I've been there eleven years and I'd be starting from zero."
> Double-sided: "Eleven years is a lot to walk away from, and you're the one who used the word 'should'."

Metaphor. Offering an image that captures the structure of the experience.

> Client: "Every time I think I'm getting somewhere something knocks it back."
> Metaphor: "Like you keep getting to the same point on the hill and then finding yourself at the bottom again."

Reframing. Reflecting the same content with a different meaning attached. Reframes should be offered lightly, because a reframe the person does not accept lands as correction.

> Client: "I'm so needy with him. I check my phone constantly."
> Reframe: "Or the checking is what happens when someone matters to you and you can't tell where you stand."

Calibration rule: complex reflections should be roughly one step ahead of the person, not three. A reflection that names a core belief in session two, when the person is describing a bad week, is not depth, it is a jump the person cannot use.

heading: Reflection of feeling and reflection of meaning
text:
Reflection of feeling names the emotion, including emotion that was shown rather than stated. It is more exposing than content reflection and should be paced accordingly.

> Client: "I found the letters when I was clearing the house. There were about forty of them." (voice tightens)
> Content reflection: "Forty letters, in among her things."
> Feeling reflection: "Something happened just then when you said forty."

Accuracy matters more than intensity. An emotion word that is slightly off invites correction, and correction is useful. An emotion word that is much too strong makes the person defend against it.

> Too strong: "You must have been devastated."
> Calibrated: "There's some grief in that, and something else I can't name."

Reflection of meaning goes beneath the emotion to what the situation signifies for the person: what it says about them, what it threatens, what it costs.

> Client: "He didn't even ask how the scan went. He just talked about the car."
> Feeling: "That stung."
> Meaning: "It's not really about the car. It's that you're going through something enormous on your own, in a house with another person in it."

The order matters. Content, then feeling, then meaning is the usual depth ladder, and skipping to meaning too early produces the response "I suppose so" delivered flatly, which is the marker that the clinician has gone deeper than the person is currently standing.

When the person's stated feeling and shown feeling differ, name the discrepancy without asserting which is true.

> "You're telling me it's fine, and you're saying it with your jaw set. I don't know what to make of that, so I'm asking you."

heading: Summarising
text:
Summaries do work that reflections cannot. They gather scattered material into a shape, demonstrate sustained attention across time, and hand the person a version of their own account they can revise.

Three types.

Collecting summaries gather several related items and end with an invitation to continue. They are short and used mid-conversation.

> "So far there's the sleep, the money, and the thing with your brother that you touched on and moved past. What else is in the pile?"

Linking summaries connect present material to something said earlier, often weeks earlier. These carry disproportionate weight because they show the clinician holds continuity.

> "What you just said about not wanting to bother the GP sounds like the same thing you described in January about not calling your daughter when you were ill. Both times, needing something felt like an imposition."

Transitional summaries close one section and open another, and are the standard way to move between agenda items or to end a session.

> "Let me pull together where we've got to. You came in wanting to work out whether to stay in the job. What's emerged is that the job is bearable and the commute isn't, and that underneath both is the sense you've given up on the thing you actually trained for. Have I got that right, or have I flattened something?"

The closing question is not optional. A summary offered without an invitation to correct is a pronouncement. Useful forms: "What did I miss?", "Where's that wrong?", "What would you add?"

In motivational interviewing, summaries are also used strategically. A summary that includes the person's change talk and their sustain talk, ordered so that change talk lands last, followed by "so where does that leave you?", is a standard move at the point of decision.

> "You've said the fatigue is affecting your work, that your daughter has noticed, and that you don't like who you are on the bad days. You've also said you don't want to be someone who can't have a drink at a wedding, and that you've stopped before and it didn't stick. And you've said the mornings are getting harder and you're tired of managing it. Where does that leave you?"

heading: Open questions and the question-to-reflection ratio
text:
Open questions invite elaboration and cannot be answered with a word. Closed questions gather specific data. Both are necessary and the error is proportion, not the existence of closed questions.

A useful working target from motivational interviewing training is at least two reflections for every question, and a majority of questions open. This is a training heuristic rather than an outcome-validated threshold [UNVERIFIED as a precise standard], but as a self-monitoring device it reliably catches the drift into interrogation.

Question quality:

> Weak, closed and leading: "Do you think that's connected to your dad?"
> Better, open: "What do you make of it?"

> Weak, stacked: "How was the week? Did you do the sleep diary? Was the medication okay?"
> Better: "How was the week?" then wait, then reflect, then ask the next.

> Weak, "why": "Why didn't you go?"
> Better: "What got in the way?" or "Walk me through the hour before you were due to leave."

"Why" questions invite justification and often produce defensiveness or a rationalisation the person then has to defend. "What" and "how" produce description.

Questions that function as advice in disguise are a specific hazard. They allow the clinician to give the advice while appearing to enquire, and clients hear them accurately.

> Disguised advice: "Have you thought about telling her how you feel?"
> Honest version if the advice is genuinely warranted: "I've got a suggestion, and I'm not sure it's right. Do you want it now or do you want to keep going?"

The scaling question is a high-yield open question because the number is less useful than the two follow-ups.

> "Nought to ten, how important is changing this right now?" ... "You said six. Why six and not three?" ... "What would need to happen to move it to seven?"

Asking why the number is not lower pulls change talk. Asking why it is not higher pulls sustain talk, and is the wrong direction unless deliberately used to explore obstacles.

heading: Silence
text:
Silence is a skill with distinct uses, and the inability to tolerate it is the most reliable marker of an untrained helper. In text-based or conversational AI contexts the equivalent skill is restraint in length: not filling the turn, not adding a second paragraph, not appending a question to a reflection that was complete.

After a question, silence gives the person time to find the real answer rather than the first available one. Most people need three to five seconds of genuine thinking time, and most helpers wait less than two before rephrasing, adding a prompt or supplying an option. The rephrasing is what destroys the answer, because it replaces the person's search with the helper's suggestion.

After the person says something significant, silence lets the significance register rather than being absorbed into the next exchange. A disclosure followed immediately by a clinician's question communicates that the disclosure was a step toward something else.

After crying starts, silence plus visible presence is usually correct. Handing tissues is an ambiguous act, since it can read as care or as a request to stop, and it is worth having them within the person's reach rather than offering them.

Before ending a difficult session, a deliberate pause changes the pace and gives the person a moment to gather themselves before standing up.

While the person is thinking mid-sentence, silence is mandatory. Completing someone's sentence takes the thought away from them.

Silence has failure modes. Extended silence with a person who is anxious, paranoid, or has a history of neglect can be experienced as withdrawal, judgement or punishment, and with a person who has been institutionalised it can read as a test. Silence in a first session, with someone who does not yet know the rules of the encounter, is usually unhelpful and should be short. Silence held because the clinician does not know what to say, extended until it becomes the client's problem to solve, is not a technique.

Naming a silence is often better than either breaking it or extending it, because it makes the pause collaborative rather than something happening to the person.

> "You've gone quiet, and I don't want to guess wrong about what that is."
> "I'm going to leave a gap here rather than fill it, because I think something's still landing."
> "Take as long as you need. I'm not waiting for anything."
> "I notice I want to fill this silence, and I think that's my discomfort rather than yours."

heading: Validation: the six levels
text:
Linehan's six levels of validation give a graded set of moves, each harder than the last, and each communicating that the person's response makes sense (Linehan, 1997; Linehan, 2015). Validation communicates that a response is understandable, not that it is correct or wise. Validating a self-destructive behaviour's function is not endorsing the behaviour.

V1, paying attention. Being present, oriented, unhurried, and visibly listening. This is validation because attention communicates worth.

> "I've got nowhere else to be for the next forty minutes. Take your time."

V2, accurate reflection. Reflecting back what was said without adding or judging, so the person hears their own account held accurately.

> "So the plan was to go, you got as far as the car park, and you drove home."

V3, articulating the unstated. Naming what the person has not said but is implied by what they have said. This is the level where the clinician guesses, and should hold it lightly.

> "You haven't said this, so tell me if I'm wrong. I imagine there was a moment in the car park where you thought this is going to happen every time."

V4, validating in terms of history or biology. Communicating that the reaction makes sense given the person's learning history or their physiology.

> "Given that the last three times you asked for help you got told you were being dramatic, of course you didn't ring anyone."

V5, validating in terms of present circumstances. Communicating that the reaction is one any reasonable person might have in this situation, independent of the person's history. This is a stronger validation than V4, because V4 says "it makes sense for you given your past" and V5 says "it makes sense full stop."

> "You found out by text, from someone who isn't even family. Anyone would be furious about that."

V6, radical genuineness. Responding to the person as an equal rather than as a patient, including being honest, being affected, and dropping the professional register. Linehan holds this to be the most powerful level, particularly for people whose experience of services has been of being handled.

> "I'm not going to do the therapist thing with this one. What happened to you was wrong, and I'm angry on your behalf."

Choosing the level. Use the highest level that is true. Do not use V4 where V5 is available, because explaining a reaction by the person's history when the situation itself justifies it subtly implies the reaction is a symptom. Do not use V5 or V6 for a response that is genuinely not warranted by the situation, because false validation is detected and costs credibility.

Validation of the invalid is the specific error to avoid. If a person says everyone at work hates them and the evidence does not support it, the clinician validates the feeling and the reasons for it, not the conclusion.

> "I'm not going to agree that they all hate you, because I don't think that's true and you'd know I was managing you. What I do believe is that you felt frozen out on Tuesday, and that when that happens it goes straight to a very old place."

heading: Invalidation by accident
text:
Most invalidation in clinical conversation is unintentional. It comes from three sources: the urge to fix, the urge to reassure, and the urge to reframe too early. All three are motivated by care, which is why they are hard to notice from the inside and easy to notice from the outside.

The structural feature they share is that each one contradicts, corrects or redirects the person's stated experience. The person has said how it is, and the reply says it is not quite like that. The effect is that the person stops elaborating, either by moving to a safer topic or by agreeing in order to end the exchange. Compliant agreement following a well-meant reassurance is the standard signature of accidental invalidation, and it is easy to mistake for the reassurance having worked.

The corrective in every case is to stay with the content one beat longer before doing anything with it.

> "At least it wasn't worse." Comparison invalidates by implying the person should be measuring against something else.
> Alternative: "That was bad enough on its own terms."

> "Everything happens for a reason." Meaning imposed from outside.
> Alternative: "I don't have a frame that makes this make sense. I don't think there is one."

> "You shouldn't feel guilty, you did everything you could." Instruction about what to feel.
> Alternative: "The guilt's there whether it's fair or not. What is it saying to you?"

> "Try not to think about it." A request to suppress, which reliably increases intrusion.
> Alternative: "What happens when you try not to think about it?"

> "But you've got so much going for you." Contradiction of the person's self-report, offered as encouragement.
> Alternative: "None of that touches it, does it."

> "I completely understand, the same thing happened to me." Redirection to the clinician plus an assumed equivalence.
> Alternative: "I don't know what that was like for you. Tell me."

> "Have you tried mindfulness?" Solution offered to a person who has not asked for one and has probably tried it.
> Alternative: "What have you already tried? I'd rather not suggest something you've been through."

> "At least it wasn't worse." Comparison invalidates by implying the person should be measuring against something else.
> Alternative: "That was bad enough on its own terms."

> "Everything happens for a reason." Meaning imposed from outside.
> Alternative: "I don't have a frame that makes this make sense. I don't think there is one."

> "You shouldn't feel guilty, you did everything you could." Instruction about what to feel.
> Alternative: "The guilt's there whether it's fair or not. What is it saying to you?"

> "Try not to think about it." A request to suppress, which reliably increases intrusion.
> Alternative: "What happens when you try not to think about it?"

> "But you've got so much going for you." Contradiction of the person's self-report, offered as encouragement.
> Alternative: "None of that touches it, does it."

> "I completely understand, the same thing happened to me." Redirection to the clinician plus an assumed equivalence.
> Alternative: "I don't know what that was like for you. Tell me."

> "Have you tried mindfulness?" Solution offered to a person who has not asked for one and has probably tried it.
> Alternative: "What have you already tried? I'd rather not suggest something you've been through."

heading: Immediacy
text:
Immediacy is talking about what is happening between the two people, in the present, out loud. It is used to address something occurring in the relationship that is either an obstacle or a resource: withdrawal, tension, an unexpected warmth, a repeated pattern being enacted.

The structure that works: describe the observable, own it as your perception, invite correction, and stop.

> "Something shifted about ten minutes ago and I've felt further away from you since. I might be wrong about that. Does it match anything for you?"

> "I notice I've been working quite hard in the last few minutes, and you've been giving me short answers. I don't want to just push on. What's going on for you?"

> "I want to say something awkward. When you thanked me at the end last week it felt like you were reassuring me that I was doing okay. I wondered if you look after me in here."

Rules. Use the present tense. Describe behaviour, not character. Do not use immediacy to discharge irritation, which is the most common misuse. Do not use it as an accusation dressed as observation ("I notice you're being defensive"). Check whether the relationship can hold it, since immediacy in session one with a mistrustful person is usually premature.

A qualitative meta-analysis of 21 studies of therapist self-disclosure and immediacy found that immediacy was associated more often with clients opening up and being immediate in return, and that both processes were linked to an enhanced therapy relationship (Hill, Knox and Pinto-Coelho, 2018, Psychotherapy).

heading: Self-disclosure and its rules
text:
Therapist self-disclosure comes in two forms. Disclosure of facts about the therapist's life outside the room, and disclosure of the therapist's in-the-moment reaction, which overlaps with immediacy. The evidence base is qualitative rather than dose-response, and the studied processes following disclosure include enhanced relationship, improved client functioning, gains in insight, and general helpfulness (Hill, Knox and Pinto-Coelho, 2018).

Working rules.

Disclose for the client's benefit, not the clinician's. If the impulse arises from wanting to be liked, wanting to seem human, or wanting relief from discomfort, do not.

Keep it brief and return the focus. A disclosure that requires the client to attend to the clinician's story has failed.

Do not disclose unresolved material. Disclosing a current struggle transfers the burden.

Do not disclose to demonstrate equivalence. "I know exactly how you feel" is almost never accurate and forecloses the client's account.

Prefer disclosure of process to disclosure of content.

> Poor: "I went through a divorce myself and what helped me was..."
> Better: "I notice I want to reassure you, and I think that's because what you're describing is genuinely hard to sit with. So instead of reassuring you I'm going to stay with it."

> Reasonable content disclosure, brief and returned: "I do have children, yes. I'm aware you asked that just after describing the school run, and I'm curious what it would have meant either way."

Answer direct personal questions with a decision rather than a deflection. Reflexively bouncing every question back ("what would it mean if I did?") is experienced as evasive and, with people who have been managed by institutions, as confirming that this is another such institution.

heading: Confrontation and challenge done well
text:
Confrontation in a clinical sense means pointing out a discrepancy: between two statements, between stated values and behaviour, between what the person says and what they show. It is not aggression, and it is not telling someone they are wrong.

The workable structure: establish credit first, name the discrepancy descriptively, do not resolve it, hand it back.

> "You've been coming for two months and you've never missed. So I'm going to say something direct, on the basis that you can take it. You've told me every week that the priority is your health, and every week the gym has come after everything else. I don't have an explanation for that. Do you?"

> "Two things you've said today don't sit together. You said you're fine with the arrangement, and you said you've been awake at three every night since it started. I'd like to understand how both are true."

Rules. Confront the discrepancy, not the person. Use their own words as the two poles. Do not add an interpretation of the motive. Do not confront while irritated, since the client will hear the irritation and not the content. Do not confront where the alliance is weak or the person is in crisis. Confront once and then stop, because repeated confrontation is nagging, and in motivational interviewing terms it directly generates sustain talk.

Softening moves that preserve the challenge: prefacing with permission ("can I put something to you?"), attributing the observation to yourself ("I might be reading this wrong"), and offering an exit ("you can tell me that's not it").

What confrontation is not: labelling ("that's denial"), diagnosing in the moment ("that's your avoidant side"), or moralising ("you're going to lose her if you keep this up"). Each of these predicts disengagement.

heading: Motivational interviewing: spirit, OARS, and the righting reflex
text:
Motivational interviewing (Miller and Rollnick, 2013; 4th edition 2023) is a collaborative conversation style for strengthening a person's own motivation and commitment to change. It is defined by its spirit as much as its techniques: partnership, acceptance, compassion, and evocation. Evocation is the load-bearing one, since it means motivation is drawn out rather than installed.

OARS names the four core skills: Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections, Summaries.

Affirmations recognise specific strengths and efforts, and differ from praise in being about the person's actions rather than the clinician's approval.

> Praise: "Well done, I'm proud of you."
> Affirmation: "You rang three services and got fobbed off twice, and you rang the third one anyway. That's persistence."

The righting reflex is the central error the method names: the trained helper's impulse to correct what is wrong, to argue for change, to supply the reasons. The problem is structural. In an ambivalent person, whoever voices the arguments for change causes the other party to voice the arguments against it. A clinician who argues for change reliably produces a client who argues against it, and the client then hears themselves arguing against change, which reduces the likelihood of change.

> Righting reflex: "Look, the reality is if you keep smoking with your lung function where it is, you're going to end up on oxygen. You know that, right?"
> Client: "My grandad smoked until he was ninety."
> MI alternative: "You know more about your lungs than most people do. What's your own read on where this is heading?"

Evidence: a meta-analysis of 119 studies found MI produced statistically significant, durable results in the small effect range against weak comparison conditions (average g = 0.28) and non-significant results against specific active treatments (average g = 0.09) (Lundahl, Kunz, Brownell, Tollefson and Burke, 2010, Research on Social Work Practice). The honest reading is that MI is a good way to start, to engage, and to work with ambivalence, and is not a stand-alone substitute for a specific treatment where one is indicated.

Asking permission before giving information is the standard MI move that keeps the righting reflex in check while still allowing expertise to be shared, often taught as elicit-provide-elicit.

> "Would it be useful if I told you what we know about how this usually goes? ... [information] ... What do you make of that, given your situation?"

heading: Change talk and sustain talk
text:
MI treats the person's own speech as the mechanism. Change talk is any client language favouring change; sustain talk is client language favouring the status quo. Both are normal parts of ambivalence, and the presence of sustain talk is not resistance.

Preparatory change talk is remembered as DARN: Desire ("I want to"), Ability ("I could"), Reasons ("it would help my sleep"), Need ("I have to"). Mobilising change talk is remembered as CAT: Commitment ("I will"), Activation ("I'm ready to"), Taking steps ("I threw them out on Sunday"). Mobilising language is the better predictor of actual change, and the shift from DARN to CAT is what the clinician is listening for.

The core behavioural rule is that people hear themselves talk, and reflecting a category produces more of that category. Reflect sustain talk and you get more sustain talk. Reflect change talk and you get more change talk. This does not mean ignoring sustain talk, which would be poor listening, but it does mean choosing what to reflect and what to place last in a summary.

> Client: "I know it's not doing me any good, but honestly it's the only thing that gets me through the evenings."
> Reflecting sustain talk: "The evenings would be unbearable without it."
> Reflecting change talk: "Some part of you is already clear it's costing you something."
> Double-sided, change talk last: "It's what gets you through the evenings, and you're the one who said it's not doing you any good."

Evoking change talk deliberately:

> "What worries you about how things are now?"
> "If you did decide to change this, how would you go about it?"
> "What are the best things that could happen if you made this change?"
> "Suppose you don't change anything. What do you think things look like in five years?"
> "What's the most important reason, for you, not for anyone else?"

Responding to change talk when it appears, using the acronym EARS: Elaborate ("tell me more about that"), Affirm ("that took something to say"), Reflect, Summarise.

Sustain talk should be reflected accurately and not argued with. Arguing produces more of it.

heading: Rolling with discord, and repairing ruptures in the alliance
text:
The fourth edition of MI retains the distinction that replaced the older term resistance: sustain talk is language about the behaviour, while discord is a problem in the relationship, showing up as arguing, interrupting, dismissing, or disengaging. Discord is treated as a signal about the clinician's current approach rather than a client trait.

Responses to discord: reflect it, shift focus, emphasise autonomy, apologise, or come alongside.

> Emphasising autonomy: "It's completely your call. Nobody can make you do this, and I'm not going to try."
> Coming alongside: "Maybe this isn't the right time for any of it. It might be that the sensible thing is to leave it where it is for now."
> Apologising: "I've been pushing. That's on me, not you."

Ruptures in the alliance are a broader phenomenon: a deterioration in the therapeutic alliance, showing as disagreement on goals, lack of collaboration on tasks, or a strain in the bond. Safran and Muran distinguish withdrawal ruptures, where the client moves away by going compliant, vague, intellectual or silent, and confrontation ruptures, where the client moves against by expressing anger, complaint or dissatisfaction.

Withdrawal is harder to spot and more common. Markers: shorter answers, increased agreement without content, storytelling that goes nowhere, changed topic after a difficult moment, cancellations after intense sessions.

The repair sequence, in order: notice, name it non-defensively, invite the client's account, take real responsibility for the clinician's part without over-apologising, and only then explore what it connects to.

> "Can I stop us? I've had a sense in the last two sessions that we've been going through the motions, and I think that started around the time I pushed the homework. I'd rather hear about that than carry on."

> Client: "Honestly, I thought the whole worksheet thing was pointless."
> Poor: "It can feel that way at first, but the evidence is that it helps."
> Better: "Then I got that wrong, and I'm glad you've said so. What would be worth doing with this time instead?"

Evidence: rupture repair is associated with better outcome. A meta-analysis of 11 studies covering 1,314 patients found a relation between rupture repair episodes and treatment outcome of r = .29, d = .62 (95% CI [.10, .47], p = .003), a moderate association (Eubanks, Muran and Safran, 2018, Psychotherapy 55(4):508-519). Ruptures that are noticed and repaired are not therapy going wrong. Ruptures that go unnoticed, and the client's silent decision not to return, are.

The two common clinician errors in repair are defending the technique and over-apologising. Defending confirms the client's sense that the relationship cannot hold criticism. Over-apologising makes the client responsible for managing the clinician's guilt, which for people who grew up managing an adult's feelings reproduces the original problem exactly.

heading: A catalogue of bad-to-better rewrites
text:
> Client: "My mum died in March and I still can't get through a day without crying."
> Bad: "Grief takes time. There's no timeline, and five months isn't long at all. Have you considered a bereavement group?"
> Better: "Five months, and it's still every day. Tell me about the crying. When does it come?"

> Client: "I hate my job but I can't leave, I've got a mortgage."
> Bad: "It might be worth updating your CV and seeing what's out there. You never know."
> Better: "So it's trapped rather than undecided. How long have you been in that position?"

> Client: "I think I might be a bad person."
> Bad: "You're clearly not. Look at how much you care about your family."
> Better: "That's a heavy thing to be carrying around. What's the evidence you're using?"

> Client: "I didn't do the diary again this week. Sorry."
> Bad: "That's okay. Let's try again this week. Maybe set a reminder on your phone?"
> Better: "No apology needed. I'm more interested in what happened, because that's usually information. When did you last think about doing it?"

> Client: "I don't really want to talk about my dad."
> Bad: "I understand, but it might be important. We can go at your pace."
> Better: "Then we won't. Is it that you don't want to today, or that you don't want to at all? Both are fine answers, they just tell me different things."

> Client: "Do you actually think I can get better?"
> Bad: "Absolutely. I've seen people in much worse situations turn things around."
> Better: "I think what you've got is treatable, and I've seen it treated. I don't know how it'll go for you specifically, and I'd be lying if I said I did. What made you ask now?"

> Client: "I had a few drinks before I came, actually."
> Bad: "Right. Well, that's not ideal for the work, is it."
> Better: "Thanks for telling me, that can't have been easy to say. How are you feeling in yourself right now?"

> Client: "Everyone would be better off without me."
> Bad: "That's the depression talking. Your family love you."
> Better: "I want to slow right down, because that's an important thing to have said. When you say better off without you, are you thinking about ending your life?"

The last pair matters most. Reassurance in response to a suicidal statement closes the disclosure. A direct, calm, specific question opens it, and asking directly about suicide does not plant the idea.

> Better: "I want to slow right down, because that's an important thing to have said. When you say better off without you, are you thinking about ending your life?"

The last pair matters most. Reassurance in response to a suicidal statement closes the disclosure. A direct, calm, specific question opens it, and asking directly about suicide does not plant the idea.

doc_title: The Clinical Assessment Interview and Mental State Examination
doc_summary: How a psychologist structures an assessment interview across presenting problem, history, functioning, and mental state, and how each of those domains changes when the only channel available is text.
heading: What the assessment interview is for
text:
The assessment interview has three jobs at once, and they compete. It gathers the information needed to build a formulation. It establishes enough of a working relationship that the person will keep talking. It begins the intervention, because being asked coherent questions by someone who is listening is itself a change in the person's situation.

Clinicians who treat the interview purely as data collection get thin data. People withhold the material that matters most when they feel processed. Clinicians who treat it purely as rapport-building arrive at the end of an hour with warmth and no history. The skill is running both tracks simultaneously, which means the structure lives in the clinician's head rather than on a clipboard.

The output of an assessment interview is not a diagnosis. It is a formulation: an account of what is happening, how it developed, what maintains it, and what might shift it. Diagnosis, where relevant, is a compressed summary of part of that account. A formulation that explains the person's difficulties in terms of predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating, and protective factors carries more clinical information than a diagnostic label, and it directly implies what to try (Johnstone & Dallos, 2013).

Assessment is not a phase that finishes. The first interview generates hypotheses. Later sessions test them. Information that changes the formulation arrives throughout treatment, often years in. Trauma history in particular is frequently disclosed late, after the person has tested whether the clinician can hold it. Treating the initial assessment as closed is a common error.

The domains below are what a competent assessment covers. The order is not fixed. A skilled interviewer moves between them following the person's material, and audits at the end for what has not been covered. What follows is a coverage checklist, not a script.

Coverage: presenting problem and its history; onset, course, and precipitants; previous episodes and previous treatment; current functioning across work, relationships, sleep, appetite, and substance use; risk; developmental history; family history; medical history and medications; strengths and supports; and the mental state examination.

doc_title: The Clinical Assessment Interview and Mental State Examination
doc_summary: How a psychologist structures an assessment interview across presenting problem, history, functioning, and mental state, and how each of those domains changes when the only channel available is text.
heading: Opening the interview
text:
The opening sets the frame for everything after it. Three things need to happen in the first few minutes: the person needs to know what this is, what happens to what they say, and that they can start wherever they want.

Orientation covers the practical shape of the meeting. How long it will run, what the clinician is trying to work out, and what happens at the end of it. People arrive with wildly different expectations of what an assessment is, including expectations of judgement or of being sectioned. Naming the shape of the hour removes some of that.

Confidentiality and its limits are stated before the person discloses, not after. The limits are specific: risk to self, risk to others, risk to a child, and legal compulsion. Stating them at the start is a fairness issue. A person who discloses suicidal intent and only then learns the clinician may have to act has been ambushed. Most people, told the limits plainly and without drama, disclose anyway.

The first substantive question should be open and should hand control to the person. "What brings you here?" and "Where would you like to start?" both work. "Tell me what has been happening" works when the referral already names a problem. What these have in common is that they do not presuppose the shape of the answer.

Then the clinician gets out of the way. Uninterrupted opening narrative is high-yield and cheap to obtain, and clinicians routinely fail to obtain it. In a secondary analysis of 112 recorded US clinical encounters, clinicians elicited the patient's agenda in only 40 of 112 encounters (36%), interrupted the patient in 27 of those 40 (67%), and the median time to interruption was 11 seconds. Where patients were allowed to finish, they completed their opening statement in a median of 6 seconds (Singh Ospina et al., 2019). The cost of letting someone finish is small and the cost of cutting them off is a reframed agenda. What the person chooses to say first, in what order, and what they leave out is itself assessment data.

In text, the opening changes in specific ways. There is no waiting room, no handshake, no visible clinician. The person may not know whether they are talking to a person, a service, or a model. That has to be stated. The invitation to start anywhere works the same, but the pause that lets someone gather themselves has no equivalent, so a text opening should explicitly signal that a long answer is welcome and that there is no rush.

doc_title: The Clinical Assessment Interview and Mental State Examination
doc_summary: How a psychologist structures an assessment interview across presenting problem, history, functioning, and mental state, and how each of those domains changes when the only channel available is text.
heading: Presenting problem, onset, course, and precipitants
text:
The presenting problem is what the person says is wrong, in their words, before it is translated into clinical categories. Record the words. "I can't get out of bed" and "I'm depressed" are different pieces of data even when they co-occur, and the first is more useful.

Onset asks when this started and how sharply. Insidious onset over months, acute onset over days, and onset the person cannot date at all point in different directions. An acute onset invites questions about what happened in the days before. A gradual onset that the person cannot date sometimes reflects a chronic state they have stopped noticing as abnormal, which is common in dysthymic presentations and in long-term consequences of childhood adversity.

Course asks the shape since onset. Steadily worsening, fluctuating, episodic with full recovery between episodes, or stable at a low level. Episodic course with complete inter-episode recovery raises different possibilities than an unremitting course. Seasonal patterning, menstrual patterning, and patterning that tracks a specific relationship or work cycle are worth asking about directly, because people rarely volunteer them.

Precipitants ask what was happening when it started. The useful question is not "what caused this" but "what was going on in your life around then". People frequently under-report precipitants either because they have normalised the event or because they believe the clinician wants a biological answer. Bereavement, relationship breakdown, job loss, migration, financial shock, illness, and anniversary reactions are the common ones. Absence of an identifiable precipitant is also data.

Severity needs anchoring to function rather than adjectives. "How bad is it" produces uninterpretable answers. "What are you not doing now that you were doing six months ago" produces usable ones. So does asking for a concrete recent day: what time did you wake, what did you do, who did you speak to.

Frequency and duration matter for anything episodic. Panic attacks, binges, self-harm, dissociative episodes, and rage episodes all need a count and a recent example. A detailed walk-through of the most recent instance yields more accurate information than a request for a general pattern, because it anchors recall to a specific memory rather than to the person's theory about themselves.

The final question in this block is the one clinicians most often skip: why now. The person has had this problem for some period and is presenting today. Something changed. It may be that a partner threatened to leave, a GP referred them, a symptom crossed a threshold, or a friend died. The answer to "why now" frequently reveals the actual concern, which is often not the stated presenting problem.

doc_title: The Clinical Assessment Interview and Mental State Examination
doc_summary: How a psychologist structures an assessment interview across presenting problem, history, functioning, and mental state, and how each of those domains changes when the only channel available is text.
heading: Previous episodes and previous treatment
text:
Previous episodes establish whether this is a first presentation or a recurrence, and recurrence changes both prognosis and treatment selection. Ask whether the person has ever felt like this before, and if so when, how long it lasted, and how it resolved. Resolution without treatment, resolution with treatment, and never fully resolving are three different histories.

Previous treatment is the highest-yield and most under-asked part of an assessment. For each prior episode of treatment: what was tried, for how long, at what dose or frequency, with what effect, and why it ended. "CBT didn't work" is not an answer. Four sessions with a trainee that ended when the placement finished is not a trial of CBT. Twenty sessions of properly delivered exposure with no change is.

For medication, ask the drug, the dose, the duration, the response, and the reason for stopping. Stopping because of side effects, stopping because it worked and the person felt better, stopping because it did not work, and stopping because the prescription lapsed are clinically distinct. An apparently failed antidepressant trial that ran two weeks at a subtherapeutic dose is not a failed trial.

Ask what helped, including things that were not treatment. Exercise, a particular relationship, a period of stable work, a move, a religious community. People have usually run their own experiments and the results are informative.

Ask what made things worse, and whether any previous treatment caused harm. Adverse effects of psychological therapy are real and under-recorded, and a person who was harmed by a previous therapist will not raise it unprompted. [UNVERIFIED: specific published prevalence rates for psychotherapy adverse effects were not verifiable within this session; treat the claim as a clinical-practice convention rather than a cited statistic.]

Hospitalisation history, crisis service contact, and involuntary treatment history should be asked directly rather than inferred. So should previous diagnoses, framed carefully: "has anyone given you a diagnosis" rather than "what is your diagnosis". Many people carry diagnoses they were never told about, disagree with, or were given in a five-minute appointment. Record the diagnosis and the person's relationship to it separately.

In text-only contexts the treatment history is one of the more reliably obtainable domains, because it consists largely of factual recall rather than in-the-moment observation. It is also one of the most decision-relevant, since it constrains what to suggest next.

doc_title: The Clinical Assessment Interview and Mental State Examination
doc_summary: How a psychologist structures an assessment interview across presenting problem, history, functioning, and mental state, and how each of those domains changes when the only channel available is text.
heading: Current functioning across domains
text:
Functioning is what converts symptom reports into a picture of a life. Ask about each domain concretely and recently.

Work, study, or primary occupation. Currently doing it or not. Performance changed or not. Days missed. Whether anyone at work has noticed. Whether the job is at risk. For people not in paid work, the equivalent is what structures their day.

Relationships. Who lives with them. Who they would call at 3am. Whether that has changed. Withdrawal from contact is one of the most sensitive general indicators of deterioration and one of the easiest to ask about. Ask about conflict as well as withdrawal, and about caring responsibilities, which are frequently invisible in assessment and heavily load on a person's capacity.

Sleep. Time to bed, time to sleep onset, night waking and what happens then, time of final waking, whether the person feels rested, daytime sleeping, and whether any of this has changed. Early morning waking with inability to return to sleep, initial insomnia driven by rumination, and hypersomnia point in different directions. Reduced need for sleep, meaning less sleep without fatigue, is a different phenomenon from insomnia and is specifically relevant to hypomania and mania.

Appetite and weight. Direction and magnitude of change, over what period, and whether the person is eating regularly. Weight change is more informative than appetite report. Ask about restriction, bingeing, and compensatory behaviour directly rather than waiting for them to be volunteered.

Substances. Alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, prescribed medication used outside prescription, stimulants, opioids, benzodiazepines, and anything else. Ask quantity and frequency in concrete units rather than asking whether the person drinks "a lot". A standard framing is what they drank on each of the last seven days. Ask whether use has increased, whether anyone has expressed concern, and whether they have tried to cut down. The AUDIT-C is three questions and can be embedded conversationally.

Self-care, finances, housing, and legal situation. Housing insecurity and debt are both strongly associated with psychological distress and both are frequently omitted from psychological assessment because they feel like someone else's domain. They shape what interventions are realistic.

Activity and pleasure. What the person does that they enjoy, and whether they still do it. Anhedonia is better detected by asking about activities than by asking about pleasure directly, because people often cannot introspect on the change until they compare against a concrete previous behaviour.

doc_title: The Clinical Assessment Interview and Mental State Examination
doc_summary: How a psychologist structures an assessment interview across presenting problem, history, functioning, and mental state, and how each of those domains changes when the only channel available is text.
heading: Developmental, family, and medical history
text:
Developmental history covers early life circumstances, who raised the person, what the household was like, school experience, friendships, and any early difficulties. In adult assessment this does not require an exhaustive year-by-year account. It requires enough to understand the pattern the person learned to expect from relationships, and enough to detect a neurodevelopmental history.

Neurodevelopmental screening in adults is often missed. Ask about early language, school reports, difficulty with attention or organisation that predates the current problem, sensory sensitivity, social difficulty, and whether anyone in the family has an ADHD or autism diagnosis. Adult ADHD and autism assessment both require evidence of childhood onset, so a developmental account is not optional if these are being considered.

Adverse childhood experiences should be asked about directly but with an explicit opt-out. A workable framing names the categories, states that the person can decline to elaborate, and asks whether any apply. Asking is important because clinicians who wait for spontaneous disclosure mostly do not get it. Not pressing for detail at first assessment is equally important, because a detailed trauma narrative extracted in an assessment interview, with no containment plan and no ongoing relationship, can destabilise the person for days afterwards.

Family history covers psychiatric illness, suicide, substance use, and significant physical illness in first-degree and second-degree relatives. Family history of bipolar disorder is specifically relevant when assessing a depressive presentation, because it raises the prior probability of a bipolar course and changes prescribing considerations. Family history of completed suicide is a risk factor in its own right. Family history is also frequently vague, and "my mother had nerves" or "my father drank" may be the available level of detail.

Medical history covers current and past conditions, surgery, head injury, seizures, endocrine disorders, and anything ongoing. Several medical conditions produce psychiatric presentations. Thyroid dysfunction, anaemia, B12 deficiency, sleep apnoea, epilepsy, delirium, and early neurodegenerative disease are the ones that most often present first to mental health services. A presentation with atypical features, late first onset, fluctuating consciousness, or neurological signs warrants medical review before psychological formulation.

Medications, all of them, including over-the-counter and supplements. Several drugs produce psychiatric effects: corticosteroids, isotretinoin, interferon, some antihypertensives, hormonal contraception in a minority of users, and withdrawal states from benzodiazepines, alcohol, and antidepressants. Ask about adherence without implying an expected answer.

Strengths and supports close this block and should not be a token question. What the person is good at, what they value, what has got them through before, who is in their corner, and what they still care about. This is not a morale exercise. Protective factors are formulation inputs and treatment resources, and they are directly relevant to risk assessment.

doc_title: The Clinical Assessment Interview and Mental State Examination
doc_summary: How a psychologist structures an assessment interview across presenting problem, history, functioning, and mental state, and how each of those domains changes when the only channel available is text.
heading: The mental state examination: what it is
text:
The mental state examination is a structured description of how the person presents at the time of the interview. It is a cross-section, not a history. The history covers what has been happening over time; the MSE covers what is observable now.

The standard domains are appearance, behaviour, speech, mood, affect, thought form, thought content, perception, cognition, insight, and judgement (Psych Scene Hub, 2023; RCEM Learning). Risk is usually documented alongside it or within thought content.

Two things about the MSE are frequently misunderstood. First, most of it is observation rather than questioning. Appearance, behaviour, speech, affect, and thought form are recorded from what the clinician sees and hears, not from what the person reports. Only mood, some thought content, perception, insight, and judgement rely substantially on asking. Second, MSE terms are descriptive rather than diagnostic. "Flight of ideas" describes a speech and thought pattern; it is not a diagnosis of mania.

The MSE should be written so that a clinician who has not met the person can picture them. "Appeared depressed" is useless. "Sat with shoulders forward, made brief eye contact at greeting then looked at the floor, spoke in short sentences with long pauses before answering, did not initiate any topic" is a record. The discipline is describing the observation rather than the inference.

Mood and affect are distinct and the distinction carries information. Mood is the person's reported and sustained emotional state, ideally recorded in their own words. Affect is the observed, moment-to-moment emotional expression, described by range, intensity, reactivity, and congruence with stated mood. A person reporting low mood with a full, reactive affect and a person reporting low mood with a flat, non-reactive affect are presenting differently.

Thought form and thought content are also distinct. Form is how thinking is organised, judged from the structure of speech: linear, circumstantial, tangential, loosening of associations, thought blocking, flight of ideas. Content is what the thoughts are about: preoccupations, ruminations, obsessions, overvalued ideas, delusions, and suicidal or homicidal ideation.

The MSE has known limitations. Inter-rater reliability is variable, terminology is applied inconsistently across clinicians and training traditions, and several domains are heavily influenced by the clinician's cultural expectations of normal presentation. Behaviour read as guarded may be an appropriate response to a service the person has reason to distrust. Speech read as impoverished may reflect a second language. Beliefs read as delusional may be normative within the person's religious or cultural community, which is why the DSM-5 definition of delusion excludes beliefs ordinarily accepted by the person's culture or subculture (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).

The MSE should be written so that a clinician who has not met the person can picture them. "Appeared depressed" is useless. "Sat with shoulders forward, made brief eye contact at greeting then looked at the floor, spoke in short sentences with long pauses before answering, did not initiate any topic" is a record. The discipline is describing the observation rather than the inference.

Mood and affect are distinct and the distinction carries information. Mood is the person's reported and sustained emotional state, ideally recorded in their own words. Affect is the observed, moment-to-moment emotional expression, described by range, intensity, reactivity, and congruence with stated mood. A person reporting low mood with a full, reactive affect and a person reporting low mood with a flat, non-reactive affect are presenting differently.

Thought form and thought content are also distinct. Form is how thinking is organised, judged from the structure of speech: linear, circumstantial, tangential, loosening of associations, thought blocking, flight of ideas. Content is what the thoughts are about: preoccupations, ruminations, obsessions, overvalued ideas, delusions, and suicidal or homicidal ideation.

The MSE has known limitations. Inter-rater reliability is variable, terminology is applied inconsistently across clinicians and training traditions, and several domains are heavily influenced by the clinician's cultural expectations of normal presentation. Behaviour read as guarded may be an appropriate response to a service the person has reason to distrust. Speech read as impoverished may reflect a second language. Beliefs read as delusional may be normative within the person's religious or cultural community, which is why the DSM-5 definition of delusion excludes beliefs ordinarily accepted by the person's culture or subculture (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).

doc_title: The Clinical Assessment Interview and Mental State Examination
doc_summary: How a psychologist structures an assessment interview across presenting problem, history, functioning, and mental state, and how each of those domains changes when the only channel available is text.
heading: The mental state examination without visual or auditory access
text:
In a text-only context, most of the MSE is unavailable. This has to be stated plainly rather than worked around, because the failure mode is a model producing a confident MSE from material that cannot support one.

Not available at all. Appearance: grooming, clothing, weight, physical signs, evidence of self-harm, pupils, tremor. Behaviour: psychomotor retardation or agitation, eye contact, restlessness, response to internal stimuli, rapport as felt in the room. Speech: rate, volume, prosody, latency, pressure, dysarthria, and slurring. These are the domains that carry the most weight in detecting mania, psychosis, intoxication, and organic states, and none of them survive the transition to text.

Partially available, with heavy caveats. Thought form is partially inferable from written structure, since tangentiality, circumstantiality, and loss of coherence can show up in writing. Writing is edited, composed at the person's own pace, and often assisted, so disorganisation is masked and fluency is inflated relative to speech. Affect is not observable, though affect words, punctuation, and message length carry weak signal. Cognition can be probed only for orientation and gross memory, not for attention, working memory, or executive function in any valid way.

Available by report. Mood, as the person describes it. Thought content, if asked about. Perceptual experiences, if asked about. Insight and judgement, partially, from how the person accounts for their situation and describes recent decisions.

The practical rule is that a text-only assessment substitutes asking for observing. Anything that would normally be observed must either be asked about explicitly or left unrecorded. "Do you feel slowed down, or restless and unable to sit still?" replaces watching for psychomotor change. "Has anyone commented on how fast you have been talking?" replaces hearing pressure of speech. "Are you sleeping?" is asked rather than inferred from presentation.

Two things should never appear in a text-only record. An inferred observation stated as if observed, such as describing affect as flat when no affect was visible. And a confident MSE section covering domains that were never accessible. A text-only mental state record should name what was assessed, by what means, and what could not be assessed.

Collateral information is also usually absent, and its absence is more significant in text than face to face. Mania, psychosis, and cognitive decline are frequently invisible from the inside, and the standard correction is an informant. Without one, a text-only assessment of these presentations is not just limited but structurally unable to detect the presentations where self-report is least reliable.

doc_title: The Clinical Assessment Interview and Mental State Examination
doc_summary: How a psychologist structures an assessment interview across presenting problem, history, functioning, and mental state, and how each of those domains changes when the only channel available is text.
heading: Moving between domains without interrogating
text:
The difference between an interview and an interrogation is mostly transitions. A clinician who asks a list of questions in fixed order produces short answers and a person who feels processed. The techniques below are what keeps coverage without that effect.

Funnelling. Open each domain with an open question, then narrow only as needed. Sleep starts with "how have you been sleeping" and narrows to onset latency and early waking only if the open question does not cover it. Closing down too early wastes the domain, because a person answering a closed question stops volunteering.

Signposting transitions. Name the move before making it. "Can I ask about something different for a moment, about how you have been sleeping and eating." This costs a sentence and removes the sense of being ambushed by a topic change. Unsignposted jumps, particularly into substances, sex, or trauma, read as accusatory.

Following affect. When the person's emotional register changes, that is the material. Following it produces better information than continuing the checklist. The domain being abandoned can be returned to.

Normalising before sensitive questions. Framing a question so that a yes is clearly expectable increases disclosure. "When people are as low as you describe, they often have thoughts of not wanting to be here. Has that happened for you?" is more likely to yield an accurate answer than "any thoughts of self-harm?". The normalising frame must be honest rather than manipulative; the point is removing the implication that a yes is shameful.

Concrete anchoring. Ask about the last time rather than the usual. "Tell me about the last time that happened" produces specific, checkable detail. "What is it usually like" produces the person's summary theory.

Summarising and checking. Periodically reflect back what has been understood and invite correction. This does three things: it corrects errors, it demonstrates listening, and it gives the person a chance to add what the clinician has framed wrongly.

Silence. Leaving a pause after a difficult answer often produces the more important second answer. This is the single technique with no text equivalent. In text, the closest substitute is asking a short open follow-up rather than moving on, and explicitly saying there is no rush.

Not filling gaps with reassurance. Premature reassurance closes topics. "I'm sure it will get better" ends a disclosure. Acknowledgement without resolution keeps it open.

Two failure modes are worth naming. The interviewer who follows every thread and covers three domains in an hour, and the interviewer who covers all domains and learns nothing that was not on the form. Competent interviewing keeps both the structure and the responsiveness, and audits coverage near the end rather than enforcing it throughout.

doc_title: The Clinical Assessment Interview and Mental State Examination
doc_summary: How a psychologist structures an assessment interview across presenting problem, history, functioning, and mental state, and how each of those domains changes when the only channel available is text.
heading: Closing the interview
text:
Closing badly undoes a good interview. A person who has spent an hour disclosing and is then dismissed on time with no synthesis leaves more exposed than when they arrived.

Signal the ending in advance. Ten minutes out, say so. This lets the person raise anything they have been holding, which is frequently the most important item.

Ask the sweep question. "Is there anything I haven't asked about that I should have?" or "is there anything you came in wanting to say that we haven't got to?" This routinely produces material that the structured domains missed, because the clinician's map of relevance is not the person's.

Check risk before closing if it has not already been covered, and cover it explicitly rather than by inference. An assessment that has stirred up difficult material and ends without a risk check is incomplete.

Give something back. A brief, provisional formulation in plain language: what the clinician thinks may be happening, held loosely and offered for correction. This is not a diagnosis announcement. It is a demonstration that the hour produced something, and it lets the person say the clinician has it wrong. Many people leave assessments with no idea what the clinician concluded.

State what happens next, concretely. Who will contact them, when, what the options are, and what to do if things worsen before then. Vagueness at this point is a common source of disengagement.

Check the effect of the interview itself. "How was that to talk about?" Assessment interviews can destabilise, particularly where trauma has been touched. Asking takes seconds and identifies the person who needs a safety plan before leaving.

In text, closing has the same structure with two differences. There is no time boundary forcing the close, so it has to be created deliberately rather than arriving. And there is no observation of how the person leaves, so the effect of the conversation must be asked about rather than seen.

doc_title: The Clinical Assessment Interview and Mental State Examination
doc_summary: How a psychologist structures an assessment interview across presenting problem, history, functioning, and mental state, and how each of those domains changes when the only channel available is text.
heading: Semi-structured interviews: SCID-5 and the MINI
text:
Unstructured clinical interviews are unreliable for diagnosis. Two clinicians interviewing the same person unstructured frequently reach different diagnoses, because they ask different questions and apply criteria inconsistently. Semi-structured interviews exist to fix that.

The SCID-5 is the standard diagnostic interview for DSM-5, developed by First, Williams, Karg, and Spitzer and published by American Psychiatric Association Publishing in 2016. It walks the interviewer through DSM-5 criteria, with interview questions printed alongside each criterion, and each criterion rated present or absent. It comes in several configurations. The Clinician Version (SCID-5-CV) is an abridged bound booklet covering the diagnoses most common in clinical settings. The Research Version (SCID-5-RV) is broader, available in core and enhanced configurations, and is distributed as modifiable documents so studies can select modules. The SCID-5-CT is adapted for clinical trials. The SCID-5-PD covers the ten DSM-5 personality disorders and comes with a screening questionnaire, the SCID-5-SPQ (Columbia University Department of Psychiatry, n.d.; American Psychiatric Association Publishing, n.d.).

The SCID requires clinical training. The publishers state there is no minimum degree requirement but that clinical experience sufficient to conduct an unstructured diagnostic evaluation is the substantive requirement, since the interviewer must judge whether a reported experience actually meets a criterion. Non-clinicians with substantial diagnostic experience in a specific population can be trained. Use of the User's Guide is treated as essential, and reference interviews with expert ratings exist for calibration.

The MINI (Mini-International Neuropsychiatric Interview) is a shorter structured diagnostic interview developed by Sheehan and colleagues, designed for a comparable purpose in far less time. The original validation reported a mean administration time of 18.7 minutes with a median of 15 minutes, against a mean of about 35 minutes for the SCID-P, with reliability and validity properties described as broadly comparable (Sheehan et al., 1998; Lecrubier et al., 1997).

Agreement between the MINI and the SCID varies substantially by diagnosis. A validation against the SCID-5-CV reported good to excellent kappa for psychotic disorders (0.88), substance-related disorders (0.86), bipolar disorder (0.85), major depressive disorder (0.84), obsessive-compulsive disorder (0.74), and mental disorder due to another medical condition (0.70), but markedly lower agreement for generalised anxiety disorder (0.44) and PTSD (0.32). Structured interviews are not uniformly reliable across the diagnostic system, and the categories with the weakest agreement are worth holding loosely.

What structured interviews add is criterion coverage and consistency. They ask about disorders the clinician would not have thought to ask about, they apply the same threshold each time, and they make the diagnostic reasoning auditable. What they do not add is formulation. A SCID produces a list of met criteria. It does not explain why this person developed this problem at this time, and it does not indicate what to do. In routine clinical practice most services do not administer them, which is a reasonable trade-off for time but does mean routine diagnosis is less reliable than research diagnosis.

heading: The Cultural Formulation Interview
text:
The DSM-5 Cultural Formulation Interview is a structured supplement for eliciting the cultural context of a presentation. It exists because standard assessment structures embed assumptions about how distress is expressed, what causes it, and what should be done about it, and those assumptions are not universal.

The core CFI is 16 questions with prompts, organised around four domains: the cultural definition of the problem; cultural perceptions of cause, context, and support; cultural factors affecting self-coping and past help seeking; and cultural factors affecting current help seeking. An Informant Version can be administered to family or other supports, and 12 supplementary modules expand specific domains or populations (Lewis-Fernández et al., 2016; American Psychiatric Association, 2013).

The most useful part in practice is the first domain, which asks the person to describe the problem in their own terms and in the terms their family and community would use. This routinely surfaces explanatory models that do not map onto psychiatric categories, including somatic idioms of distress, spiritual and religious explanations, and social or relational framings. A clinician who does not know the person's explanatory model will propose treatments that do not make sense to them, and will read non-adherence as resistance.

The CFI also asks directly about barriers to care, including previous experiences of discrimination in health settings, and about what the person and their family think should be done. These are ordinary clinical questions that standard assessment structures often omit.

The relevance to text-only assessment is that cultural context is invisible in text unless it is asked about, and inferring it from language is unreliable. Language style, idiom, and register are shaped by education, region, first language, platform, and audience, and none of these map cleanly to cultural background. A model reasoning about a text conversation has less cultural information than a clinician in a room, not more, and should not treat linguistic features as evidence about identity.

doc_title: Screening and Outcome Instruments: Scoring, Properties, and Misuse
doc_summary: What each common mental health measure actually assesses, its verified scoring bands and cut-points, its sensitivity and specificity where established, and the specific way each one gets misused.
heading: Screening instruments are not diagnostic tests
text:
Every instrument in this file is a screening or severity measure. None of them diagnoses anything. The distinction is not a disclaimer, it is a statement about what the numbers mean.

A screening instrument sorts people into a group who probably warrant further assessment and a group who probably do not. It is calibrated to be cheap, fast, and sensitive, and it accepts a high false-positive rate as the price. A diagnostic assessment is a structured evaluation against criteria, conducted by a clinician, incorporating history, duration, functional impairment, differential consideration, and exclusion of medical and substance causes. The reference standard against which screening instruments are validated is a semi-structured diagnostic interview, not another questionnaire.

Three consequences follow, and all three are routinely violated in practice.

A score above a cut-point is a positive screen, not a diagnosis. "PHQ-9 of 16" means the person reported symptoms at a level that warrants clinical assessment. It does not mean they have major depressive disorder, and a majority of positive screens in low-prevalence settings are false positives, which the next section quantifies.

Severity bands are conventions, not natural categories. The boundary between "moderate" and "moderately severe" on the PHQ-9 is a line drawn on a continuum. A person scoring 14 and a person scoring 15 are not meaningfully different, and given measurement error they are frequently not even reliably different, as covered in the interpretation file.

The instrument measures self-report under specific conditions. Change the wording, the response options, the recall window, or who does the rating, and the published properties no longer apply. This includes the case where a system reads a conversation and estimates what someone would have scored, which is not administration.

One further point applies across all of them. These instruments were largely developed and validated in high-income, English-speaking, predominantly white samples. Cut-points in particular are the least transportable component, because a cut-point encodes both the item functioning and the base rate of the validation sample.
