doc_summary: What each common mental health measure actually assesses, its verified scoring bands and cut-points, its sensitivity and specificity where established, and the specific way each one gets misused.
heading: Base rates and positive predictive value: a worked example
text:
Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test. Positive predictive value is a property of the test in a population, and it is what a clinician actually needs to know. The gap between them is the most consequential piece of arithmetic in screening.

Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the condition who screen positive. Specificity is the proportion of people without the condition who screen negative. Positive predictive value (PPV) is the proportion of people who screen positive who actually have the condition. PPV depends on prevalence, and it collapses as prevalence falls.

Take the PHQ-9 at its standard cut-point of 10. The individual participant data meta-analysis by Levis, Benedetti and Thombs (2019), pooling 29 studies and 6,725 participants against a semi-structured interview reference standard, found sensitivity 0.88 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.92) and specificity 0.85 (95% CI 0.82 to 0.88). Hold those fixed and vary prevalence.

Scenario A, general adult population screening. Take an 8% prevalence of past-year major depressive episode, close to the NIMH figure of 8.3% for US adults in 2021. In 10,000 people, 800 have the condition and 9,200 do not.
True positives: 800 × 0.88 = 704.
False negatives: 96.
False positives: 9,200 × 0.15 = 1,380.
True negatives: 7,820.
PPV = 704 / (704 + 1,380) = 704 / 2,084 = 33.8%.
Roughly two out of every three positive screens are wrong.

Scenario B, community screening at a lower point prevalence of 2%. In 10,000 people, 200 have the condition.
True positives: 176. False positives: 9,800 × 0.15 = 1,470.
PPV = 176 / 1,646 = 10.7%.
Nearly nine out of ten positive screens are wrong.

Scenario C, a psychiatric outpatient clinic where prevalence is 30%. In 10,000 people, 3,000 have the condition.
True positives: 2,640. False positives: 7,000 × 0.15 = 1,050.
PPV = 2,640 / 3,690 = 71.5%.

The test did not change. Its sensitivity and specificity are identical in all three. What changed is the prior probability, and PPV moved from 11% to 72%. Levis et al. flag this directly, noting that at cut-point 10 in low-prevalence settings PPV can be around 49%, meaning about half of positive screens are false.

Negative predictive value moves the opposite way and is high in low-prevalence settings. In Scenario A, NPV is 7,820 / 7,916 = 98.8%. A negative screen in a low-prevalence population is fairly informative; a positive one is not.

Three practical rules. Interpret any positive screen against the setting it was administered in. Expect most positives in unselected populations to be false and plan the follow-up assessment accordingly rather than treating the screen as the finding. [03-assessment / instruments.md] Screening and Outcome Instruments: Scoring, Properties, and Misuse

Base rates and positive predictive value: a worked example

Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test. Positive predictive value is a property of the test in a population, and it is what a clinician actually needs to know. The gap between them is the most consequential piece of arithmetic in screening.

Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the condition who screen positive. Specificity is the proportion of people without the condition who screen negative. Positive predictive value (PPV) is the proportion of people who screen positive who actually have the condition. PPV depends on prevalence, and it collapses as prevalence falls.

Take the PHQ-9 at its standard cut-point of 10. The individual participant data meta-analysis by Levis, Benedetti and Thombs (2019), pooling 29 studies and 6,725 participants against a semi-structured interview reference standard, found sensitivity 0.88 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.92) and specificity 0.85 (95% CI 0.82 to 0.88). Hold those fixed and vary prevalence.

Scenario A, general adult population screening. Take an 8% prevalence of past-year major depressive episode, close to the NIMH figure of 8.3% for US adults in 2021. In 10,000 people, 800 have the condition and 9,200 do not.
True positives: 800 × 0.88 = 704.
False negatives: 96.
False positives: 9,200 × 0.15 = 1,380.
True negatives: 7,820.
PPV = 704 / (704 + 1,380) = 704 / 2,084 = 33.8%.
Roughly two out of every three positive screens are wrong.

Scenario B, community screening at a lower point prevalence of 2%. In 10,000 people, 200 have the condition.
True positives: 176. False positives: 9,800 × 0.15 = 1,470.
PPV = 176 / 1,646 = 10.7%.
Nearly nine out of ten positive screens are wrong.

Scenario C, a psychiatric outpatient clinic where prevalence is 30%. In 10,000 people, 3,000 have the condition.
True positives: 2,640. False positives: 7,000 × 0.15 = 1,050.
PPV = 2,640 / 3,690 = 71.5%.

The test did not change. Its sensitivity and specificity are identical in all three. What changed is the prior probability, and PPV moved from 11% to 72%. Levis et al. flag this directly, noting that at cut-point 10 in low-prevalence settings PPV can be around 49%, meaning about half of positive screens are false.

Negative predictive value moves the opposite way and is high in low-prevalence settings. In Scenario A, NPV is 7,820 / 7,916 = 98.8%. A negative screen in a low-prevalence population is fairly informative; a positive one is not.

Three practical rules. Interpret any positive screen against the setting it was administered in. Expect most positives in unselected populations to be false and plan the follow-up assessment accordingly rather than treating the screen as the finding. And never quote a sensitivity or specificity figure as though it told you the probability that this person has the condition, because it does not; that is the inverse probability and it requires the base rate.

heading: PHQ-9
text:
What it measures. Depressive symptom severity over the past two weeks, mapped onto the nine DSM criteria for major depressive episode. Developed by Kroenke, Spitzer and Williams (2001). Public domain and free to use.

Structure and scoring. Nine items, each rated 0 (not at all), 1 (several days), 2 (more than half the days), 3 (nearly every day). Total range 0 to 27. A tenth question about functional difficulty is asked but not scored into the total.

Severity bands. 0 to 4 minimal, 5 to 9 mild, 10 to 14 moderate, 15 to 19 moderately severe, 20 to 27 severe.

Psychometrics. The original validation (Kroenke et al., 2001, N = 580, against independent structured mental health professional interview) reported sensitivity 88% and specificity 88% at a cut-point of 10. The individual participant data meta-analysis by Levis et al. Accuracy varied by reference standard: against fully structured interviews sensitivity fell to 0.70 with specificity 0.84, and against the MINI sensitivity was 0.77 with specificity 0.87. This variation is itself informative, since it shows that a substantial part of what looks like test accuracy is a property of what the test is being compared against.

Item 9. The final item asks about thoughts of being better off dead or of self-harm. It is treated differently from the other items: any endorsement counts, regardless of the frequency selected. A positive response requires direct suicide risk assessment by someone competent to conduct one. It is a prompt to ask, not a risk assessment in itself, and it has poor predictive value for suicide as a standalone item.

heading: GAD-7
text:
What it measures. Generalised anxiety symptom severity over the past two weeks. Developed by Spitzer, Kroenke, Williams and Löwe (2006). Public domain.

Structure and scoring. Seven items, each rated 0 to 3 on the same frequency anchors as the PHQ-9. Total range 0 to 21.

Severity bands. 0 to 4 minimal, 5 to 9 mild, 10 to 14 moderate, 15 to 21 severe.

Psychometrics. At a cut-point of 10, the original validation reported sensitivity 89% and specificity 82% for generalised anxiety disorder (Spitzer et al., 2006). [UNVERIFIED against primary text: the original paper is paywalled with no open deposit; these figures were confirmed only through direct quotation in a peer-reviewed secondary source.] Kroenke et al. (2007, Annals of Internal Medicine 146(5):317-25) reported that the GAD-7 and GAD-2 performed well across four anxiety disorders with areas under the curve ranging from 0.80 to 0.91. [UNVERIFIED: the frequently quoted per-disorder sensitivity and specificity pairs for panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and PTSD could not be confirmed against the primary text.] A meta-analysis by Plummer et al. (2016) across 12 samples and 5,223 participants reported acceptable performance at cut-points 7 to 10 with optimal performance at 8 (sensitivity 0.83, specificity 0.84). [UNVERIFIED: secondary-sourced only.]

The critical caveat. The cut-point of 10 does not transport to psychiatric or high-comorbidity populations. In a specialty outpatient anxiety and mood clinic sample (N = 536), a cut-point of 10 yielded sensitivity 79.5% but specificity of only 44.7%, and no cut-point achieved an acceptable balance, with AUCs of 0.65 to 0.74 (Rutter & Brown, 2016). Kertz et al. (2013) reported a comparable pattern in a psychiatric sample with sensitivity 83% and specificity 46%. The authors concluded the GAD-7 works better as a dimensional severity index in such settings than as a binary screener. This is the clearest available demonstration that a published cut-point belongs to a validation population.

Misuse to avoid. Reading a high GAD-7 as evidence specifically of generalised anxiety disorder; it is elevated across anxiety, depressive, and trauma presentations, and the GAD-7 and PHQ-9 correlate strongly with each other. Using it to screen in a psychiatric population at the primary care cut-point.

heading: DASS-21
text:
What it measures. Three correlated dimensions of negative emotional state over the past week: Depression, Anxiety, and Stress. Derived from the 42-item DASS by Lovibond and Lovibond (1995). Free for research and clinical use; the manual is purchased.

Structure and scoring. Twenty-one items, seven per subscale, each rated 0 to 3. Subscale scores are summed and then multiplied by 2 so they are comparable to DASS-42 norms. Each subscale therefore ranges 0 to 42 after doubling.

Severity bands, applied to the doubled scores.
Depression: Normal 0 to 9, Mild 10 to 13, Moderate 14 to 20, Severe 21 to 27, Extremely Severe 28 and above.
Anxiety: Normal 0 to 7, Mild 8 to 9, Moderate 10 to 14, Severe 15 to 19, Extremely Severe 20 and above.
Stress: Normal 0 to 14, Mild 15 to 18, Moderate 19 to 25, Severe 26 to 33, Extremely Severe 34 and above.

What the subscales cover. The Depression scale assesses dysphoria, hopelessness, devaluation of life, self-deprecation, lack of interest, anhedonia, and inertia. The Anxiety scale assesses autonomic arousal, skeletal muscle effects, situational anxiety, and subjective anxious affect. The Stress scale assesses chronic non-specific arousal: difficulty relaxing, nervous arousal, being easily upset, irritability, and impatience.

The explicit non-diagnostic statement. The DASS scoring documentation states directly that the instrument is built on a dimensional rather than categorical conception, that differences between normal and clinical populations are differences of degree, and that the DASS-21 therefore "has no direct implications for the allocation of patients to discrete diagnostic categories postulated in classificatory systems such as the DSM and ICD" (DASS-21 scoring instructions, Lovibond & Lovibond, 1995). This is the clearest statement of the screening-versus-diagnosis distinction that any of these instruments makes about itself, and it is routinely ignored by people reporting "severe depression on the DASS".

Misuse to avoid. Treating the Anxiety subscale as a general anxiety measure; it is weighted toward physiological arousal and under-detects worry-dominant presentations, which is why Stress and Anxiety often behave unexpectedly. Forgetting to double the subscale scores, which produces spuriously normal results. Reporting band labels as if they were diagnoses. Note also that the recall window is one week, shorter than the PHQ-9 and GAD-7, so the scales are not interchangeable across timeframes.

heading: K10
text:
What it measures. Non-specific psychological distress, meaning the anxiety and depressive symptom load that is common across conditions rather than specific to any one. Developed by Kessler and colleagues (Kessler et al., 2002, Psychological Medicine 32(6):959-976). Widely used in Australian services and population surveys.

Structure and scoring. Ten items about frequency of distress symptoms, each rated 1 (none of the time) to 5 (all of the time), with a four-week recall period. Total range 10 to 50.

Interpretation bands. The Australian bands, attributable to Andrews and Slade (2001, Australian and New Zealand Journal of Public Health 25(6):494-497) and used by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, are: Low 10 to 15, Moderate 16 to 21, High 22 to 29, Very High 30 to 50.

A discrepancy worth knowing about. Alternative band systems circulate in clinical software and service documentation, including one that sets the boundaries at 20, 25, and 30. These are not interchangeable with the Andrews and Slade bands and a score can fall in different categories depending on which set is applied. Check which convention a given score was interpreted under before comparing across services. [UNVERIFIED: an alternative 0 to 40 scoring convention, with items scored 0 to 4, is sometimes referenced; no citable source confirming it was located, so treat the 10 to 50 range as the standard and verify the range before interpreting any K10 score.]

Psychometrics and what it is for. The K10's value is as a brief distress screen and a population-level monitoring tool. It performs reasonably at detecting the presence of a common mental disorder and poorly at saying which one, by design, since non-specificity is the construct. A high K10 tells you someone is distressed and warrants assessment. It tells you nothing about whether that distress is depression, anxiety, trauma-related, substance-related, or a response to circumstances.

Misuse to avoid. Using it as a depression measure. Using it as an outcome measure without a reliable change threshold. Using band labels as severity of a disorder rather than severity of distress. And treating "Low" as reassurance in someone reporting suicidal ideation, since distress and risk are different constructs and the K10 does not assess risk at all.

doc_summary: What each common mental health measure actually assesses, its verified scoring bands and cut-points, its sensitivity and specificity where established, and the specific way each one gets misused.
heading: BDI-II
text:
What it measures. Depressive symptom severity over the past two weeks including today. Developed by Beck, Steer and Brown (1996) as a revision of the original BDI, realigned to DSM-IV criteria.

Structure and scoring. Twenty-one items, each a set of four statements graded 0 to 3 in increasing severity, from which the respondent selects the one that best fits. Total range 0 to 63.

Severity bands. 0 to 13 minimal, 14 to 19 mild, 20 to 28 moderate, 29 to 63 severe.

Copyright status. The BDI-II is proprietary and owned by Pearson. It requires purchase and user qualification, and reproducing the items is copyright infringement. This matters practically: it is the main reason the PHQ-9 has displaced it in routine care, since the PHQ-9 is free, shorter, and directly criterion-mapped.

Psychometrics. Unlike the PHQ-9 and GAD-7, the BDI-II does not have a single canonical screening cut-point with a universally reported sensitivity and specificity pair. The severity bands are the primary interpretive framework, and reported cut-point accuracy varies substantially by the population assessed, particularly in medically ill samples where the somatic items inflate scores. No single figure should be quoted as the BDI-II's sensitivity.

Misuse to avoid. Using it in medically unwell or older populations without accounting for somatic item confounding. Comparing BDI-II scores directly to PHQ-9 scores, which is a different scale with a different range and different bands. Reproducing the items.

heading: PCL-5
text:
What it measures. The severity of the 20 DSM-5 PTSD symptoms. Maintained by the US Department of Veterans Affairs National Center for PTSD and freely available to clinicians and researchers.

Structure and scoring. Twenty items, each rated 0 (not at all) to 4 (extremely), with a past-month default recall period; past-week and extended versions with Criterion A assessment exist. Total range 0 to 80.

Two interpretation methods, which the VA presents side by side rather than preferring one.

Cut-point method. The VA states that initial research suggests a cut-point between 31 and 33 is indicative of probable PTSD across samples, with the explicit guidance that a lower cut-point should be considered when screening or when maximising detection is desirable, and a higher cut-point when attempting a provisional diagnosis or minimising false positives. The underlying study is Bovin et al. (2016, Psychological Assessment 28(11):1379-1391), which examined two veteran samples (N = 468) against the CAPS-5 and found 31 to 33 optimally efficient, reporting kappa of 0.58. [UNVERIFIED: exact sensitivity and specificity percentages at the 31 to 33 cut-point could not be confirmed against the primary text; secondary sources report inconsistent figures. Do not quote a specific sensitivity or specificity for this cut-point.]

DSM-5 symptom cluster method. Treat each item rated 2 (moderately) or higher as endorsed, then require at least one Criterion B item (questions 1 to 5), one C item (6 to 7), two D items (8 to 14), and two E items (15 to 20).

Change interpretation. The VA suggests 10 points as an indicator of response, and a post-treatment score below 28 as an indicator of clinically significant change, citing Marx et al. (2022, Psychological Assessment 34(2):197-203). That study was conducted in male veterans, so the thresholds carry the population caveat that applies to every other number in this file.

Misuse to avoid. Treating a score above 33 as a PTSD diagnosis; the reference standard remains a structured clinical interview, the CAPS-5. Administering it without establishing a Criterion A event, since the items ask about responses to a specific stressful experience and are uninterpretable without one. Using it to screen general populations, where PPV will be low. And administering it in a text conversation as a way of extracting a trauma narrative, which risks destabilising the person with no containment available.

heading: AUDIT and AUDIT-C
text:
AUDIT. The Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test, developed by the WHO (Babor, Higgins-Biddle, Saunders & Monteiro, 2nd edition, 2001). Ten items: three on consumption, three on dependence symptoms, four on alcohol-related problems. Items 1 to 8 are scored 0 to 4 and items 9 to 10 are scored 0, 2, or 4. Total range 0 to 40.

Risk zones from the WHO manual, which map to actions rather than to diagnoses. Zone I, 0 to 7: alcohol education. Zone II, 8 to 15: simple advice. Zone III, 16 to 19: simple advice plus brief counselling and continued monitoring. Zone IV, 20 to 40: referral to a specialist for diagnostic evaluation.

Psychometrics. The manual states that at the recommended cut-off of 8, most studies have found very favourable sensitivity and usually lower but still acceptable specificity. In the original multinational development sample (Saunders et al., 1993), sensitivities were generally in the mid-0.90s and specificities averaged in the 0.80s. A cut-off of 10 trades sensitivity for greater specificity.

Population adjustment. The manual states that setting the cut-off one point lower, at 7, for all women and for men over 65 will increase sensitivity in those groups. One cited study of elderly hospital patients found low sensitivity and high specificity above age 65 at the standard cut-off.

AUDIT-C. The first three consumption items, used as a very brief screen. Range 0 to 12.

Cut-point attribution, which is commonly reported wrongly. Bush, Kivlahan, McDonell et al. (1998, Archives of Internal Medicine 158(16):1789-1795) validated the AUDIT-C in a male-only VA outpatient sample (n = 243 analysed, mean age 67; the six women in the sample were excluded from the analytic set). AUDIT and AUDIT-C

AUDIT. The Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test, developed by the WHO (Babor, Higgins-Biddle, Saunders & Monteiro, 2nd edition, 2001). Ten items: three on consumption, three on dependence symptoms, four on alcohol-related problems. Items 1 to 8 are scored 0 to 4 and items 9 to 10 are scored 0, 2, or 4. Total range 0 to 40.

Risk zones from the WHO manual, which map to actions rather than to diagnoses. Zone I, 0 to 7: alcohol education. Zone II, 8 to 15: simple advice. Zone III, 16 to 19: simple advice plus brief counselling and continued monitoring. Zone IV, 20 to 40: referral to a specialist for diagnostic evaluation.

Psychometrics. The manual states that at the recommended cut-off of 8, most studies have found very favourable sensitivity and usually lower but still acceptable specificity. In the original multinational development sample (Saunders et al., 1993), sensitivities were generally in the mid-0.90s and specificities averaged in the 0.80s. Population adjustment. The manual states that setting the cut-off one point lower, at 7, for all women and for men over 65 will increase sensitivity in those groups. One cited study of elderly hospital patients found low sensitivity and high specificity above age 65 at the standard cut-off.

doc_summary: What each common mental health measure actually assesses, its verified scoring bands and cut-points, its sensitivity and specificity where established, and the specific way each one gets misused.
heading: ASRS v1.1
text:
What it measures. Adult ADHD symptoms, mapped to DSM-IV criteria. Developed with the World Health Organization. Freely available.

Structure and scoring. The full instrument has 18 items. Part A is a six-item screener, which is the part most commonly used. Scoring uses per-item thresholds rather than a simple sum: for questions 1 to 3, a response of "sometimes" or higher counts as positive; for questions 4 to 6, only "often" or higher counts. Four or more positive items on Part A is a positive screen warranting further evaluation. [The scoring rule is taken from a widely reproduced version of the official instructions; the primary Harvard-hosted document was not directly accessible for confirmation.]

Psychometrics. Kessler et al. (2005, Psychological Medicine) validated it in an NCS-R clinical reappraisal subsample (n = 154, oversampled for childhood ADHD and adult persistence). The six-item Part A screener achieved sensitivity 68.7%, specificity 99.5%, total classification accuracy 97.9%, and kappa 0.76. The full 18-item version performed worse as a classifier: sensitivity 56.3%, specificity 98.3%, accuracy 96.2%, kappa 0.58. Kessler et al. (2007, International Journal of Methods in Psychiatric Research 16(2):52-65) replicated in a representative health plan sample and reported an AUC of 0.90, but did not report sensitivity and specificity, so the 68.7% and 99.5% figures belong specifically to the 2005 paper.

Note the shape of those numbers. Specificity is very high and sensitivity is moderate, which is unusual for a screener and means the ASRS Part A misses roughly a third of cases while rarely producing false positives in that validation sample. That trade-off inverts in low-prevalence unselected populations and in self-selected populations seeking assessment.

A separate instrument. A DSM-5-updated ASRS exists (Üstün et al., 2017, JAMA Psychiatry) with different properties, reported sensitivity around 91% and more variable specificity of 74% to 96%. It is a different revision and its numbers should not be attached to the v1.1 screener.

Misuse to avoid. Treating a positive Part A as an ADHD diagnosis. Adult ADHD diagnosis requires evidence of childhood-onset symptoms, impairment in more than one setting, and exclusion of alternative explanations including anxiety, depression, trauma, sleep disorder, and substance use, all of which produce inattention. Self-administered ASRS results from people who have already concluded they have ADHD carry substantial expectancy effects.

doc_summary: What each common mental health measure actually assesses, its verified scoring bands and cut-points, its sensitivity and specificity where established, and the specific way each one gets misused.
heading: AQ-10
text:
What it measures. A brief screen for autistic traits, abbreviated from the 50-item Autism Spectrum Quotient. Developed by Allison, Auyeung and Baron-Cohen (2012, Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry 51(2):202-212).

Structure and scoring. Ten items, one point per item scored in the autism-consistent direction. Range 0 to 10. The adult cut-point is 6 or above.

Psychometrics as originally reported. At a cut-point of 6 or above, sensitivity 0.88, specificity 0.91, positive predictive value 0.85 (Allison et al., 2012).

Psychometrics in clinical populations, which are much worse. Ashwood et al. (2016, Psychological Medicine 46(12):2595-2604) studied 476 adults seen consecutively at a national ASD diagnostic referral service, of whom 73% received a clinical diagnosis of ASD against expert ICD-10 assessment informed by ADOS-G and ADI-R. Self-report AQ scores did not significantly predict receipt of a diagnosis. Sensitivity was 0.77 (95% CI 0.72 to 0.82) and PPV 0.76 (95% CI 0.70 to 0.80), but specificity was only 0.29. Important scope note: this study used the full self-report Autism-Spectrum Quotient, not the 10-item AQ-10, so it is evidence about the AQ family in clinical referral samples rather than about the AQ-10 specifically. Bezemer, Blijd-Hoogewys and Meek-Heekelaar (2021, Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders 51(7):2402-2415) evaluated adults referred for autism assessment in clinical practice and concluded that predictive values were considerably lower in this clinical population than in general population research, and that psychometric results in the core publications appear less representative of clinical practice. [UNVERIFIED: exact sensitivity, specificity and PPV figures from this study were not available in the accessible abstract.]

[UNVERIFIED: NICE guidance. Secondary sources consistently report that NICE CG142 recommends the AQ-10 as a screening tool for adults where autism is suspected, but the primary NICE text could not be accessed to confirm the wording.]

Misuse to avoid. This is the instrument in this file with the widest gap between its published properties and its behaviour in the setting it is actually used in. A score below 6 should not be used to rule out autism in someone referred for assessment. A score of 6 or above in a self-referring population is weak evidence. Autism assessment requires developmental history, ideally informant history, and multi-domain assessment; the AQ-10 is a triage tool at best.

doc_title: Screening and Outcome Instruments: Scoring, Properties, and Misuse
doc_summary: What each common mental health measure actually assesses, its verified scoring bands and cut-points, its sensitivity and specificity where established, and the specific way each one gets misused.
heading: MDQ
text:
What it measures. A screen for lifetime history of manic or hypomanic symptoms, used to detect bipolar spectrum disorder in people presenting with depression. Developed by Hirschfeld et al. (2000, American Journal of Psychiatry).

Structure and scoring. Thirteen yes/no items about manic and hypomanic symptoms, plus a question about whether several of the endorsed symptoms co-occurred in the same time period, plus a question about the degree of functional problems caused. A positive screen requires all three: seven or more "yes" responses, plus co-occurrence, plus at least moderate functional impairment.

Psychometrics, and the reason this instrument is the best base-rate lesson in this file. In the original validation of 198 psychiatric outpatients across five mood disorder clinics, sensitivity was 0.73 and specificity 0.90 (Hirschfeld et al., 2000). In a general population study of 711 respondents drawn from 85,358 sampled, with 695 completing telephone SCID-based interviews, sensitivity fell to 0.281 with specificity 0.972 (Hirschfeld et al., 2003, American Journal of Psychiatry 160(1):178-180). Sensitivity dropped from 0.73 to 0.28 moving from a clinical to a community sample. The same instrument, the same scoring rule, and it detects roughly a quarter of cases instead of three quarters.

The false positive problem. Zimmerman et al. (2010, Journal of Clinical Psychiatry) assessed 480 psychiatric outpatients and found borderline personality disorder diagnosed four times more often in MDQ-positive than MDQ-negative patients (21.5% versus 4.1%). Among MDQ-positive patients, roughly as many received a borderline personality disorder diagnosis (27.6%) as a bipolar diagnosis (23.5%). Their conclusion was that positive results on the MDQ were as likely to indicate borderline personality disorder as bipolar disorder.

Misuse to avoid. Treating a positive MDQ as evidence of bipolar disorder, which the Zimmerman finding directly contradicts. Treating a negative MDQ as ruling out bipolarity, which in community settings it emphatically does not. Using it to justify a mood stabiliser or to withhold an antidepressant. The MDQ's legitimate use is prompting a careful clinical enquiry into past elevated mood, which then has to be conducted properly, ideally with collateral history, since hypomania is the symptom people are least able to report retrospectively about themselves.

heading: WHODAS 2.0
text:
What it measures. Functioning and disability, independent of diagnosis, grounded in the WHO's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health. This makes it different in kind from every other instrument in this file: it measures what the person can do rather than what symptoms they have.

Domains. Six: cognition (understanding and communicating), mobility (moving and getting around), self-care, getting along with others, life activities (domestic, leisure, work, school), and participation in society.

Structure. A 36-item version taking roughly 20 minutes and giving domain-level scores, and a 12-item version taking about 5 minutes which accounts for 81% of the variance in the longer version. A 12+24 configuration also exists. Self-administered, interviewer-administered, and proxy versions are available. The recall period is the past 30 days, chosen because recall accuracy is best over about a month.

Scoring. Items are rated none (0), mild (1), moderate (2), severe (3), extreme or cannot do (4). Simple scoring sums the item scores without weighting, which is practical for hand scoring. Complex scoring uses an item response theory algorithm that differentially weights items and severity levels, producing a summary score converted to a 0 to 100 metric where 0 is no disability and 100 is full disability. The two methods do not produce the same number and should not be compared.

Why it matters clinically. Symptom severity and functional impairment dissociate. Two people with identical PHQ-9 scores can differ enormously in what they are able to do, and functioning is usually what the person actually cares about and what determines eligibility for support. DSM-5 included the WHODAS 2.0 as its recommended disability measure partly for this reason.

Misuse to avoid. Comparing simple-scored and IRT-scored results. Assuming the domains are equally relevant to everyone, since mobility and self-care items have limited range in physically well adults and can flatten the profile. Treating a low disability score as evidence that a mental health problem is not serious, since many people maintain function at high cost.

doc_title: Screening and Outcome Instruments: Scoring, Properties, and Misuse
doc_summary: What each common mental health measure actually assesses, its verified scoring bands and cut-points, its sensitivity and specificity where established, and the specific way each one gets misused.
heading: ORS and SRS
text:
What they are. The Outcome Rating Scale and Session Rating Scale, developed by Miller and Duncan, designed for routine session-by-session measurement rather than for diagnosis. They are the most widely used instruments in feedback-informed treatment.

ORS structure. Four items presented as 10cm visual analogue lines, covering personal or symptom distress, interpersonal wellbeing, social role functioning, and overall wellbeing. Each line scores 0 to 10 by measured position, giving a total range of 0 to 40, where higher means better functioning. This is the opposite direction to every symptom scale in this file, and mixing the directions up is a common error.

ORS interpretation. The adult clinical cut-off is 25. Scores of 25 or below fall in the clinical range. Reported normative data place non-clinical samples around 28.0 and clinical samples around 19.6. The reliable change index is commonly reported as 5 or 6 points depending on the normative sample used. Change that both meets the reliable change threshold and crosses the clinical cut-off of 25 is treated as clinically significant change, following the Jacobson and Truax framework.

ORS reliability. Internal consistency is high, with reported coefficient alpha estimates of .93 and .97. Test-retest reliability estimates vary widely across studies, reported in ranges of .58 to .66 and .80 to .84.

SRS structure and interpretation. Four items on the therapeutic alliance, covering the relationship, goals and topics, approach or method, and overall fit, in the same visual analogue format, total range 0 to 40. The cut-off is 36 out of 40. Scores below 36 are the signal to discuss the alliance.

The SRS ceiling problem. A cut-off of 36 out of 40 exists because almost everyone scores high. Reported figures suggest around a quarter of cases fall below 36. This is a severe ceiling effect and it reflects demand characteristics: the client is rating their therapist, to their therapist's face, in a relationship they depend on. The SRS should be read as a prompt for a conversation, not as a measurement of alliance quality, and a perfect score is close to uninformative.

Misuse to avoid. Treating a four-item visual analogue scale as a precise measure. Using the ORS as a symptom measure, which it is not; it measures subjective wellbeing across four broad domains. Interpreting single-session movement, which is well inside measurement error. And using aggregate ORS improvement to demonstrate that a service works, since routine outcome data selected on high baseline distress is exactly the setup that generates regression to the mean.

doc_title: Screening and Outcome Instruments: Scoring, Properties, and Misuse
doc_summary: What each common mental health measure actually assesses, its verified scoring bands and cut-points, its sensitivity and specificity where established, and the specific way each one gets misused.
heading: Choosing and sequencing measures
text:
Instruments answer specific questions and the first decision is which question is being asked.

To detect something that may be present but unmentioned, use a sensitive screener and accept false positives: PHQ-9 and GAD-7 for common mental disorders, AUDIT-C for alcohol, MDQ for past hypomania in a depressed presentation with the caveats above.

To grade severity of something already established and track it, use a dimensional measure with known change properties: PHQ-9, GAD-7, DASS-21, PCL-5, or ORS, applied repeatedly with a reliable change threshold.

To capture what the problem is costing the person, use a functioning measure: WHODAS 2.0. Symptom scales do not answer this.

To decide something diagnostically, use a structured interview and clinical assessment. No questionnaire in this file does this job.

Sequencing rules. Screen broadly before narrowing, because a person presenting with anxiety frequently has depression, trauma, or substance involvement that a single-target instrument will not surface. Screen for bipolarity before treating depression, because the treatment implications diverge. Screen for substances always, because they change every other interpretation. Establish a baseline before starting treatment, and use at least two baseline points where the situation allows, since a single pre-treatment score taken at the point of maximum distress guarantees apparent improvement.

Administration rules that preserve the properties. Use the actual items in their actual wording. Use the specified response options and recall window. Let the person do their own rating on self-report instruments. Record which version and which scoring convention was used, particularly for the K10 and WHODAS where multiple conventions exist. Record the setting, since the setting determines the base rate and therefore what a positive result means.

The stopping rule. Adding more questionnaires does not add information proportionally, because these instruments correlate strongly with each other. The PHQ-9, GAD-7, DASS subscales, and K10 all load heavily on a general distress factor, so administering all four mostly measures the same thing four times while increasing burden. Two well-chosen measures plus a functioning measure is usually more informative than six symptom scales.

Let the person do their own rating on self-report instruments. Record which version and which scoring convention was used, particularly for the K10 and WHODAS where multiple conventions exist. Record the setting, since the setting determines the base rate and therefore what a positive result means.

The stopping rule. Adding more questionnaires does not add information proportionally, because these instruments correlate strongly with each other. The PHQ-9, GAD-7, DASS subscales, and K10 all load heavily on a general distress factor, so administering all four mostly measures the same thing four times while increasing burden. Two well-chosen measures plus a functioning measure is usually more informative than six symptom scales.

heading: Reliability: what it is and what it constrains
text:
Reliability is the proportion of variance in observed scores that reflects true score variance rather than measurement error. It is a property of scores in a population, not a fixed property of a test. The same instrument can be reliable in one sample and unreliable in another, which is why reporting "the scale has an alpha of .90" without naming the sample is incomplete.

Several distinct things are called reliability and they are not interchangeable.

Internal consistency, usually reported as Cronbach's alpha or McDonald's omega, indexes how far items on a scale covary. It answers whether the items are measuring something in common. It does not establish that they measure one thing, and a high alpha is routinely misread as evidence of unidimensionality. Alpha rises with the number of items, so a long scale can post a high alpha while being multidimensional.

Test-retest reliability indexes stability of scores across time in the absence of real change. It matters most for traits and least for states. A depression measure with a two-week recall window should not have high test-retest reliability across six months if the depression is changing, so a low correlation there is not necessarily a defect.

Inter-rater reliability indexes agreement between raters, usually as kappa or an intraclass correlation. It applies to clinician-rated instruments and to diagnostic interviews. Diagnostic agreement is not uniform across the diagnostic system. In one validation of the MINI against the SCID-5-CV, kappa was 0.88 for psychotic disorders and 0.85 for bipolar disorder but 0.44 for generalised anxiety disorder and 0.32 for PTSD, meaning that agreement on some categories is close to chance-corrected marginal.

The practical consequence of reliability is that it caps validity. A score that is substantially error cannot correlate strongly with anything real. It also determines the width of the uncertainty band around an individual score, which is the next section. The single most common misuse of reliability is reporting it at the group level and then interpreting an individual score as if it were exact.

doc_summary: How to reason about a psychological test score, including the error around it, what counts as real change, why an instrument validated in one population can fail in another, and why inferring a score from free text is not administration of the instrument.
heading: Standard error of measurement and the band around a score
text:
A test score is a point estimate of an unobservable true score. The standard error of measurement (SEM) quantifies how far the observed score is likely to sit from the true score, and it is expressed in the units of the test, which makes it directly usable.

The formula is SEM = SD × √(1 − r), where SD is the standard deviation of scores in the relevant population and r is the reliability coefficient (National Council on Measurement in Education, Module 9). Reliability and SEM move in opposite directions: as reliability approaches 1, SEM approaches 0; as reliability falls, the band widens.

Treating measurement error as approximately normally distributed, a confidence interval around an observed score is the score plus or minus a multiple of the SEM: roughly ±1 SEM for about 68% confidence, ±1.96 SEM for 95%, and ±2.58 SEM for 99%.

Worked example. A cognitive test with a mean of 100, an SD of 15, and a reliability of .96 has an SEM of 15 × √(1 − .96) = 15 × 0.2 = 3. A person scoring 100 has a 95% interval of roughly 94 to 106. A second person scoring 106 has an interval of roughly 100 to 112. These two people are not reliably different from each other, and reporting them as "average" and "above average" overstates what the test can support.

The same logic applies to symptom scales. Any instrument with reliability below about .90 has a band wide enough to cross its own severity boundaries. If a depression scale has an SD of 6 and reliability of .85, SEM = 6 × √0.15 ≈ 2.3, so the 95% band on any score is about ±4.5 points. A score of 14 on such a scale cannot be confidently distinguished from a score of 10 or a score of 18, and if 10 and 15 are the boundaries of a severity band, a single score near a boundary carries almost no information about which band the person belongs in.

Two rules follow. Never treat a score as a number that means something exact. And never make a categorical decision on the basis of a score sitting one or two points either side of a cut-point, because the cut-point is a convention imposed on a continuum and the score has error in it. Clinicians who say "you scored 10, so you have moderate depression" are misreporting the measurement.

This applies with particular force in text-only contexts, where the SEM of the underlying instrument is not even the relevant quantity, because the instrument was not administered.

doc_title: Interpreting Measurement: Reliability, Error, Change, and Bias
doc_summary: How to reason about a psychological test score, including the error around it, what counts as real change, why an instrument validated in one population can fail in another, and why inferring a score from free text is not administration of the instrument.
heading: Reliable change and clinically significant change
text:
A score changing between two time points does not mean anything has changed. The observed difference contains measurement error at both time points, and the error compounds.

The Reliable Change Index (RCI) is the standard correction. Jacobson and Truax (1991) defined it as the difference between pre-treatment and post-treatment scores divided by the standard error of the difference between the two scores. The standard error of the difference is S_diff = SD₁ × √2 × √(1 − r), where SD₁ is the standard deviation at baseline and r is the reliability of the instrument. The RCI is interpreted as a z score: values above 1.96 indicate reliable improvement, values below −1.96 indicate reliable deterioration, and values between the two indicate no reliable change.

Note the √2 term. The error band on a change score is about 1.41 times wider than the error band on a single score, because both measurements carry error. This is why a small pre-post difference is uninformative even when it looks meaningful on a chart.

Reliable change alone is not clinical significance. Jacobson and Truax paired the RCI with a cut-off separating a functional from a dysfunctional distribution, producing four outcome categories: recovered (reliable change and crossed into the functional range), improved (reliable change but still in the dysfunctional range), unchanged (no reliable change), and deteriorated (reliable change in the wrong direction). Reporting only mean group change hides how many people fall in each category, and a treatment producing a moderate mean improvement can contain a substantial deteriorated subgroup.

Published RCI values exist for common instruments. For the Outcome Rating Scale, the adult clinical cut-off is 25 and the reliable change index is commonly reported as 5 or 6 points depending on the normative sample used, with change that both meets the RCI and crosses 25 treated as clinically significant. For the PCL-5, the VA's National Center for PTSD suggests 10 points as an indicator of response and a post-treatment score below 28 as an indicator of clinically significant change, citing Marx et al. (2022, Psychological Assessment 34(2):197-203), a study conducted in male veterans.

The general principle is that any claim about change needs to specify which of three questions it answers: did the score move, did it move more than measurement error, and did the person's clinical status change. These are increasingly demanding and increasingly informative.

doc_summary: How to reason about a psychological test score, including the error around it, what counts as real change, why an instrument validated in one population can fail in another, and why inferring a score from free text is not administration of the instrument.
heading: Regression to the mean
text:
Regression to the mean is a statistical artefact that generates false evidence of treatment effect, and it operates most strongly in exactly the situation clinical services find themselves in.

Whenever a measure is imperfectly reliable, extreme scores are extreme partly because of real standing on the construct and partly because of error. On re-measurement, the real component persists and the error component resamples, so the expected second score is closer to the population mean than the first. The effect is proportional to unreliability: a perfectly reliable measure shows none, and a measure that is entirely noise regresses fully to the mean.

The clinical setup that maximises this artefact is selection on an extreme score. People enter treatment when they are at their worst, often crossing a threshold on a screening measure to be admitted. Their baseline score is therefore selected for being high, which means it is selected for having positive error. The expected follow-up score is lower whatever the treatment does. A single-arm pre-post design in a service that admits on the basis of a high score will show improvement even if the treatment is inert.

Three consequences follow. First, uncontrolled pre-post outcome data from routine services systematically overstate treatment effect and cannot be used to establish that a treatment works. Second, the magnitude of the artefact is larger for less reliable measures and for more extreme selection thresholds. Third, the same logic applies within a single case: a person presenting on their worst day will usually report feeling somewhat better at the next contact, and attributing that to the intervening session is unwarranted.

The corrections are a control group, or in a single case a baseline period with repeated measurement before intervention rather than a single pre-treatment point. Where neither is available, the honest statement is that the direction of change is consistent with improvement but does not establish it.

Regression to the mean also explains a family of clinical superstitions. Any intervention applied at the point of maximum distress will appear to help, which is why practices with no active mechanism accumulate confident practitioners.

heading: Statistical significance versus clinical significance
text:
These answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other.

Statistical significance answers whether an observed difference is larger than would be expected from sampling variability under a null hypothesis. It is heavily determined by sample size. With a large enough sample, a difference of half a point on a 27-point scale reaches p < .001. That p value says the difference is probably not zero. It says nothing about whether it is worth anything.

Clinical significance answers whether the difference matters to the person. It is assessed with effect sizes, with the reliable change and recovery categories described above, and with anchors based on patient report, such as the minimal clinically important difference (MCID), which is the smallest change a person can detect as beneficial.

The two dissociate in both directions. A large trial can produce a statistically significant benefit too small for any individual to notice. A small trial can fail to reach significance while containing a large effect that is simply underpowered, and reporting that as "no difference" is a misreading; absence of evidence of an effect is not evidence of absence.

Two further distinctions matter when reading outcome literature. Mean group change is not individual change: a mean improvement of 6 points is compatible with half the sample improving 12 points and half not moving. And between-group differences at endpoint are the relevant comparison in a controlled trial, not within-group change from baseline, because within-group change absorbs regression to the mean, natural remission, and expectancy.

Effect sizes have their own trap. Cohen's benchmarks of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 for small, medium, and large were offered as rough conventions in the absence of better information, not as a scale of clinical value. In psychotherapy research, where typical effects cluster in the medium range, the benchmark contributes little. A standardised mean difference should be translated back into the units of the instrument and then into a description of what the person can now do.

doc_title: Interpreting Measurement: Reliability, Error, Change, and Bias
doc_summary: How to reason about a psychological test score, including the error around it, what counts as real change, why an instrument validated in one population can fail in another, and why inferring a score from free text is not administration of the instrument.
heading: Measurement invariance
text:
Measurement invariance is the property that an instrument measures the same construct, in the same metric, across groups. Without it, comparing scores across groups compares two different things.

Invariance is tested in a hierarchy. Configural invariance holds when the number of factors and the pattern of loadings is the same across groups, meaning the same broad structure applies. Metric invariance additionally requires the factor loadings to be equal across groups, meaning a one-unit change in the latent construct produces the same change in item responses in each group; this licenses comparing associations and regression slopes. Scalar invariance additionally requires equal intercepts, meaning that at the same level of the latent construct the groups give the same item responses; this is what licenses comparing group means. Scalar or at least partial scalar invariance is a prerequisite for comparing latent means between groups.

The failure mode is concrete. Suppose an item on a depression scale asks about crying. If one cultural group reports crying at a lower threshold of distress than another, the intercept for that item differs, and at identical true depression severity the two groups produce different total scores. Comparing raw totals then produces a spurious group difference in depression that is actually a difference in item functioning. This is the same phenomenon known in the item response theory literature as differential item functioning.

Non-invariance arises from translation, from culture, from age, from clinical versus community setting, and from mode of administration. Somatic items on depression scales are a recurring source of it, because they conflate depression with physical illness in medically unwell and older populations. Items referencing work or study misfire for people not in either.

The practical rule for interpreting any score is to ask who the instrument was validated on and whether this person resembles them. An instrument developed and normed on US undergraduates or on treatment-seeking adults in high-income health systems has not been shown to behave the same way elsewhere. The score is not invalid, but its relationship to the underlying construct and to any published cut-point is unestablished, and cut-points in particular are the least transportable part of an instrument because they depend on both item functioning and local base rates.

doc_summary: How to reason about a psychological test score, including the error around it, what counts as real change, why an instrument validated in one population can fail in another, and why inferring a score from free text is not administration of the instrument.
heading: Response bias and social desirability
text:
Self-report instruments measure what the person reports, which is not the same as what is true. The gap has structure and the structure is predictable.

Social desirability is the tendency to answer in a way that presents the self favourably. It operates both as impression management, which is deliberate, and as self-deceptive enhancement, which is not. It suppresses reported symptoms and it is strongest where the answer has consequences. Assessments attached to employment, custody, immigration, fitness to practise, insurance, or firearms licensing are systematically under-reported, and treating a low score in those contexts as reassurance is a serious error.

Symptom exaggeration operates in the opposite direction and is likewise driven by context, most obviously in medicolegal, disability, and compensation settings. Neither direction should be assumed as a default; both should be considered as a function of what the person stands to gain or lose.

Acquiescence is the tendency to agree with items regardless of content. It inflates scores on scales where all items are keyed in the same direction, and it is more pronounced in people with lower literacy, in people answering in a second language, and in cultures with stronger norms against disagreeing with an interlocutor. Reverse-keyed items partially control it and introduce their own problem, because a proportion of respondents miss the reversal.

Extreme and midpoint responding are stylistic tendencies to use the ends or the centre of a scale, and they vary systematically across cultural groups. This produces group differences in scores that have nothing to do with the construct.

Recall bias affects any item with a retrospective window. Current mood colours recall of past mood, so a person who is currently low reports the last two weeks as worse than a contemporaneous diary would show. This inflates apparent severity at intake and contributes to apparent improvement later.

Demand characteristics operate in clinical relationships. A person who likes their therapist and wants to be a good patient reports improvement. This is a specific problem for session-by-session outcome measures administered by the treating clinician, and it is the main reason to be cautious with alliance measures like the SRS, which show strong ceiling effects.

The corrections available are limited. Establishing that the answers have no consequences where that is true, asking about behaviour rather than about self-assessment, seeking collateral report, and using multiple methods rather than multiple self-report questionnaires. In a text-only context the correction set is smaller still: there is no collateral, no observation, and no behavioural sample, so response bias is uncorrectable and must be treated as a permanent limit on the inference.

heading: Cultural and linguistic bias in assessment
text:
Bias in assessment is not confined to the instrument. It enters at the level of the construct, the item, the administration, the norm, and the interpretation.

Construct bias occurs when the underlying construct is not equivalent across groups. Depression as operationalised in DSM-based instruments emphasises mood and cognitive symptoms, and idioms of distress in many populations are predominantly somatic or relational. An instrument that indexes the construct as defined in one tradition will under-detect distress expressed in another, and it will do so invisibly, since the output is still a plausible-looking number.

Item bias is differential item functioning as described above. Translation is a frequent source. A translated instrument is a new instrument and requires revalidation, including of its cut-points; back-translation establishes semantic correspondence, not psychometric equivalence.

Method bias covers everything about administration. Familiarity with Likert-type formats varies. Test-taking motivation varies. The identity of the assessor changes responses, particularly on questions about discrimination, substance use, immigration status, and sexuality. Language of administration matters even in fluent second-language speakers, and emotional vocabulary in a second language is generally less differentiated than in a first.

Norm bias occurs when a person is compared against a reference sample they do not belong to. Most widely used instruments were normed on samples that overrepresent white, educated, high-income, treatment-seeking populations in a small number of countries. The published cut-point of an instrument is a property of the validation sample and of the base rate in that sample, and it is the component least likely to transport.

Interpretation bias is the clinician's. Diagnostic disparities are well documented, including long-standing overdiagnosis of schizophrenia and underdiagnosis of mood disorders in Black patients in the US and UK. These do not require conscious prejudice; they follow from differential thresholds for reading behaviour as pathological, from misreading justified mistrust of services as paranoia, and from unfamiliarity with normative expression.

Language-based automated assessment inherits all of these and adds its own. Rai et al. (2024) examined whether established language markers of depression generalise across race in a matched sample of 868 Black and White US Facebook users with PHQ-9 scores. Greater depression severity predicted first-person singular pronoun use in White participants but not in Black participants, and five negative-emotion topics related to depression severity in White but not Black participants. Models trained on White participants' language correlated r = 0.392 with depression severity in a held-out White test set but only r = 0.132 in a Black test set. A model trained exclusively on Black participants' language performed poorly on Black participants (r = 0.126). The authors conclude that language-based depression models need to demonstrate racial invariance before clinical integration. This is a direct, quantified demonstration that a language-based inference pipeline can fail for a whole population while continuing to output confident numbers.

doc_title: Interpreting Measurement: Reliability, Error, Change, and Bias
doc_summary: How to reason about a psychological test score, including the error around it, what counts as real change, why an instrument validated in one population can fail in another, and why inferring a score from free text is not administration of the instrument.
heading: Inferring a score from free text is not administration
text:
This is the most important limit in this file for a system that reasons over conversation.

An instrument is a standardised procedure. Its psychometric properties belong to the procedure, not to the construct it names. Those properties were established under specific conditions: fixed item wording, fixed response options, a fixed recall window, a fixed order, and self-completion by the respondent. Change any of those and the published reliability, validity, sensitivity, specificity, and cut-points no longer apply, because they were never estimated under the changed conditions.

Reading a conversation and producing "this appears to be around a 14 on the PHQ-9" is not a PHQ-9 score. It is an impression with a number attached. The impression may have some validity as an impression. The number imports a false precision and an unearned evidentiary status, because a PHQ-9 of 14 carries a specific meaning derived from validation studies, and that meaning attaches to the administered instrument, not to a similar-sounding judgement.

The specific failures are these. The items were never asked, so the person never considered several symptom domains and never had the chance to report symptoms they did not spontaneously mention. The recall window was never applied, so a mention of poor sleep might refer to last night or to last year. The response anchors were never used, so there is no calibration between "not at all" and "several days". The person did not self-rate, so the rating reflects the model's inference about the person rather than the person's report about themselves, and self-report instruments derive their validity precisely from being self-report. And the ordering, framing, and completeness that make item responses comparable across people are absent.

The same applies to diagnostic criteria. Concluding from a conversation that someone meets criteria for a disorder is not a diagnostic assessment. Diagnosis requires systematic criterion coverage, duration and functional impairment thresholds, exclusion of substance and medical causes, differential consideration, and usually collateral information. None of these are available from a conversation, and the most consequential differentials, such as bipolar versus unipolar depression, depend precisely on the information self-report in a single conversation is worst at supplying.

The permitted operations are narrower and still useful. Asking the actual questions of a public-domain instrument, in its actual wording, with its actual response options and recall window, and having the person answer them, is administration, and it is a legitimate thing to do in text where the instrument permits self-completion. Noting that a person has described several features that overlap with a recognised pattern, and naming that as a hypothesis to be checked, is legitimate. Recommending that the person complete a validated measure with a clinician, or seek assessment, is legitimate.

What is not legitimate is producing a score, a severity band, a percentile, a probability of diagnosis, or a diagnosis, from inference over text, and presenting it in the vocabulary of measurement. The vocabulary of measurement carries an implicit claim about procedure that has not been met.

doc_title: What Can and Cannot Be Assessed From Text Alone
doc_summary: The genuine but weak signal available in language, the clinical channels that text removes entirely, and how to flag a hypothesis and ask the question instead of inferring an answer.
heading: The honest starting position
text:
A text conversation is a narrow channel. It carries what the person chose to write, after editing, at their own pace, to an audience they are modelling. It does not carry how they look, how they sound, how they move, how they were last month, or what anyone else says about them.

Face-to-face clinical assessment draws on several parallel channels and cross-checks them. A person who says they are fine while sitting motionless, speaking in a monotone with long response latencies, and not tracking the conversation has told the clinician two different things, and the discrepancy is the finding. Text collapses those channels into one. There is nothing left to cross-check the self-report against.

This matters most precisely where clinical stakes are highest. The presentations that self-report is worst at detecting are the ones where insight is impaired: mania, psychosis, and cognitive decline. Face-to-face assessment compensates through observation and collateral history. Text-only assessment has neither compensation, so its blind spot aligns exactly with the conditions that most need detecting.

The available research supports a modest claim. Language carries real, statistically detectable signal about mental state at the group level. It carries weak signal about any individual. The gap between those two statements is where most misuse lives.

The correct posture is not refusal to engage. It is engaging with the channel that exists, which is conversation, and using it the way a clinician uses conversation: to ask. A clinician cannot see inside anyone either. What they can do is ask a good question, listen to the answer, and ask a better one. That capability transfers to text almost intact. What does not transfer is observation, and observation is what most pseudo-clinical inference from text is pretending to substitute for.

doc_title: What Can and Cannot Be Assessed From Text Alone
doc_summary: The genuine but weak signal available in language, the clinical channels that text removes entirely, and how to flag a hypothesis and ask the question instead of inferring an answer.
heading: What language genuinely carries
text:
Several features of language have replicated associations with mental state. They are real, and they are small.

First-person singular pronoun use is the most studied. Edwards and Holtzman (2017) meta-analysed 21 studies with a combined N of 3,758 and found a correlation between depression and first-person singular pronoun use of r = 0.13, 95% CI [0.10, 0.16]. The correlation was not moderated by gender or by publication status. An r of 0.13 corresponds to roughly 1.7% of variance explained. This is the best-established linguistic marker of depression, and it is nowhere near strong enough to classify an individual.

Negative emotion words show a similar pattern: reliable group-level association, small individual-level signal. Absolutist language, meaning words like "always", "never", "completely", and "totally", has been reported as elevated in depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation forums.

Beyond word counts, the following carry clinical information when read as conversational content rather than as automated features.

Content. What the person talks about, what they return to, and what they never mention. This is the strongest signal available in text and it is not a linguistic feature; it is ordinary listening.

Coherence and narrative structure. Whether the account hangs together, whether events are sequenced, whether causal links are made. Loss of coherence is meaningful, though writing conceals disorganisation better than speech does.

Temporal orientation. Whether the person talks about the past, present, or future, and whether the future appears at all. Absence of any future reference in someone describing distress is worth asking about directly, since hopelessness is more strongly associated with suicide than depressed mood is.

Self-referential density. How much of the account is about the self versus about others and circumstances. Related to the pronoun literature and subject to the same effect-size limit.

Avoidance patterns. What the person deflects, minimises, changes the subject away from, or answers a different question than the one asked. This is observable in text and is often the most informative thing in a transcript.

Agency and attribution. Whether the person describes themselves as acting or as being acted upon, and how they explain causes. This maps onto formulation-relevant material about control and self-blame.

The last five are not measurable features. They are clinical reading of content, and their value comes from being followed up with a question, not from being scored.

doc_title: What Can and Cannot Be Assessed From Text Alone
doc_summary: The genuine but weak signal available in language, the clinical channels that text removes entirely, and how to flag a hypothesis and ask the question instead of inferring an answer.
heading: What text removes entirely
text:
These channels are absent, not degraded. No amount of careful reading recovers them.

Prosody and paralinguistics. Rate, volume, pitch, latency, pressure, monotony, tremor in the voice, tearfulness. These are central to detecting mania, melancholic depression, intoxication, and some neurological presentations. Pressure of speech is one of the more specific indicators of a manic state and it has no text analogue; long messages sent rapidly is not the same phenomenon and is confounded by typing habit, platform, and device.

Appearance. Grooming, weight, clothing appropriate to weather and context, physical signs of self-harm, injection sites, jaundice, tremor, pupil size, sweating. Self-neglect is often the first visible sign of deterioration and it is invisible here.

Psychomotor signs. Retardation and agitation are observed, not reported, and they carry substantial diagnostic weight. A person who is markedly slowed frequently does not experience themselves as slowed.

Behaviour in interaction. Eye contact, responsiveness, whether the person appears to be responding to internal stimuli, and the felt quality of rapport. The clinician's own emotional response to being with the person is informative and has no text equivalent.

Physical examination and investigations. Vital signs, neurological examination, thyroid function, B12, full blood count, toxicology. Several conditions that present psychiatrically are diagnosed medically, and a text conversation cannot exclude them.

Collateral history. Family, partners, friends, GP records, previous notes, and other clinicians. Collateral is the standard correction for impaired insight and for the systematic distortions of self-report. Its absence is the single largest structural limitation of text-only assessment.

Longitudinal observation. A clinician who has seen someone across a year knows their baseline and can detect change against it. A single conversation has no baseline. "Speaking more than usual" requires knowing what usual is.

Context outside the conversation. Whether the person is safe where they are, who is present, whether they have eaten, and whether anyone is coercing them.

The practical rule is that anything from this list that matters must be asked about explicitly and taken as report rather than observation, and its status as report should be preserved in whatever is written down.

doc_title: What Can and Cannot Be Assessed From Text Alone
doc_summary: The genuine but weak signal available in language, the clinical channels that text removes entirely, and how to flag a hypothesis and ask the question instead of inferring an answer.
heading: What the performance research actually shows
text:
The empirical literature on automated mental state inference from text is worth stating in numbers, because the numbers are more sobering than the abstracts.

Rai et al. (2024) tested whether established language markers of depression generalise across race, using a matched sample of 868 US Facebook users with self-reported PHQ-9 scores. Depression severity predicted first-person singular pronoun use in White participants but not in Black participants. Five negative-emotion topics related to depression severity in White but not Black participants. A model trained on White participants' language correlated r = 0.392 with depression severity in a held-out White test set, but only r = 0.132 in a Black test set. A model trained exclusively on Black participants' language correlated r = 0.126 when tested on Black participants. The authors state that language-based depression models need to demonstrate racial invariance before integration into research or clinical practice. A model of this kind fails silently: it continues producing numbers for the population it does not work on.

Teferra et al. (2025) evaluated LLMs predicting individual PHQ-8 items from clinical interview transcripts in the DAIC-WOZ dataset using zero-shot prompting on 100 transcripts. On binary scoring of items, GPT-4o achieved mean accuracy of 75.9% (SD 6.8) and mean F1 of 0.74. On the actual four-point Likert scoring the instrument uses, GPT-4o achieved mean accuracy of 48.9% and F1 of 0.43. The authors list text-only analysis as a limitation, specifically the absence of tone of voice, speech cadence, and facial expressions. The collapse from binary to graded scoring is the finding that matters: the model can partially detect presence, and it cannot grade severity, which is what a score is for.

Xu et al. (2025) evaluated 15 current LLMs on mental health knowledge tests and on classification from social media posts. Best accuracy on depression classification was 76.98%; best on suicidal ideation was 69.53%. Failure modes were symptom overlap between conditions, ambiguous or metaphorical language, and absence of clinical context, with models defaulting to high-frequency categories under uncertainty. The authors state outputs must be reviewed by qualified professionals.

Two cautions apply to reading any of these figures. Accuracy on a roughly balanced research dataset does not transfer to a population with a low base rate; a classifier at 77% accuracy on a balanced set will generate mostly false positives where prevalence is 5%. And these systems were given a defined classification task on a curated corpus, which is a substantially easier problem than open-ended assessment of an unknown person in an unstructured conversation.

doc_title: What Can and Cannot Be Assessed From Text Alone
doc_summary: The genuine but weak signal available in language, the clinical channels that text removes entirely, and how to flag a hypothesis and ask the question instead of inferring an answer.
heading: Hypothesis-flagging without pseudo-diagnosis
text:
There is a legitimate operation between saying nothing and delivering a diagnosis. It is naming a pattern as a question.

The structure of a properly flagged hypothesis has four parts. The observation, stated as what the person actually said. The pattern it might belong to, named without diagnostic vocabulary where possible. The explicit uncertainty. And the next step, which is almost always a question or a referral.

Worked example. "You have mentioned three times that you are waking around four and cannot get back to sleep, and that food has stopped being appealing. Those two things often travel together with the low mood you described, and they are the kind of thing worth taking to a GP because they sometimes point to something treatable. Can I ask how long the early waking has been going on?"

That does the work. It names the observation, links it to a pattern, avoids asserting a diagnosis, and ends with a question that gathers the missing duration information.

Compare the failure mode. "Based on what you've described, you're showing classic signs of major depressive disorder, probably moderate severity, and you should consider medication." This asserts a diagnosis from an unstructured conversation, imports a severity grading with no measurement behind it, and recommends a treatment class without knowing the person's medical history, medications, previous trials, bipolar history, or family history.

Rules for the flagged-hypothesis form.

Attribute the observation to the person's own words rather than to inference. "You said you have not been able to face work" is checkable. "You appear to have significant functional impairment" is not.

Use plain description over diagnostic labels when the plain description does the work. "Low mood that has lasted several months and is affecting your sleep and appetite" conveys more to the person than "depression" and makes fewer claims.

Hold the alternatives open. Fatigue, low mood, and poor concentration have a wide differential that includes anaemia, thyroid disease, sleep apnoea, medication effects, and grief. A single-hypothesis flag is worse than none because it forecloses the alternatives a clinician would consider.

Never grade severity from inference. Mild, moderate, and severe are measurement terms tied to specific bands on specific instruments, and using them without administering the instrument imports authority that does not exist.

Never assert what has not been asked. If duration, functional impact, previous episodes, substances, or medical history were not discussed, the hypothesis is missing the information that would most change it, and saying so is part of stating the hypothesis honestly.

Distinguish flagging from escalation. Risk is the exception to the "hold it loosely" posture. Where something in the conversation suggests risk of harm, the correct response is a direct question and a safety response, not a carefully hedged hypothesis.
